_comment: Last research result per problem (key = algorithm_taxonomy.json problem_id). Written by the research-pr job of algorithm-audit-drift.yml; read by the next run's agents as previous_results.json.

analytic-derivatives.note: The closed-form score and information are at the lower bound per observation; AD (TMB/CppAD) is not faster for small hand-coded models. The one improvement is to evaluate them once per distinct (x, y) pattern with count weights instead of once per subject: the same sums, O(G(K+p)) instead of O(n(K+p)) (finding 2). The CR Hessian's structured form is already catalogued (v1.0.5 catalog §2 TODO-3). beta-regression hessian rows are mapped here but belong to beta regression; nothing new for them.

lbfgs.note: Updated. Both the AC-logit fit (fast_adjacent_category_logit_internal) and the CR fit (fast_continuation_ratio_internal) still default to L-BFGS. The randomization kernel compute_adj_cat_logit_distr_parallel_cpp already uses Newton. External evidence fetched this run: Harrell's 2024/2025 benchmark of ordinal logistic fits (k=10 intercepts, p=5, n=1e5) has Newton-Raphson at 0.084 s against BFGS at 0.39 s, about 4.7x. That supports the catalogued v1.0.5 catalog §2 TODO-1/TODO-2 (Newton default), which the previous result had folded into 'already catalogued'. Separately, the covariate-pattern compression finding makes each L-BFGS evaluation cheaper too.

log-sum-exp.note: Trivial, O(K) per call. The max-shifted form is the accurate standard (Blanchard, Higham & Higham, IMA JNA). Nothing faster at equal accuracy.

newton-raphson.note: Updated. Newton (step-halving, with an L-BFGS fallback) is the right optimizer here: it is quadratic for canonical concave AC/CR at small d, and the same algorithm as ordinal::clm, rms::lrm/orm and VGAM Fisher scoring. Nothing newer beats it at EDI's sizes: trust-region Newton (Lin et al. 2008) targets large d, and Böhning–Lindsay was already rejected. The faster option is a change to its input: on treatment-only or discrete designs, the per-iteration O(nK²) Hessian/gradient pass drops to O(G·K²) over G distinct (x, y) patterns (finding 2).

findings.candidate: Sufficient-statistic / covariate-pattern compression. Tabulate the data once per fit into G distinct (x row, y) patterns with integer counts c_g; for treatment-only, G ≤ 2K, a 2×K table. Then evaluate NLL, gradient and Hessian as count-weighted sums over the G patterns. For AC this is the grouped form of the Poisson-log-linear / multinomial equivalence used by brglm2::bracl with frequency weights. For CR, the existing fast_continuation_ratio_regression_weighted_cpp already accepts subject weights and can take the counts directly. The NLL is exactly the ungrouped NLL: identical (x, y) rows are summed with multiplicity, so no multinomial constant appears. The MLE, vcov and neg_loglik are therefore unchanged up to floating-point summation order.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. Theoretical: after one O(n) (or O(n log n) for general X) tabulation, the per-evaluation cost goes from O(nK) to O(G·K). Treatment-only means G ≤ 2K, so roughly n/(2K) fewer flops per eval: about 50x at n=500, K=5. A whole fit then costs about one pass over the data instead of ~30–45 L-BFGS evaluations or ~5–8 Newton gradient+Hessian passes. In the randomization kernel, tabulating each permuted w column is O(n).
findings.suggested_action: Prototype: add a compressed-pattern path to AdjacentCategoryLogitNegLogLik/hessian and route CR through the weighted kernel with counts when the number of distinct (x, y) rows is below about n/2. Start with treatment-only fits and compute_adj_cat_logit_distr_parallel_cpp. Gate on equality of b, ssq_b_1, neg_loglik to 1e-10 against the current path. This mirrors the category-tabulation trick the catalog already adopted for JT/ridit (catalog §6 TODO-9, §10 TODO-1).

findings.candidate: Damped Newton-Raphson with step-halving on the analytic Hessian, with L-BFGS as the fallback. It is already implemented (optimization_alg="newton_raphson") and already used in compute_adj_cat_logit_distr_parallel_cpp; this means making it the default (catalogued as v1.0.5 catalog §2 TODO-1/TODO-2). New external evidence: a benchmark of ordinal logistic MLE (Harrell, fharrell.com, 2024-11-28, revised 2025-06-20) with k=10 intercepts, p=5, n=100,000 timed NR at 0.084 s against optim BFGS at 0.391 s, and at k=1000, p=1 NR at 0.0095 s against BFGS at 0.0375 s. Its stated conclusion: NR is the best Hessian-using algorithm for speed and convergence, and BFGS is appealing only with very many intercepts.
findings.claimed_speedup: About 4–5x wall-clock over BFGS on cumulative-logit ordinal fits at d≈15 (Harrell's benchmark, rms lrm.fit, not the AC/CR models or LBFGSpp). The catalog's theoretical estimate is 1–2x fewer gradient-equivalents.
findings.suggested_action: Run the A/B harness for catalog §2 TODO-1/TODO-2 (wall clock and iterations, AC and CR, n in 50–2000, K in 3–7, p in 1–10). Then switch the defaults to newton_raphson with the existing L-BFGS fallback.

atkinson-da-biased-coin.note: Rechecked the previous result (2026-11-16, run 43903509109). There are no code commits since then, and the code still rebuilds X'X and runs FullPivLU per (b,t) (generate_permutations.cpp:80-119, atkinson_assign.cpp:24-63). The fastest acceptable method for the hot path, the null draws (draw_ws_raw / generate_permutations_atkinson_internal), is still the block-inverse / Schur-complement rewrite. The catalog already lists it as Adopt (P6, v1.0.5 TODO-5/TODO-3): precompute C_t^-1 once per t, then O(p^2) per (b,t). It is not implemented yet. The new searches found nothing faster than that. They covered the problem itself, synonyms (Atkinson biased coin, DoptBCD), the broader family (sequential D-optimal design, covariate-adaptive randomization, RLS), the narrower variants (Sherman-Morrison, Cholesky up/downdate via Eigen LLT::rankUpdate, rank-revealing QR updating for the per-t column selection, rank-Greville RLS for rank-deficient designs) and the software (carat 2.3.0, covadap, randomizeR, CRAN ClinicalTrials task view). Sequential D-optimal work uses the same Sherman-Morrison/greedy kernel, which the catalog has already considered and rejected for drift and column-set changes. Rank-Greville (doi 10.1016/j.amc.2021.125996) could in principle avoid explicit column selection, but it would only speed up the once-per-t precompute, which is not the hot path after the Schur rewrite, and no licensed code is published. carat's DoptBCD uses the same closed-form probability and gives no performance claims. The 2026 arXiv covariate-adaptive papers (2611.08378, 2608.13442) are about different designs or theory and say nothing on computation. The per-arrival assign_wt is O(tp^2+p^3) once per arrival and not hot; the LDLT micro is already catalog P5/TODO 6.

branch-and-bound-milp.note: All three previous findings still stand and are re-reported: the p = 1 BLDM+CKK route, scip as a low-rank MIQCP backend, and HiGHS. What was checked this run: (1) scip 1.10.1-1 (2026-10-04, Apache ≥ 2) is still the current CRAN version and supports quadratic constraints on binary variables. (2) The CRAN highs NEWS for 1.15.1-2 confirms that all 177 HiGHS C API functions are registered with R_RegisterCCallable. (3) HiGHS still has no MIQP; the maintainers say they 'don't have the resources'. (4) ompr 1.0.4 supports only linear objectives, so a scip route has to bypass ompr/ROI and use the scip model API directly. Two new papers were checked and rejected: Singh & Sun 2026 (Kybernetika, interval branch and bound for cardinality-constrained QP) targets continuous best-subset/portfolio problems and reports no Gurobi comparison; the SDP k-cluster branch and bound (Krislock, Malick & Roupin) is the SDP option the catalog already rejects as overkill at n ≤ 30. The Fortet/RLT literature (heaviest/densest k-subgraph) has nothing newer than catalog table (a).

cholesky-ldlt.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. Here it is a one-off O(np²) whitening per setup, and the reuse of the rank-p factor is already tracked (v1.0.5-TODO-1/-2).

dinkelbach.note: No 2025–26 binary fractional-programming result was found. The Charnes-Cooper versus Dinkelbach literature favours Dinkelbach when few outer iterations are needed (the case here), and no benchmark for the binary case exists. Gains still come from cheaper subproblems: enumeration (v1.0.5-TODO-1), seeding (v1.0.5-TODO-13) and the backend findings.

qr-decomposition.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. It runs once per setup; the thin-Q̂ storage of P is already recorded in the inventory.

simulated-annealing.note: The p = 1 BLDM+CKK finding stands. A re-read of Mertens confirms that BLDM is O(n log n) time and O(n) space and that the anytime guarantee covers the balanced case |m| ≤ 1. For other n_T (prob_T ≠ 0.5), CKK needs cardinality pruning and its first solution may not be feasible. For p > 1, arXiv 2603.13607 (March 2026) reports that SA and memetic tabu fall short of enhanced parallel tempering at equal time on hard HUBO instances. That supports the comparison already tracked in quantum_upgrade.md TODO-5 and is not a new finding. No source tests SA, tabu and PT under an equal-cardinality swap neighbourhood. The threshold-accepting and LAHC literature shows no advantage over Metropolis. BRAIN (arXiv 2312.17230) is a rerandomization sampler, which would change the design rather than speed up the solver.

size-based-dispatch.note: Trivial orchestration. The cutoff should depend on the solver and on p (route p = 1 to BLDM+CKK if that finding is adopted); there is no algorithmic alternative.

findings.candidate: (Re-reported, unchanged.) With p = 1, mahal_dist, D and l1 are all monotone in |Σ_T x̃ − Σ_C x̃|, which is balanced number partitioning (Kallus 2018, eq. 2.8). Use the balanced largest differencing method (BLDM, O(n log n) time, O(n) space) as the start and Mertens' BLDM + complete Karmarkar-Karp to search towards a certified optimum. The algorithm is anytime and deterministic. The anytime guarantee holds for |n_T − n_C| ≤ 1. Other n_T need Mertens' cardinality pruning, and the first solution is then not guaranteed to be feasible.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for EDI. Mertens reports BLDM at O(n log n). CKK node counts grow exponentially below n_c ≈ 30 (25-bit numbers) and fall above it. With 12 or fewer significant digits, problems of arbitrary size are solvable in practice; double-precision covariates push the hard region to larger n. No source compares this with SA or MILP.
findings.suggested_action: Prototype a C++ BLDM+CKK kernel with a node/time cap behind a p == 1 branch in optimal_solve_auto. Validate it against enumeration at n ≤ 24 and against SA at n = 50/100/200. Add a row to catalog §12 tables (a)/(b).

findings.candidate: (Re-reported, updated.) A low-rank convex MIQCP through the CRAN package scip 1.10.1-1 (Apache ≥ 2): minimize θ subject to θ ≥ ||z||², z = Mw (p continuous), Σw = n_T, w binary. This removes the commercial-solver objection recorded in catalog table (a). New this run: ompr 1.0.4 supports only linear objectives, so this has to use scip's own model API (scip_add_quadratic_cons), not the existing ompr path.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified; no source benchmarks this problem.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look: benchmark scip low-rank MIQCP against GLPK Fortet at n = 15/20/25/30 (p = 5), behind requireNamespace('scip'), and against the enumeration prototype.

findings.candidate: (Re-reported, unchanged.) Use HiGHS as the MILP backend, either through ROI.plugin.highs (GPL-2 | GPL-3) or by calling the HiGHS C API from EDI's C++ through highs 1.15.1-2. The 1.15.1-2 NEWS confirms that all 177 C API functions are registered with R_RegisterCCallable (LinkingTo: highs). HiGHS still has no MIQP, so it helps only the linearized models.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. Earlier evidence suggests results depend on the formulation.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look: benchmark GLPK against HiGHS on milp_solve_quadratic at n = 15/20/25 and on milp_solve_l1 at n = 20–200, with HiGHS threads fixed at 1 for determinism.

bayesian-bootstrap.note: Re-checked what is new since 2026-11-16 (no code commits since). Weight generation is still one vectorized rgamma(B*n_units,1) call, O(Bn), with the context built once per call. It is negligible next to the B weighted refits. The rexp/uniform-spacings routes give the same distribution but change the realized draws, and the saving does not matter. Every recent proposal that avoids the B refits is an approximation of the refit distribution, so each is an estimator change: amortized generators (GMS/GBS, Shin-Wang-Liu JCGS 2024; Sohn-Rockova arXiv 2608.02480; Lopes-Polson-Sokolov 2025/26), influence-function linearization (Ribbon, arXiv 2606.27269, Jun 2026) and one-step Newton replicates (Davidson-MacKinnon; Moulton-Zeger 1991). Owen's 2025 Beta(1/2,3/2) / power weights (fwb 0.6.0) and Lam's cheap bootstrap (fwb 1.0.0) change the weight law or the interval, not the cost per replicate; they are accuracy and interval-method options, not speedups. fwb 1.0.0 adopts seed-only weights independent of worker count, which matches EDI's determinism model and needs no change. Per-replicate weighted refits (g-comp weighted logistic) are already warm-started; a fully iterated weighted MLE is needed to keep the estimand.

analytic-derivatives.note: Exact O(np) NLL+gradient and O(np²) observed/expected information (Ferrari–Cribari-Neto closed forms) are at the cost lower bound for an exact likelihood. Checked since 2026-11-16: betareg 3.2-6 (2026-08-26) only adds analytic score/hessian to the BetaR distribution class; TMB/glmmTMB use AD, which is no faster than hand-coded analytic derivatives for a fixed-effects model (TMB paper: similar performance without random effects). The dead all-n mu pass in ZeroOneInflatedBeta::operator() is an already-recorded incidental (catalog §3 TODO 2a).

closed-form.note: Trivial: Smithson–Verkuilen squeeze and the lgamma/lbeta loglik/deviance/AIC sums are single O(n) passes; nothing faster. Alternatives for 0/1 responses (XBX extended-support betareg, ordered beta, scale-location-truncated beta arXiv 2509.13167) are estimator changes, not speedups.

lbfgs.note: Rivals: betareg (optim BFGS + Fisher-scoring polish, φ start from Ferrari–Cribari-Neto moment formula; vignette example 51 BFGS + 3 FS iterations) and BetaRegression.jl (pure Fisher scoring, max 100 iterations). Both are already covered by catalog §1 v1.0.5 TODO-7 (moment φ₀ + Fisher-scoring polish, Prototype) and options-table row O12. The ZOIB joint L-BFGS split is already Adopt/Prototype (catalog §3 TODO 2a/2b, §11 TODO-1). EDI's C++ L-BFGS is already 28x faster than betareg.fit at N=1000 per its own benchmark. No new LBFGSpp release or line-search evidence was found after 2026-11-16. Warm starts for bootstrap refits are only weakly supported (a single IceCube analysis reports a 3.6x median reduction in evaluations when the inverse Hessian is also carried over), and EDI's reusable worker already warm-starts.

likelihood-factorization.note: Re-checked the code at 8b718ae: the ZOIB BB replicate still calls betareg::betareg (inference_proportion_zero_one_inflated_beta.R:290) although fast_beta_regression_weighted_cpp exists, and the PB simulator still calls rbeta(1) per row in a loop (:799). Both findings stand. Separability is reconfirmed by Queiroz & Ferrari (arXiv 2605.14011, May 2026) and by the Stata Journal hurdle note. gamlss.dist BEINF uses nu=p0/p2, tau=p1/p2 with log links, which is the same multinomial-logit (mid baseline) parameterization as EDI's C++ softmax, and gives a reference implementation for the plogis-vs-softmax mismatch question (an estimator question, not a speedup).

findings.candidate: Call EDI's existing fast_beta_regression_weighted_cpp on the interior rows with the BB weights (the same weighted beta MLE), keeping betareg/lm.wfit as fallbacks. Skip the zero/one logits unless the estimand is marginal.
findings.claimed_speedup: From EDI's own benchmark page (fetched): at N=1000, the C++ beta regression takes 0.88 ms vs 24.85 ms for betareg.fit (28.4x). The formula betareg() call adds model.frame overhead on top. Not measured on this exact path.
findings.suggested_action: Prototype: swap betareg::betareg for fast_beta_regression_weighted_cpp in the ZOIB BB replicate, gate the logits on the marginal estimand, verify coefficient agreement with betareg, then time a B=1000 run.

findings.candidate: One vectorized call over the interior indices: rbeta(length(idx), pmax(mu[idx]*phi,1e-4), pmax((1-mu[idx])*phi,1e-4)). R recycles the shape arguments to the result length.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. Removes an O(n) interpreted loop of n separate rbeta calls per PB replicate.
findings.suggested_action: Adopt as a low-priority cleanup, gated on an identical() check of y_sim against the loop under a fixed seed.

analytic-derivatives.note: Closed-form score Xᵀ(y−μ) and Hessian −XᵀWX (and the probit generalized-residual forms) cost O(np²), which is the price of reading X, so nothing can beat them asymptotically. AD rivals were re-searched (TMB arXiv 1509.00660; the phylogenetics AD study, arXiv 2211.02168). No source shows AD beating a fused hand-written GLM gradient. No code commits since the 2026-11-16 result.

irls.note: C++ LDLT IRLS (logit = Newton; probit = Fisher scoring) remains the right algorithm at small p: no 2026 arXiv paper on accelerating IRLS/Newton for binary GLMs turned up. Recent arXiv work targets large-step gradient descent on separable data, not unpenalized small-p MLE. Correction to the previous note: per fastglm's CRAN NEWS, 0.1.4 (2026-11-11) is maintenance only. The probit/cloglog tail and capped-scoring-update changes are in 0.1.3 and apply to its bias-reduction path. They still back the catalogued Incidental 3 and v1.0.5 TODO-2 step-halving items, but say nothing new about plain MLE. Re-verified in code: inference_proportion_fractional_logit.R:165 still calls glm.fit(quasibinomial) on the estimate_only + harden=FALSE path, while :257 uses the C++ kernel for the same QMLE. fastglm's benchmark vignette (2026-11-06) still shows glm.fit 2.75 ms vs Cholesky IRLS 0.67 ms at n=1,000, p=30. fracreg 1.1.0 (CRAN 2026-08-20) fits the Papke–Wooldridge QMLE through maxLik, a general optimizer and no faster.

lbfgs.note: Re-verified at commit 8b718ae1: the R wrappers fast_logistic_regression (helper_glm_fit.R:852) and fast_logistic_regression_with_var (:923) still default to optimization_alg = "lbfgs", while the C++ kernel and the helper docs at :33 say "irls" is the default. The scikit-learn 1.9.1 docs still recommend newton-cholesky for n_samples >> n_features. RcppNumerical fastLR (L-BFGS) beats glm.fit only in a third-party p=100 benchmark, with no comparison against Newton-Cholesky. LBFGSpp (MIT) has had no change relevant to line-search speed. The previous finding stands.

lu-decomposition.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. Here it is a single p×p LU log-det in the uncalled Firth evaluator, so not a hot path. Rival Firth fitters (fastglm firth, brglm2, logistf; Zietkiewicz–Kosmidis bounded-memory IWLS arXiv 2307.07342) use modified-score IWLS rather than an LU objective. That matters only if the evaluator ever gets a caller.

findings.candidate: Make "irls" (Newton with LDLT, already in C++) the wrapper default, matching the C++ default and the catalog row that calls L-BFGS the non-default alternative.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for EDI. scikit-learn 1.9.1 docs recommend newton-cholesky for n_samples >> n_features. fastglm's vignette shows Cholesky-IRLS as the fastest exact GLM fit. The 5–8 Newton iterations vs tens for L-BFGS is the catalog's estimate, not a measurement.

balanced-clustering.note: anticlust 0.8.18 (2026-09-15) is still the CRAN version, and balanced_clustering is still equal-size only (centroid/ilp), so the Ward holdout is still needed. The fastcluster finding stands, but its keeps_estimator is now flagged: fastcluster's own tests note ward.D2 ties 'may be resolved differently' from stats::hclust, so held-out subjects could differ on ties. K-way is about 6 ms per replay draw at n=40, so this is low priority. Newer balanced k-means heuristics (BalLOT, arXiv 2512.05926; MCF-based constrained k-means) are heuristics with a different estimator and are not drop-ins.

branch-and-bound-milp.note: solve_optimal_blocks builds an n²B/2-binary McCormick MILP and solves it with GLPK. The roxygen in design_fixed_optimal_blocks.R:132-144 shows this is a hot path: every randomization-bootstrap replay draw re-solves the blocking. Measured cost per draw is about 1.7 s at n=12, B=3 and about 79 s at n=16, B=4. New this run: (1) An exact bitmask/subset dynamic program over the same objective (anchor the lowest unassigned subject, enumerate its block-mates) solves EDI's ompr sizes (n ≤ ~20) exactly in O(2^n·C(n−1, s−1)) or better, with no solver. It works for any D, including custom or negative distances. (2) When the blocks are pairs (n = 2B), the problem is exactly min-weight perfect non-bipartite matching; nbpMatching, already an EDI import, solves that exactly in polynomial time. Still standing from the earlier run: the HiGHS backend, now with stronger evidence (designmatch 0.5.5, 2026-02, made highs its default solver; highs 1.15.1-2 was released 2026-11-02), and the equal-size MSSC exact methods. The arXiv 2025–2026 scan found no newer exact method for fixed-size blocking. Karmakar 2022 confirms NP-hardness for block size > 2.

greedy-blocking.note: blockTools is still 0.6.6 (2025-01-22) and quickblock still 0.2.2 (threshold blocking with a variable block count, so not a drop-in). scclust 0.2.5 has a minimum size only and does not restrict the number of clusters. Karmakar's 2022 approximation algorithm optimises a bottleneck objective, which is a different estimator, and has no R implementation. The quantile-binning strata builder runs once per design; rsample/stratamatch use the same quantile approach. At about 27–33 ms per draw for greedy, there is nothing to replace.

linear-search.note: largest_divisor_at_most scans down from floor(sqrt(n)), O(√n) modulo operations run once per design construction. Trial division is the usual baseline, and factoring would not pay off at any realistic n.

findings.candidate: An exact subset dynamic program written in C++ (deterministic, no solver). Let f(S) be the minimum cost of partitioning the set S of unassigned subjects, with a count of how many size-⌈n/B⌉ blocks are still allowed. The lowest-index subject in S always opens the next block; enumerate its s−1 block-mates among S (s ∈ {⌊n/B⌋, ⌈n/B⌉}), add that block's within-pair distance sum, and recurse. Anchoring on the lowest element removes the B! label symmetry the MILP suffers from. States are bitmasks (2^n, about 1M at n=20, 8 MB of doubles). Transitions per state are at most C(n−1, s−1), so the total is well under 3^n, and 3^16 ≈ 4.3e7 already fits in about 2 s per the cited DP write-up. Exact for any D: custom, negative or asymmetric-symmetrised. Above a size cap, keep the MILP as a fallback.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not benchmarked by any source for this problem. The source for the general submask-partition DP solves N=16 (3^16 ≈ 43M transitions) within 2 s. The fixed-block-size version enumerates far fewer transitions: for n=16, s=4, about 16.5k reachable states × ≤455 transitions, versus EDI's measured 79 s for the MILP. Any ratio is my own estimate, not a measurement.
findings.suggested_action: Add a row to catalog §12 options table (c): 'exact subset DP with lowest-element anchoring (C++, no solver), n ≤ ~22'. Prototype it as an arm of the v1.0.5-TODO-5 benchmark against the current MILP at n ∈ {8, 12, 16, 20}, checking objective equality (not block-id equality). If it wins, dispatch method='ompr' to the DP below the cap. This directly fixes the documented hours-long replay cost at n=16.

findings.candidate: When ⌊n/B⌋ = ⌈n/B⌉ = 2, the objective Σ_blocks D_ij is exactly minimum-weight perfect non-bipartite matching. Dispatch to nbpMatching::nonbimatch, which is already an EDI import used by helper_matching.R. It runs the Derigs/Edmonds blossom algorithm, exact and polynomial (O(n³)). blockTools' algorithm='optimal' uses the same approach for n.tr=2.
findings.claimed_speedup: Exponential to O(n³). Not quantified by a source at EDI's sizes. Pair blocking is optimally solvable while blocks larger than two are NP-hard (Karmakar 2022, citing Greevy et al. 2004 and Lu et al. 2011).
findings.suggested_action: In solve_optimal_blocks, add a fast path when n == 2B: call the existing compute_binary_match_structure / nbpMatching::nonbimatch on D and convert the pairs to block ids. Add a test that the objective equals the MILP's at n=8, B=4.

findings.candidate: Use HiGHS as the open-source MILP backend, through ROI.plugin.highs if it accepts binary/integer types, or through the highs package's model API directly. designmatch 0.5.5 (2026-02-20), a CRAN matching/blocking-design package, now uses highs as its default solver. The scip CRAN package (1.10.1-1, 2026-10-04, Apache-2.0) is a second option through its own model-building API.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for this model. The general MIPLIB 2017 figures from Mittelmann (via arXiv 2312.13527, cited in the previous run) give a shifted geometric mean of 7317 for GLPK vs 3114 for HiGHS, about 2.3×. This is far smaller than the reformulation and DP gains.
findings.suggested_action: In the v1.0.5-TODO-5 benchmark, first confirm that ROI.plugin.highs solves a binary model. If it does, time GLPK vs HiGHS on the current and reformulated models above the DP cap, and add 'highs' to the closed roi_solver set if it wins.

findings.candidate: For dist ∈ {euclidean, mahal}, the kernels return squared distances, so when n mod B = 0 the objective is (n/B) × equal-size MSSC. Exact cardinality-constrained MSSC methods then apply: Piccialli & Sudoso's SDP branch-and-cut, and Brusco-style repetitive branch-and-bound. Re-reported from the previous run; nothing newer turned up in the 2025–2026 arXiv scan.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified against GLPK. Piccialli & Sudoso say they solve instances '10 times larger than ... state-of-the-art exact methods'.
findings.suggested_action: Keep as a note in catalog table (c), below the subset DP. Do not pursue unless exact blocking at n ≫ 20 becomes a requirement.

findings.candidate: fastcluster::hclust, a drop-in replacement for stats::hclust (or hclust.vector to avoid materialising dist). Re-reported from the previous run.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified; the package page says only 'much faster' algorithms. K-way already costs only about 6 ms per replay draw at n=40 and about 21 ms at n=400.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look only if profiling shows the hclust holdout as a hotspot at large n. If so, A/B fastcluster against stats for identical cutree output, including tied-covariate fixtures.

bca-interval.note: Re-checked the arXiv BCa listing through 2026-10: no cheaper way to compute the acceleration has appeared. bcaboot 0.2-3 (CRAN, 2021) is unchanged, and SciPy 1.18 BCa still uses a jackknife-type acceleration with batching. The earlier conclusion stands. z0, a and the quantiles are O(B). The jackknife refits are the cost; the influence-function acceleration is already v1.0.5-TODO-7, and grouped jackknife / ABC were already rejected because they change â or need no fewer evaluations.

double-bootstrap.note: Reading `ci_calibrated_bootstrap` (inference_all_abstract_non_param_boot.R:1986-2042) shows the loop draws a new set of n_outer ≤ 101 outer resamples, each with an inner bootstrap of 51, for every one of the 5 grid values of α. The inner distribution of each outer resample does not depend on α, so one outer×inner set can be stored and scored at all 5 grid α. That keeps the grid search and its nearest-coverage pick, cutting about 26.8k refits to about 5.8k. It is the estimator-preserving sub-step of v1.0.5-TODO-2, without the switch to continuous prepivoted α, which needs an A/B test. Since the previous run (same day): Chang & Hall (doi 10.1093/biomet/asu060) and the arXiv listing still give single-inner-sample (warp-speed / fast double bootstrap) schemes no gain for CIs, so the rejection stands. Hall, Lee & Young 2000 (interpolation at the second level) is already effectively in place, because the inner type-8 quantiles interpolate. Lee & Young 1996 (sequential SPRT stopping at the inner level) and 1995 (analytic coverage correction) are further possible savings, but no fetched source quantifies them at EDI's sizes.

percentile-bootstrap-interval.note: Percentile, basic, studentized and symmetric intervals, tail-count p-values, the Wald fallback and the smoothed percentile interval all run on a precomputed distribution in O(B) to O(B log B), which costs microseconds next to the B refits. New searches found no 2025–26 primary work that changes this. The cheap bootstrap and BLB change the estimator. Besag–Clifford / anytime-valid sequential p-values (arXiv 2409.18908, 2404.15586) are already tracked as v1.0.5 catalog TODO-8 / TODO-156. Smoothed-bootstrap bandwidth papers (Polansky–Schucany 1997, Ho–Lee 2005) concern accuracy, not speed.

findings.candidate: Draw the outer×inner set once (101 outer refits, each with 51 inner refits) and store each sorted inner distribution, or equivalently u_b, the inner-CDF position of θ̂. Then score coverage at all 5 grid α from the same set, with common random numbers across the grid. The grid and the nearest-coverage pick stay as they are. This is the half of v1.0.5-TODO-2 that keeps the estimator; going to continuous prepivoted α can follow separately after its A/B test.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not a source claim; this is arithmetic on the code. About 26.8k → 101·52 + 501 ≈ 5.8k refits (≈4.6×). MetricGate's documentation describes the same trick ('store the sorted inner distributions up front', so each candidate α becomes a lookup), but gives no timing.
findings.suggested_action: Hoist the outer×inner loop out of the α-grid loop in ci_calibrated_bootstrap. This can be done now, ahead of or as step 1 of v1.0.5-TODO-2, and needs no coverage A/B beyond a regression check.

cluster-block-resampling.note: Unchanged since 2026-11-16 and there are no code commits since. resample_group_rows_internal does one counting pass plus O(G) Lemire draws and an O(output) expansion, which is optimal. The pair-preserving draw is O(n_R + m) per replicate. The faster cluster methods found this run do not apply: MacKinnon's precomputed per-cluster sums, aggregated-matrix resampling (arXiv 2311.15829) and the wild cluster bootstrap (boottest, MacKinnon-Nielsen-Webb 2023) are all OLS-specific statistic shortcuts or estimator changes, not faster index generation. fwildclusterboot was archived from CRAN on 2024-05-29. Balanced group-level resampling is still tracked under audit J.

iid-index-resampling.note: No new 2025-2026 work beats Lemire draws for one fixed range; Lemire's method is also what NumPy's Generator.integers cites. The batched-ranged finding still stands, now with its journal DOI (10.1002/spe.3369, SPE 55(1)). New this run: Randompack (arXiv 2605.05099, May 2026, MIT) benchmarks bounded integers at 0.6-3 ns per value, which is a reference, not a new algorithm. The Poisson bootstrap was checked again; it gives random replicate sizes, so it is an estimator change. For sample_group_units with replace = FALSE, the bitset-instead-of-unordered_set finding is merged with the stratified one. dqrng 0.4.1 (2024-05-28) has no sampling changes since the last run; its license is AGPL-3, so take the idea, not the code.

largest-remainder-allocation.note: Trivial: a closed-form apportionment, O(G log G) over a handful of strata and run once per call. Any other rounding rule changes the allocation, which is an estimator change.

sort-and-sweep.note: build_draw's stable_sort runs only when preserve_order is set, on the PRW subsampling path, next to a full refit. A stable counting sort keyed on row index (keys at most n) would be O(N+n) and give the identical order. Sources found this run (Apache Arrow ARROW-7526, the Boost list) confirm counting sort wins on small key ranges, but the inventory already records this as immaterial. No new evidence.

stratified-resampling.note: stratified_bootstrap_indices_cpp and exchangeable_resampling_draws_cpp with replace = TRUE are already optimal (Lemire draws). For replace = FALSE, the dqrng-style hybrid still stands, merged into one finding with iid-index-resampling: a bitset at moderate sampling rates, partial Fisher-Yates above 50%. Balanced stratified resampling is still tracked under audit J; a 2021 efficiency-balanced design paper and Nigam-Rao (1996) add nothing that changes this. rsample 1.3.2 (2026-01-30) group_bootstraps(strata=) is an R-level reference implementation, not faster.

findings.candidate: (a) The same rejection loop, but mark seen positions in a dense, reusable std::vector<uint8_t> or bitset of length n. The RNG calls happen in the same order, so the output is bit-identical. (b) Rate-based dispatch as in dqrng: partial Fisher-Yates on a reusable scratch copy of the ids when k/n > 0.5 (this is v1.0.5-TODO-2 and changes the stream), the bitset otherwise.
findings.claimed_speedup: From the CRAN dqrng vignette, measured against base R rather than EDI. At m=1e6, n=1e4 (1% rate), bitset rejection takes 103 µs, R's hash variant 658 µs and sample.int 1.94 ms. At a 60% rate, partial Fisher-Yates takes 10.3 ms against 63.7 ms for sample.int. Not quantified at EDI's n of roughly 100-1e4, and negligible end to end next to B refits.
findings.suggested_action: When v1.0.5-TODO-2 is picked up, first swap the unordered_set for a reusable dense marker (bit-identical) and microbenchmark it at k/n in {0.25, 0.5, 0.9} with n up to 1e4. Adopt partial Fisher-Yates for k > n/2 only if it is still materially faster. Add the bitset row to the catalog §7 options table.

findings.candidate: Batched ranged random integer generation (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, SPE 2025): several unbiased bounded integers from one 64-bit word, with one multiplication and no division per value in the common case.
findings.claimed_speedup: The paper reports 1.5-2.5x on shuffles with fast 64-bit generators and 2.6-4.7x with ChaCha, on in-cache arrays. It was not benchmarked for repeated draws from one fixed range or with 32-bit MT19937. Not quantified at EDI sizes.
findings.suggested_action: No action unless profiling shows RNG/index time matters. If it does, prototype a batched bounded_rand in RNG.h and bundle it with the v1.0.5-TODO-2/TODO-3 stream-change window.

brt-monte-carlo.note: Per-draw work is unchanged: O(n) masked sums is the floor for a fresh resample and assignment, and draw materialization is already Adopt under catalog §9 TODO-4 (parallelize, results identical). No new BRT kernel algorithm was found. The studentized-permutation and approximate-randomization papers (Toulis 1908.04218, prepivoting 2102.04423) are about validity, not speed. New since the previous result, for the 'early stopping' variant: compute_two_sided_brt_pval_with_sequential_mc (inference_all_abstract_rand_bootstrap.R:930) stops on a Clopper–Pearson band checked at every batch with no multiplicity control across looks, and Besag–Clifford (TODO-156) stops early only for futility. Fischer & Ramdas' Monte Carlo testing by betting (JRSSB 2025) is anytime-valid and stops early for both rejection and futility. On Fisher's sharp null it needed a mean of 85 permutations, against 160–200 for Besag–Clifford. See the finding. It changes the reported p-value (a stopping-rule and policy change), so the speed gain comes with a validity gain, not the same estimator.

kaplan-meier-product-limit.note: Checked FastSurvival 2.0.0 on CRAN (MIT, 2026-11-16), the scikit-survival 0.26–0.28 notes and the 2024–26 arXiv RMST resampling papers (2408.15607, 2501.05836). Nothing beats the already-Adopt presort-once plus O(n) counting pass per arm (catalog §5, TODO-18). Multinomial-weight and Poisson-bootstrap formulations (arXiv 1412.1735) are the same idea as that planned presort.

logrank-sweep.note: Already Adopt (presort + merge, TODO-18). FastSurvival survdiff_fast (two-pointer merge, FH weights), nph 2.1, coin 1.4-6 (2026-09-30) and the cheap quadratic-form permutation log-rank (arXiv 1807.05504) bring nothing faster for the BRT draw loop. 1807.05504 changes the statistic.

ridit-scoring.note: The O(n+L) level-slot rebuild (ridit_kernel_level_slots.md TODO-3) is still the only faster option. Ridit (CRAN) is archived and pridit adds nothing algorithmic.

sort-and-sweep.note: The O(n+K) counting variant for the JT kernel is already tracked as TODO 9. Sources put radix sort behind std::sort at n ≤ 1000 for general keys, and base R's radix itself falls back to insertion sort below n=200, so only counting by level helps at EDI's sizes. That is already tracked.

streaming-moments.note: Trivial: an O(n) single pass, bounded by reading the input. The shifted one-pass accuracy fix is already Adopt (TODO-4).

value-space-bisection-selection.note: No 2025–26 work on HL or X+Y selection found. Monahan (DescTools), Antille's O(n log n) linearization and Johnson–Mizoguchi are all already weighed in catalog §6 (tie-safe early stop, wilcox_hl_kernel_hoisting.md TODO-3/4).

findings.candidate: Sequential Monte Carlo testing by betting (Fischer & Ramdas, JRSSB 2025). A test martingale bets on whether each BRT draw's statistic is at or beyond the observed one, and its p-process is valid at any stopping time, including the B cap. The binomial and binomial-mixture strategies stop early for rejection and for futility. The updates are closed form, so they slot into the existing batch loop over the common-random-number prefix (get_brt_distribution_prefix) with O(1) extra work per draw.
findings.claimed_speedup: Source claim, not measured on EDI. On Fisher's sharp-null real data at α=0.05, the binomial strategy needed a mean of 85 permutations (median 53) and the binomial mixture 147, against 160–200 for Besag–Clifford (h=8–10) and a fixed T=1000 in the simulations (arXiv 2401.07365v5 §7.4). The simulations say substantially fewer permutations than Besag–Clifford under strong alternatives. Not quantified against EDI's current Clopper–Pearson band.
findings.suggested_action: Fold the BRT sequential-MC path into the TODO-156 / v1.2.0 anytime-results proposal (algorithm_choice_audit.md TODO-43). Prototype the binomial betting strategy as an opt-in alternative to the Clopper–Pearson band in compute_two_sided_brt_pval_with_sequential_mc, then compare draws used and the error across looks on existing benchmark workloads. Also cite DOI https://doi.org/10.1093/jrsssb/qkaf014 (taken from the arXiv record; not fetched).

adaptive-quadrature.note: QUADPACK oracle in ordinal_clmm_cloglog_link_probe runs once per session per ordinal version (2 clmm fits plus 80 integrate() calls). It must stay independent of GH, and its cost is negligible. Checked Boost.Math tanh-sinh / GSL QUADPACK material: tanh-sinh only wins on endpoint-singular integrands, and this integrand is smooth. Re-checked ordinal NEWS: no clmm link-swap fix through 2026.7-26, so the probe is still needed.

analytic-derivatives.note: OrdinalLikelihood interval probability is closed form, O(K) per observation per node. The remaining speedup, an analytic Louis-identity observed information replacing the FD Hessian, is already catalog §4 TODO-2 (Adopt). New supporting evidence: rms 8.2-0 (2026-10-22) uses a Louis-identity sparse information for its random-intercept orm. TMB/CppAD AD is not faster than hand-coded gradients (AD review arXiv 1811.05031).

gauss-hermite-quadrature.note: Two findings. (1) Weighted Bayesian-bootstrap path (weighted_ordinal_random_intercept_fit → ordinal::clmm nAGQ=20, used by KKCLMM and KKGLMM). New evidence from the clmm source: nlminb gets no gradient, so it uses finite differences, and every objective call reruns the inner Newton for the conditional modes; the Hessian comes from numerical deriv12. More importantly, clmm case weights multiply each observation's log-probability inside the integral (getNAGQ/getNGHQ_C: SS1 += weights[j]*log(pr)). With EDI's pair-level weights, clmm therefore maximizes Σ_g log∫∏p^{w_g}φ, not the cluster-weighted Σ_g w_g log∫∏pφ. That answers the previous run's open 'confirm weight semantics' question: they do not match. A native cluster-weighted GH kernel would be both faster and the right replicate estimator. (2) The Stringer 2024 exact-gradient AGQ finding still stands; arXiv 2310.01589 is still at v2 with no journal DOI. Also checked: rms 8.2-0 orm(cluster) adds AGQ with escalating nodes and a Louis-identity sparse information. It uses a block-alternating outer loop with linear convergence and a profiled σ, and it targets many intercepts, so it is not faster than EDI's native L-BFGS at small K. mixor (Fortran, Fisher scoring) and tramME (TMB Laplace, an estimator change) are not better at EDI sizes either.

lbfgs.note: The Stringer exact-gradient AGQ + L-BFGS (LBFGSpp) finding stands and is re-reported jointly with GH. LBFGSpp (MIT) still shows no new release. Nothing new on warm starts: lme4 refit and MixedModels.jl already warm-start replicates, and EDI's CLMM already warm-starts from the fixed-effects fit. The single cold start of fast_ordinal_clmm (log σ = −3) remains a robustness item that is already catalogued (catalog §4 Incidental).

model-simplification-surrogate.note: The inventory row is stale. At 8b718ae1, compute_weighted_clmm_estimate (inference_ordinal_KK_clmm_abstract.R:256) and the KKGLMM weighted path (inference_ordinal_KK_combined.R:485) both call weighted_ordinal_random_intercept_fit (ordinal::clmm with a random intercept), not a fixed-effects surrogate. weighted_ordinal_bootstrap_surrogate_fit is still used only by non-mixed ordinal classes. The speed and estimand question has moved to the GH weighted-path finding. Recommend retiring or rewriting this row.

multistart.note: The 5-start log σ grid plus L-BFGS plus FD-Hessian Newton polish is cheap at d = K+p. The only real speedup, an analytic Hessian in the polish, is TODO-2. nloptr MLSL (L-BFGS local, low-discrepancy starts) is meant for unknown multimodality and costs more than a 1-D σ grid. No 2025–2026 evidence against deterministic σ-start grids was found.

findings.candidate: Add cluster weights to the native C++ GH objectives (_glmm_engine.h GLMMObjective, used by fast_ordinal_clmm for all 4 links, and fast_ordinal_glmm). Each group's log-integral and its gradient are multiplied by w_g, the weight being constant within a KK pair or singleton, so the replicate maximizes Σ_g w_g·log∫∏_i p_ig(u)φ(u)du with the analytic gradient and L-BFGS, warm-started from the point estimate. This matches the cluster Bayesian bootstrap (context row_to_unit = match cluster), uses the same estimator family and quadrature as the point estimate, and needs neither the R model frame nor the cloglog link-swap probe.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. Mechanism, from the clmm source: d+1 objective evaluations per FD gradient, each with an inner mode-finding Newton and 20-node AGQ, versus one analytic-gradient pass at 20 fixed nodes, plus R formula/model-frame overhead and a fallback ladder of up to 10 fits per replicate. Order-of-magnitude gains per replicate are plausible but unmeasured.
findings.suggested_action: Investigate, prioritised above speed: (1) confirm the weight-semantics mismatch numerically: for one KK dataset and one weight draw, compare clmm's weighted -logLik with a direct Σ_g w_g·log∫ evaluation at the same θ; (2) add a w_g argument to the GLMMObjective/OrdinalGLMMObjective value and gradient (group-level multiply); (3) switch weighted_ordinal_random_intercept_fit callers to it, A/B the Bayesian-bootstrap CIs, and time one replicate against the clmm path. Also retire the stale model-simplification-surrogate inventory row.

findings.candidate: Adaptive GH with an exact gradient of the AQ approximate log-likelihood for a single grouping factor (Stringer, arXiv 2310.01589 v2): implicit differentiation of the per-group mode, reusing the inner Newton factorisation, optimised with L-BFGS via LBFGSpp and followed by a Newton polish. This answers the catalog's TODO-153 objection that the AGQ gradient lacks an envelope identity.
findings.claimed_speedup: Paper (Bernoulli GLMM): typically 2–4× faster than lme4/GLMMadaptive at m=1000, n=5; up to 7–10× on toenail data. These are relative to other packages, not to fixed-node GH. Against EDI's 20 fixed nodes the saving is probably modest, since the paper needs about 7–17 AGQ points at small clusters. Not quantified for ordinal models.
findings.suggested_action: Unchanged from the previous run: cite Stringer 2024 in v1.0.5 TODO-153 and catalog T1, with a lowered node-saving expectation for 20-node ordinal kernels. Prototype AGQ on the 60-node Poisson GLMM before the ordinal kernels.

bernoulli-coin-flips.note: Trivial (one draw per subject or pair, using the R-parity MT stream). Checked what is new since 2026-11-16: the bit-efficient Bernoulli literature (binary-expansion and geometric methods, ~2 bits/draw) and randomness recycling (Draper & Saad, SODA 2026) save random bits, not wall time, with MT words this cheap. Bit-packing and non-MT generators were already rejected in catalog P1 because they break the stream. Change from the previous result: the Koning & Hemerik subgroup sign-flip test (Biometrika 2024, doi 10.1093/biomet/asad050) is dropped as a finding here. It changes the reference set and the p-value (an estimator change), and the current arXiv v3 abstract claims more power at the same number of transformations, not fewer draws, so it belongs to the randomization-test problem, not to the draw kernel. Per-column MT seeding cost stays under v1.0.6 performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md TODO-149(c) (counter-based child streams). The 2026 Philox-vs-MT preprint could not be fetched (403).

fisher-yates-shuffle.note: The explicit Durstenfeld shuffle on Lemire bounded_rand is the standard optimum: O(n), one word per position. The Randompack paper (arXiv 2605.05099, 2026) benchmarks C++ permutation at ~1.7 ns/value, against 30–60 ns for base R, which confirms EDI's C++ kernels are already at the floor. MergeShuffle and parallel in-place shuffles (Penschuck 2023) pay off only for one huge permutation; EDI shuffles many small vectors, already parallel across draws. Floyd, Vitter D and Floyd rank recycling (arXiv 2607.14302, with no runtime claim) help only when k ≪ n; EDI has k ≈ n/2. Two constant-factor options stand, both re-reported: (1) batched ranged integers (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, doi 10.1002/spe.3369), a stream change; (2) a C++ kernel for block_ra_batch. New evidence for (2): randomizr 2.0.1 (CRAN 2026-08-27) moved block_ra to C++ and reports a 6–17× speedup over per-block R calls.

findings.candidate: A small C++ kernel. For each draw column, a partial Fisher–Yates of k = min(n_T, N−n_T) positions per block, using edi_rng::bounded_rand. It keeps the block_ra law (random rounding of N·prob_T, Bernoulli for singleton blocks) and seeds per draw index so results do not depend on thread count. randomizr 2.0.1 made the same kind of move: blocked assignment now runs in one C++ call.
findings.claimed_speedup: From the randomizr 2.0.1 NEWS (CRAN, Apple M4 Pro, R 4.6.0): block_ra went from 8.9 ms to 1.1 ms at N=20,000 with 2,000 blocks, and from 46 ms to 6.5 ms at N=100,000 with 10,000 blocks, when moving from per-block R calls to C++. EDI's baseline is already vectorized, not per-block, so the gain for EDI is smaller and not quantified.
findings.suggested_action: Profile block_ra_batch at typical N·r (1e5–1e6) against a design's per-draw statistic time. Write the kernel under v1.0.5-TODO-11 only if draws are a material share; otherwise close v1.0.5-TODO-11 as Keep. Bundle any stream change with v1.0.6 TODO-149(c).

findings.candidate: Batched ranged random integer generation (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, Software: Practice and Experience 55(1), doi 10.1002/spe.3369). It takes two or more unbiased bounded indices from one random word; with 32-bit words, two indices fit while i(i−1) < 2^32, which covers EDI's n.
findings.claimed_speedup: From the arXiv abstract: it 'can more than double the speed of unbiased random shuffling for small to moderately large arrays'. The paper measured this with 64-bit PCG and Lehmer generators, not MT19937 and not specifically at n = 100–10,000.
findings.suggested_action: Record this as an option in the catalog P2 table. Consider it only together with another planned stream change, such as v1.0.6 TODO-149(c), so seeds are refreshed once, and only if profiling shows RNG words are material.

analytic-derivatives.note: Closed-form score/info at O((n_d+n_R)p²), which is at the input-reading lower bound. AD (TMB/CppAD) adds tape overhead at small p. Caching lgamma(y+1), which is constant in the parameters, and a SYRK-style fused sqrt(W)X crossprod (scikit-learn sandwich_dot discussion) are constant-factor micro-optimizations already noted. Nothing new.

bfgs.note: compute_weighted_combined_estimate (inference_count_KK_cond_poisson.R:2117-2152) is still R optim(BFGS) on R-coded NLL/score, maxit 300, reltol 1e-8, in every bootstrap replicate. The C++ Newton kernel with a weights argument is the catalog §10 Adopt item (v1.0.5 TODO-2) and is still not implemented. It is re-reported because it remains the faster same-estimator option and was not rejected. Nothing new in BFGS literature changes this: for small p and a concave canonical-link likelihood, Newton wins.

clogit-logistic-reduction.note: The reduction itself (an exact identity, O(n_d p) design build) is still optimal. The 2026 papers (bclogit arXiv 2602.08212, log-F penalized clogit arXiv 2607.28899) change the estimator and do not speed it up. New: the 2026-11-16 inventory row fit_clogit_reservoir_logit (inference_incidence_KK_cond_logit_glmm_abstract.R:591) fits the stacked problem with R-level stats::glm.fit, plus an R pivoted QR in assemble. This runs in every bootstrap replicate (compute_clogit_reservoir_logit_weighted_estimate) and every null refit of likelihood-test CI inversion (fit_null). The sibling entries already use EDI's C++ fast_logistic_regression kernel. That kernel has fixed_idx/fixed_values (the offset case) but no prior-weights argument. See finding 1.

closed-form.note: Trivial: for m=2 strata the conditional likelihood is expit((x1-x2)'b), O(n_d p) per evaluation. GLR recursion (survival::clogit exact) collapses to the same 2-term sum.

newton-raphson.note: fast_cpoisson_combined_internal is a C++ Newton at small p on a concave canonical-link likelihood, so convergence is quadratic. Trust-region / truncated Newton (Lin-Weng-Keerthi) targets large sparse p. glm2-style step-halving (Marschner RJ 2011) and the fastglm step-halving IRLS are robustness changes, matching the existing halving/LDLT-check Adopt item (catalog §1, v1.0.5 TODO-2), not speedups. No commits since the last research.

findings.candidate: Route the fit through a compiled IRLS/Newton with prior weights and an offset (or fixed index). Option (a): add a case-weights argument to EDI's existing C++ fast_logistic_regression[_with_var]_cpp, which already supports fixed_idx/fixed_values and warm starts. This is the same change as the cpoisson weights item, v1.0.5 TODO-2. Option (b): use the fastglm-style RcppEigen IRLS (pivoted QR default, step-halving, weights+offset) as a reference.
findings.claimed_speedup: fastglm's own vignette claims 2.2x (QR) to 4.1x (Cholesky) over glm.fit for logistic n=1000, p=30, rising to 2.9x/7.2x at n=1e5. These are the source's claims, not measured on EDI. More gain is likely at EDI's small n, where R per-call overhead dominates (not quantified).
findings.suggested_action: Fold into v1.0.5 TODO-2: add a prior-weights argument to fast_logistic_regression[_with_var]_cpp. Then switch fit_clogit_reservoir_logit (full fit, bootstrap and fit_null) to it, with an equivalence test against glm.fit and a microbenchmark at typical KK sizes.

findings.candidate: The C++ Newton kernel fast_cpoisson_combined_with_var_cpp with a row-weights argument and step-halving: the same concave optimum, quadratic convergence and compiled evaluation. This is the existing catalog §10 Adopt item (v1.0.5 TODO-2), still unimplemented. glm2/fastglm-style deviance-decrease step-halving gives the needed robustness.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by a source for this model. Expected gains: fewer iterations (Newton, about 5 vs BFGS 20-100) and the R-to-C++ move (cf. fastglm's 2-7x for compiled vs R IRLS).
findings.suggested_action: Implement v1.0.5 TODO-2 (weights argument plus halving in fast_cpoisson_combined). Replace the optim call and benchmark the bootstrap loop.

active-set-projection.note: Checked: projected-Newton and gradient-projection literature (Bertsekas; Forsgren–Murray; Davis SSC 2008), small dense QP solvers (qpOASES/qpmad/Eiquadprog per arXiv 2510.21773), and aRD/BSW (SQP via osqp/quadprog). The projection reuses the iteration's LDLT at O(|A|p²+|A|³), negligible next to O(np²). A QP or conic solver would replace the whole scheme rather than speed up this step (see the irls finding).

cholesky-ldlt.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. Here it is one LDLT plus one solve per variance call, O(p³) against an O(np²) build of X'WX; nothing problem-specific to reuse.

finite-differences.note: Changed from no_faster: at commit 8b718ae the production score and Hessian (constrained_binomial_{score,hessian}[_weighted]_cpp_impl, fast_log_binomial_regression.cpp:840-920) are still central-FD stencils (h=1e-6 / 1e-4, 4·p(p+1)/2 log-likelihood evaluations). The closed form (catalog O5, v1.0.5 TODO-1 'Adopt') has not landed. Schwendinger et al. 2021 §2 give the analytic gradient X'(y−μ)/(1−μ) and a Gram-matrix (X'DX) Hessian for the log link. AD and complex-step were rejected in the catalog and are not cheaper than the 2-line closed form. Re-reported as a still-open adopted improvement, not a new option.

irls.note: The previous conic-solver finding stands, now backed by numbers from the open copy of Schwendinger, Grün & Hornik 2021 (doi:10.1007/s00180-021-01084-5), which I extracted from https://d-nb.info/1231156651/34. In simulation C (hard boundary scenarios, n=500, 10/20/50/100 covariates), default glm/glm2 IRLS has a non-convergence rate of 99.9/99.9/99.5/97.9%; with tuned settings (maxit 10,000) it is 1.6–4.4%. ECOS is at 0% throughout. At 10 covariates the timings of ECOS, ipopt* and auglag* are 'rather similar'; ECOS is 'among the quickest' at 100 covariates. So the gain is reliability, not speed, at EDI's p. EDI's IRLS already adds an active-set projection and a KKT gate that plain glm/glm2 lack, so the paper's glm failure rates are an upper bound for EDI. No code commits since 2026-11-16. New since then: aRD 0.1.0 (CRAN 2025-08-22), a modified Newton method under box constraints for the identity link using osqp/quadprog, in the same family as BSW and the catalog's 'active-set / projected Newton QP' row, so no new finding. lbm 0.9.0.2 (2021, exact method / boundary-vector reparametrisation) and logbin 2.0.6 (a vcov change only) bring no faster method. ECOSolveR 0.6.2 (2026-10-16) and clarabel 0.11.3 (2026-08-23) are current R bindings of the conic candidates.

kkt-boundary-analysis.note: Checked: chi-bar-squared and constrained score-test literature (arXiv 2206.15178, 2601.03909), and the log-binomial MLE-finiteness LP (Schwendinger 2021, implemented in detectseparation). The multiplier solve reuses the LDLT and is tiny. An interior-point conic solver returns the duals directly but is not cheaper. Robustness side note, not speed: EDI could add the LP finiteness check (detectseparation::detect_infinite_estimates) before fitting, to tell infinite-MLE data apart from slow convergence. The earlier note on dropping all negative multipliers at once instead of following Lawson–Hanson NNLS still applies.

findings.candidate: Exponential-cone program: maximise Σ y·η + (1−y)·log(1−exp η) subject to Xβ ≤ 0 for the log link, or the identity-link analogue with log μ and log(1−μ) terms. Solve it with a primal-dual interior-point conic solver: ECOS (GPL-3, R binding ECOSolveR) or Clarabel (Apache-2.0, needs Rust). This form needs no feasible start and returns certified dual multipliers. Use it as a fallback when IRLS fails the KKT gate, or as the main solver.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not a speedup at EDI's sizes. Schwendinger, Grün & Hornik 2021 (§4.6, n=500, hard boundary scenarios), as extracted from the open PDF: only ecos, ipopt* and auglag* always reached the optimum, and their timings are 'rather similar' at 10 covariates. ECOS is 'among the quickest' at 100 covariates. Default glm/glm2 IRLS had 99.9% non-convergence at 10 covariates (1.6% with maxit 10,000), against 0% for ECOS. The timings appear only in a figure, so no IRLS-versus-ECOS ratio is quantified.
findings.suggested_action: Add 'exponential-cone interior point (ECOS/Clarabel)' to catalog §1 O4. In the v1.0.5 TODO-32 constrained-solver Prototype, A/B test an ECOS fallback for fits that fail kkt_verdict_at_bounds, on boundary-MLE fixtures (e.g. Schwendinger's simulation C designs), measuring converged rate and wall-clock at EDI's n and p.

findings.candidate: Closed-form score X'(w∘∂ℓ/∂η) and observed Hessian X' diag(w∘∂²ℓ/∂η²) X. For the log link these are (y−μ)/(1−μ) and −(1−y)μ/(1−μ)²; for the identity link, y/μ−(1−y)/(1−μ) and −y/μ²−(1−y)/(1−μ)². Schwendinger et al. 2021 §2 state the gradient X'(y−μ)/(1−μ) and the Gram (X'DX) form of the Hessian.
findings.claimed_speedup: Theoretical, from the catalog's O5 operation counts (not measured): about p× fewer flops (O(np²) against O(2np³)) and about 2p² fewer exp/log1p calls per Hessian. It also removes the NaN/Inf Hessians that FD stencils produce when they cross the boundary.
findings.suggested_action: Implement the already-adopted v1.0.5 TODO-1 analytic score and Hessian for the log- and identity-binomial links, weighted and unweighted, and keep an FD test that cross-checks them at interior points.

analytic-derivatives.note: The closed-form Poisson score X'(y−μ) and information X'WX cost O(np) and O(np²), the floor for reading X. AD (TMB/CppAD, Stan math) at best matches hand-coded derivatives and adds overhead. Fusing the likelihood, gradient and Hessian into one pass, or SIMD exp, gives only a constant-factor micro-optimization. Nothing new since 2026-11-16.

closed-form.note: Trivial: Pearson χ²/(n−p) dispersion times the inverse diagonal is O(n + p³), the standard quasi-Poisson estimator; nothing faster.

irls.note: fast_poisson_internal is canonical-link Newton (= IRLS/Fisher scoring) with an Eigen LDLT solve and step-halving (≤10 halvings, cached Δη, so each probe is O(n)). Checked what is new since 2026-11-16. fastglm 0.1.4 (2026-11-11) NEWS lists no Poisson algorithm change. Its vignette's fastest Poisson path (LLT Cholesky, ~0.6 ms at n=1000, p=30, per its own benchmark) is the same normal-equation Cholesky IRLS that EDI runs in C++. glm2 and speedglm are unchanged, and statsmodels and scikit-learn newton-cholesky are the same algorithm. The shrinkage-IRLS preprint (Asimit et al. 2025) changes the estimator. One-step or warm-start bootstrap shortcuts change the estimator, or are already present (EDI accepts warm_start_beta and a warm Fisher information). The modified-Poisson and cluster-sandwich work since then (rqlm 4.5-1, Noma 2026) is about finite-sample inference, not fitting speed. Nothing faster at EDI sizes.

lbfgs.note: L-BFGS is an option only; the default is IRLS (fast_poisson_regression.cpp:96/406). Sources (BranchGLM docs, scikit-learn solver guidance) place quasi-Newton ahead of Fisher scoring only at large p (≳50). EDI's p is small and the likelihood is strictly concave, so exact-Hessian Newton converges quadratically. LBFGSpp (MIT) is still the right L-BFGS backend if one is needed. Nothing new since 2026-11-16.

analytic-derivatives.note: SE = sqrt([I^-1]_jj) from an information matrix that is already computed in closed form and cached through shared(). Checked AD alternatives (TMB JSS paper, nabla 0.7.2 released 2026-10-28, CppAD speed suite) for anything new since 2026-11-16. AD only matches hand-coded derivatives at best on small simple models, and the sources found compare AD with ADMB, not with analytic derivatives. Nothing faster that keeps the same estimator. The count-family LR-CI bisection 'Investigate' item is a CI-inversion question, not an information-inversion one.

cholesky-ldlt.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. How this problem uses it: one LDLT plus a single-RHS solve for one diagonal entry, at p up to about 20. Selected-inversion work (arXiv 2025-2026: Serinv, sTiles, incomplete-LDL^T) targets large sparse matrices and saves nothing on small dense ones. The R wrapper compute_variance_from_information_matrix does an R qr() rank check before the Eigen LDLT, which factors twice. That constant factor is already tracked in v1.1.0-TODO-155. The ordinal Hessian-built-twice redundancy is recorded as incidental.

eigen-pseudo-inverse.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. This is a post-fit fallback, not a hot path. An eigendecomposition Moore-Penrose inverse is also what SAS CALIS uses for singular information below 60 parameters, which confirms it as the standard choice. Nothing new.

lu-decomposition.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. Previous finding still stands: invert_free_information runs FullPivLU and then a separate .inverse(), so it factors twice. Re-fetched the Eigen benchmark: at 8x8, FullPivLU costs 1.9x LLT, PartialPivLU 1.5x and LDLT 1.3x. Already tracked as v1.1.0-TODO-155. No code commits since the last run.

qr-decomposition.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. chol2inv on an R factor that already exists is a closed form. The QR rank check before LDLT in the R wrapper is the constant-factor double factorization tracked in v1.1.0-TODO-155. No code changes since the last run.

findings.candidate: Factor once. Either reuse the FullPivLU (lu.inverse()), or, for SPD information, use LDLT/LLT with a pivot-based definiteness check and then solve(Identity).
findings.claimed_speedup: From Eigen's dense decomposition benchmark (float; the page says to roughly double the times for double). At 8x8: LLT 0.05 ms, LDLT 0.07 ms (1.3x), PartialPivLU 0.08 ms (1.5x), FullPivLU 0.10 ms (1.9x). At 100x100, FullPivLU is 10.6x LLT. FullPivLU plus PartialPivLU is about 2.6x one LDLT on the factorization step at 8x8. Not quantified for a whole fit.
findings.suggested_action: No new work item. Keep this attached to v1.1.0-TODO-155. The minimal fix is lu.inverse(), which reuses the one factorization. Run an A/B on the vcov fixtures before considering LDLT.

breslow-risk-set-cumsum.note: The previous finding still stands, and I re-checked the code. .breslow_hazard (helper_survival_fits.R:582-600) still rescans `y_o >= event_times[k]` once per event, which is O(nK). kk_cox_fully_fixed_null_fit (inference_survival_KK_strat_cox.R:7) still calls the R rescan .cox_neg_loglik_breslow_r. The arXiv listing sorted by date (through 2026-11-02) and the coxdev 0.4.0 page show no algorithm better than the sort plus reverse cumsum, which is O(n log n). FastSurvival (arXiv 2410.19081) restates the O(n) exact derivative computation.

finite-differences.note: Checked the complex-step and FD Hessian literature again: complex-step second derivatives are worse than FD, and Richardson extrapolation costs more evaluations. The FD helpers (.cox_score_breslow_fd_r, .cox_information_breslow_fd_r) appear to be dead code and have analytic replacements. Nothing new.

lbfgs.note: No new benchmark of L-BFGS against Newton on the Cox objective at small p. FastSurvival notes that quasi-Newton is cheaper per iteration but makes less progress. At p ≤ ~10, the analytic-Hessian Newton is the faster choice, and L-BFGS remains an option path.

linear-scan.note: Trivial: a single O(n) pass, and the O(n·S) which() incidental is already recorded. Nothing faster.

newton-raphson.note: No new exact, faster unpenalized fitter appeared (arXiv listing to 2026-11-02; survival NEWS through 3.8-12 has no fitting change; Cyclops 3.7.1 and coxstream 0.1.0 are unchanged). FastSurvival (NeurIPS 2024) and the Cox MM algorithms (Zhang-Huang 2022, Ding et al. 2015) use quadratic or cubic surrogates. Those help robustness and large p, but bring no speed win over damped Newton at small p. Spectral survival analysis (arXiv 2505.22641) targets stationary points in high-dimensional and deep settings. Warm starts per bootstrap draw already exist (warm_start_beta / warm_start_fisher_info). Both earlier findings stand: the lazy design ladder, and coxdev for the weighted Efron kernel (coxdev 0.4.0 is header-only via LinkingTo, GPL>=3 on CRAN, BSD-3 upstream).

sandwich-estimator.note: SAS PHREG documents the Lin-Wei sandwich via DFBETA, and the coxdev manual gives O(n)-per-column score residuals. Both match EDI's prefix-sum form, which is already optimal.

sort-and-sweep.note: The radix-vs-comparison crossover is still in the hundreds to thousands of elements (djbsort speed notes 2026, ska_sort). The sort runs once per dataset and is cached via XPtr, so it is not a hot path. Keep.

findings.candidate: After the existing order(), take a single within-stratum reverse cumsum of exp(eta - max eta) and read off one risk sum per failure time. This gives the Breslow cumulative hazard and the NLL, and is the same identity coxdev's header and EDI's own compute_cox_neg_ll_only use.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. The complexity drops from O(nK) or O(n^2) to O(n) after the sort.

analytic-derivatives.note: The finding here is about robustness and accuracy, not speed. The derivative formulas are closed form and cost about as little as reading the data, so nothing is faster. However, FixedOrdinalRegression::neg_log_likelihood and operator() (ordinal_fixed_link_helpers.h:244-300) compute the cell probability as cdf(z_u) - cdf(z_l), and as 1 - cdf for the top category. This loses precision in the tails, and the result is then floored at 1e-12. rms 8.2-0 (2026-10-22) reworked orm.fit to avoid this. Its celldiff uses exact-width forms: logistic 2 sinh(dl/2) sqrt(f1 f2), cloglog via expm1, Cauchy via atan2, and probit by differencing the small-valued tail. The catalog lists this only as an incidental note; the rms rework is new evidence. See finding.

bfgs.note: weighted_ordinal_bootstrap_surrogate_fit (globals.R:177) runs MASS::polr (optim BFGS, R model-frame overhead, reltol 1e-10) on every bootstrap draw for the probit, cauchit and cloglog classes (and for the adjacent-category and stereotype logistic surrogates). EDI's own FixedOrdinalRegression already supports observation weights (m_weights, obs_weight). Only the probit, cloglog and cauchit Rcpp wrappers fail to expose them, and the PO class already uses fast_ordinal_regression_weighted_cpp. Harrell's benchmark (n=100k, 10 intercepts, p=5) has polr at 2.40 s against 0.084 s for compiled Newton-Raphson. See finding. The PPO polr rung is the last rung of a robustness ladder and is not hot, so Keep.

irls.note: The previous finding still stands: fastglm_ordinal(nonparallel=) is a compiled PPO fit that could precede the VGAM::vglm rung. fastglm 0.1.4 (CRAN, 2026-11-11) only fixes edge cases (empty predictor block, zero-weight rows). The vignette describes weights= as frequency counts, so how it behaves with fractional bootstrap weights is undocumented. VGAM 1.1-14 (2025-12-04) has no change to cumulative() or Fisher scoring beyond the optional bhhh. No timings found.

lbfgs.note: New quantified evidence for the catalog's existing Prototype item (§2 option table, Newton default, v1.0.5 algorithm-audit TODO-1). Harrell's rms 7.0 optimizer comparison on ordinal data (n=100k, 10 intercepts, p=5) has Newton-Raphson at 0.084 s against optim BFGS at 0.391 s. It also reports that BFGS stops with a large residual gradient when tight absolute convergence is required. That is the same f-plateau weakness the catalog flags for EDI's LBFGSpp stop rule. The comparison is BFGS, not L-BFGS, and the sizes are larger than EDI's. Cauchit is excluded because it is nonconcave. LBFGSpp: no new release notes found.

multistart.note: The previous cloglog finding still stands. I re-checked Kosmidis (arXiv 1204.0105, DOI 10.1111/rssb.12025): a log-concave g implies a concave log-likelihood with a unique MLE (Pratt 1981). So the 4 deterministic restarts in .cloglog_full_data_multistart can only repair non-convergence. A convergence certificate or a Newton polish is cheaper. Recent multistart literature (arXiv 2602.13450, Bayesian basin-size inference) is heuristic and gives no certificate for this problem.

newton-raphson.note: Newton with step-halving is still the reference and the fastest in Harrell's benchmarks: NR and Levenberg-Marquardt were best, nlminb close behind. ordinal 2026.7-26 (CRAN) still uses modified Newton. rms 8.0-0 and 8.2-0 add step-halving refinements: a -2LL tolerance of eps/10 and halving when the linear predictor changes by a large amount. Its Levenberg-Marquardt option is claimed to converge better with large offsets, a robustness alternative rather than a speedup at EDI's d of about 3-15. Nothing faster.

reparameterization.note: Centering and scaling is one O(np) pass. The log-increment threshold reparameterization (statsmodels OrderedModel, polr) was already rejected in catalog §2 because it destroys concavity. No new evidence.

solver-fallback-ladder.note: Trivial orchestration. The rungs run only on failure. Checked VGAM 1.1-14 NEWS, ordinal 2026.7-26 and fastglm 0.1.4: nothing changes the ladder logic.

findings.candidate: Expose the weights argument that FixedOrdinalRegression (ordinal_fixed_link_helpers.h:230) already has through the probit and cloglog C++ wrappers, the same way fast_ordinal_regression_weighted_cpp does for logit. Fit each draw with EDI's C++ Newton, warm-started from the full-data fit. This gives the same weighted cumulative-link MLE, which is concave for probit and cloglog. Cauchit is nonconcave and should keep a multistart or polr check. Mind the cloglog sign convention (eta_sign=+1) when mapping coefficients.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not measured for EDI. Harrell's benchmark (fharrell.com/post/mle, rms 7.0, n=100,000, 10 intercepts, p=5): MASS::polr 2.40 s, optim BFGS 0.391 s, compiled Newton-Raphson 0.084 s, about 28x faster than polr. At EDI's smaller n, polr's fixed R overhead (model.frame, glm.fit start) dominates even more.
findings.suggested_action: Prototype: add weights to fast_ordinal_{probit,cloglog}_regression_cpp, route weighted_ordinal_bootstrap_surrogate_fit for probit and cloglog through them with Newton and a warm start, and A/B against polr for coefficient agreement and wall-clock time on EDI's bootstrap fixtures.

findings.candidate: Damped Newton on the analytic observed Hessian, which is already implemented as optimization_alg='newton_raphson'. This is the catalog's Prototype (v1.0.5 algorithm-audit TODO-1); this run adds source evidence that quantifies the gain.
findings.claimed_speedup: From Harrell's rms 7.0 comparison (ordinal, n=100k, 10 intercepts, p=5): Newton-Raphson 0.084 s against optim BFGS 0.391 s, about 4.7x. The post also reports that BFGS ends with a large residual gradient when tight absolute convergence is needed. That benchmark is dense BFGS, not L-BFGS, at larger n than EDI's.
findings.suggested_action: Use this evidence to move v1.0.5 algorithm-audit TODO-1 (Newton default for concave ordinal fits) forward. Run the A/B harness at EDI's sizes.

findings.candidate: Use the exact-width cell differences from rms orm_links.f90 celldiff (reworked in rms 8.2-0, 2026-10-22). Logistic: 2 sinh(dl/2) sqrt(f1 f2). Cloglog: g2 * (-expm1(-t2 * expm1(dl))). Cauchit: atan2(dl, 1 + x1 x2)/pi. Probit: difference the smaller-valued tail (Phi-bar when x2 > 0). The top and bottom categories use the complementary CDF through argument flipping.
findings.claimed_speedup: None. This is a robustness and accuracy improvement at the same cost: O(1) per observation, a few extra transcendental calls.
findings.suggested_action: Investigate: add a tail-accurate cell-probability helper per link in ordinal_fixed_link_helpers.h, and test it against high-precision references for extreme eta. This upgrades the catalog §2 incidental note on cancellation, using the rms 8.2-0 rework as evidence.

findings.candidate: fastglm::fastglm_ordinal(nonparallel=) (fastglm >= 0.1.3, CRAN 0.1.4 dated 2026-11-11). It is a compiled C++ PPO maximum-likelihood fit (logit, probit, cloglog) using observed-information Newton steps, with a block factorization when there are many categories.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified: the NEWS and the ordinal vignette give no timings against vglm, clm or polr.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look, as in the previous run: A/B fastglm_ordinal(nonparallel=) against vglm on EDI's PPO fixtures for agreement, improper-fit handling and wall-clock time. Check fractional weights.

findings.candidate: The cumulative cloglog log-likelihood is concave in (alpha, beta), because the extreme-value density is log-concave (Pratt 1981, as stated in Kosmidis). The MLE is therefore unique, and restarts only repair non-convergence. Gate the restarts on a failed convergence certificate (gradient norm plus a positive-definite Hessian, or the Newton decrement), or replace them with a damped-Newton polish.
findings.claimed_speedup: No source quantifies it. From the code structure, up to 4 fewer fits per call when the certificate passes. This is theoretical, not measured.
findings.suggested_action: As in the previous run: gate the cloglog restarts on a convergence certificate, or replace them with a Newton polish, then A/B on the null-refit multistart cases.
