cholesky-ldlt.note: At p<30 the LDLT factorization costs microseconds. Eigen's own benchmark puts LDLT at 1.3-1.5x LLT (8x8 and 100x100), and catalog O2 already weighed LLT vs LDLT, so no change there. The one new constant-factor win is in a hot resampling loop: compute_rand_bootstrap_ols_parallel_cpp forms M'M with a full GEMM (M.transpose()*M) in every replicate, and that Gram build dominates at n>>p. A symmetric rank-k update (Eigen selfadjointView().rankUpdate, or the existing symmetric_crossprod/dsyrk) computes only one triangle. See finding 1. Batched/compact SIMD Cholesky across replicates (MKL mkl_?potrf_compact; Lemaitre & Lacassagne) speeds up only the p^3 part, which is not the bottleneck here, and MKL is not an open GPL-compatible dependency. Diagonal-of-inverse via a solve against e_j is already optimal for a single entry. A dense selected inversion gives no saving over O(p^3).

eigen-pseudo-inverse.note: It runs only as a fallback (covariance_from_information after LDLT fails) or where the null-space eigenvectors are needed (fast_zinb identified_pseudo_inverse_free_information), so it needs a spectral decomposition. CompleteOrthogonalDecomposition is ~4x faster than SVD at 8x8 (Eigen benchmark), but it does not give the eigenvector loadings and would change the truncation semantics, which is an estimator change on rank-deficient information. At p<30, SelfAdjointEigenSolver costs microseconds.

gauss-jordan-elimination.note: The faster option (LLT whitening once, then Euclidean distances: O(np^2+n^2p) instead of the O(n^2p^2) per-pair S^-1 matvec in distance_matrix_mahal_cpp) is already Adopt in catalog P1 / TODO 1, so it is not re-reported. Searches found nothing beyond that: Gauss-Jordan and Cholesky inversion are both O(p^3), and Cholesky has the better constant for SPD.

lu-decomposition.note: In invert_free_information, FullPivLU followed by information.inverse() (a second, partial-pivot LU) is already tracked in v1.1.0 TODO-155 and kept for bit-compatibility. On SPD information, LLT/LDLT would be ~1.5-2x faster at 8x8 (FullPivLU x1.9 vs LLT in the Eigen benchmark), but only at the O(p^3) level, which the O(np^2) Hessian build dominates. The LU log-determinant in evaluate_penalized_neg_loglik_at could be 2*sum(log diag(L)) from LLT, but the function has no caller and its sign issue (Investigate) matters more.

qr-decomposition.note: Column-pivoted Householder QR is still the standard rank revealer at these sizes. The newer rank revealers do not fit EDI. Randomized CPQR/HQRRP (Duersch & Gu; RandLAPACK, arXiv 2507.00976) target large matrices and are RNG-dependent. Local-max-volume pivoting (arXiv 2405.04330) costs up to 2x CPQR. Pivoted Cholesky (dpstrf) is cheaper but squares the conditioning. QR updating (Bernardi, Busatto & Cattelan arXiv 2412.05905, v3 2026; CRAN fastQR 1.1.5, 2026-11-10, GPL>=2) is the reference implementation for options already rejected or tracked: catalog O11 (incremental column-append QR for qr_reduce_preserve_cols_cpp) and kk14_incremental_covariance.md (per-arrival rebuild). It is new evidence, but it does not overturn the keep-set flip risk the catalog recorded. The per-draw R loop in compute_rand_bootstrap_ci_affine_coefs and the double factorization in drop_linearly_dependent_cols are already tracked as implementation-level work.

schur-complement.note: score_test_from_score_information forms the full covariance_from_information(I_nn) and then a matvec. One LDLT of I_nn solved against I_n,psi (or a block LDLT/Cholesky of the whole I, where the trailing block is the Schur complement, per Higham 2023) avoids the explicit inverse. This is already noted in the inventory verdict and in v1.1.0 TODO-155, and it is a constant factor at p<30. Nothing new found.

sherman-morrison.note: The per-group closed form in fast_gaussian_lmm neg_ll_and_grad is already O(n). Nothing is faster. The finding is about robustness: W_g = Q_g - (v_b/a_g) S_g^2 is a difference of two large quantities and loses about log10(1+v_b/v_e) digits when v_b>>v_e. The algebraically equal form SSW_g + (v_e/a_g) S_g^2/m_g has no subtraction. See finding 2. lme4's general sparse-Cholesky machinery is slower for this compound-symmetry case.

findings.candidate: Form only one triangle with a symmetric rank-k update: `MtM.setZero(); MtM.selfadjointView<Eigen::Lower>().rankUpdate(M.transpose());` and pass the selfadjoint view to LDLT. This is Eigen's SYRK path; only the meaningful triangle is updated. Inside the OpenMP region, prefer Eigen's rankUpdate over the BLAS-backed symmetric_crossprod (cblas_dsyrk) to avoid nested multithreaded BLAS. Optionally accumulate MtM row by row while M is filled, so the n x p matrix is never stored.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by a source. Theoretical: about half the flops of the dominant Gram build (n p(p+1)/2 vs n p^2 multiply-adds), so up to ~2x on that term per replicate.
findings.suggested_action: Swap the Gram build for selfadjointView().rankUpdate in compute_rand_bootstrap_ols_parallel_cpp. Benchmark paired ABBA at typical n (100-1000) and p (3-20), and check results match to 1e-12.

findings.candidate: Use the algebraically identical form W_g = SSW_g + (v_e/a_g) * S_g^2/m_g, where SSW_g = sum (r - rbar_g)^2 is computed by a two-pass or Welford pass over the group. Both terms are nonnegative, so there is no cancellation. The cost is the same O(n) (one more pass over a small group, or Welford in the same pass).
findings.claimed_speedup: none (robustness finding, same O(n) cost)
findings.suggested_action: Add a unit test with v_b/v_e = 1e8 and singleton groups that compares W against long-double or MPFR. If it shows error above 1e-8 relative, switch to the centred form in neg_ll_and_grad and the matching Hessian code.

linear-scan.note: Trivial. which_cols_vary_cpp compares each column against row 0 and exits early, O(np) in the worst case, which is the cost of reading the input. It still has no R caller outside RcppExports. No commits since the 2026-11-16 result, and the problem-level searches found nothing new.

pairwise-correlation-filter.note: Previous finding stands: the repeat loop in drop_highly_correlated_cols always stops after round 2, so the second cor() call is redundant. New this run, from reading the callers: five call sites run drop_highly_correlated_cols on the SAME matrix for each rung of a threshold ladder. These are cox_design_candidates (12 thresholds), KK strat Cox (12), KK rank-regression IVWC (12), the KK GEE candidates (12) and the Weibull frailty fit (3). Constant-column removal and the pairwise correlations do not depend on the threshold, so one cor() per call can serve every rung, with an identical keep-set at each rung. That is 1 cor instead of up to 24 per call, and it runs per replicate on BB/bootstrap paths. Rival tools fetched this run add nothing faster for a fixed rule. caret 7.1-0 (2026-11-15) did not change findCorrelation. corrselect 3.3.0 uses exact clique enumeration, a different keep-set. usdm vifcor is VIF-based, also a different keep-set. coop::pcor (BLAS crossprod) speeds up the cor kernel itself, but its gain needs large p and a tuned BLAS.

qr-decomposition.note:
Researched in dense-linear-algebra. The reason to look here anyway is how this problem uses it: qr_reduce_preserve_cols_cpp does a fresh ColPivHouseholderQR for every required and every candidate column, O(n p^3). The previous finding still stands and I re-confirmed it this run. LAPACK DGEQP3 'leading' JPVT columns (fetched netlib page) force the required columns first in ONE pivoted QR, though DGEQP3 does not report rank, so a threshold on |R_kk| is needed. Column-append QR updating (Hammarling & Lucas, MIMS EPrint 1192, fetched) is 'much faster' than refactoring. New this run: the fastQR CRAN package (1.1.5, 2026-11-10, GPL>=2) provides column add/delete QR updates usable from R/C++. UpdatableQRFactorizations.jl (MIT) reports add_column! about 30x cheaper than a fresh qr at n=1000, m=128. 2025-2026 column-subset-selection preprints (arXiv 2503.18496, 2509.03198, 2604.14418) target wide n<

>p designs. This is the existing Prototype-lite TODO-6 (v1.0.5 catalog §1 item 6).

streaming-moments.note: Trivial. scale_columns_cpp computes the mean and SD with two passes, O(np) and memory-bound. arXiv 2410.21922 (seen again this run) confirms that two-pass is more accurate than Welford at large offsets, and a one-pass sum-of-squares formula cancels catastrophically. The function has no R caller. Nothing new since 2026-11-16.

findings.candidate: Add a helper, e.g. drop_highly_correlated_cols_ladder(M, thresholds), that removes constant columns once and computes R = cor(M) once. For each threshold t, it takes pairs = which(abs(R) > t, upper triangle), drops unique(pairs[,2]) and returns the kept js. That is exactly what the current function returns at each t. It holds because each Pearson r_ij uses only columns i and j, stats::cor computes each pair from per-column quantities, constant-column removal does not depend on t, and the previous finding showed round 2 never fires. Remove the repeat loop in the single-threshold function as well (previous finding).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. By the argument above, the correlation work per call drops from up to 24 cor() calls (12 rungs × 2 rounds) to 1, and from 6 to 1 for the 3-rung frailty ladder. The downstream QR and fit per candidate are unchanged, so the end-to-end gain depends on how cor cost compares with the fits.
findings.suggested_action: Implement a single-cor threshold-ladder helper and use it at the five ladder call sites. Combine it with the catalog §10/§11 incidental notes to cache the candidates per call, since the predictors do not depend on the bootstrap weights. Gate on a test that the per-rung keep-sets are identical to the current function's across the test corpus.

findings.candidate: Use a single column-pivoted QR with the required columns forced to the front (LAPACK DGEQP3 JPVT 'leading columns'), with rank taken from a |R_kk| threshold. Or keep the greedy order and append columns with O(np) QR updates instead of refactoring (Hammarling & Lucas; fastQR on CRAN provides add/delete-column updates under GPL>=2).
findings.claimed_speedup: Hammarling & Lucas say updating is 'much faster' than refactoring, with no number given. The UpdatableQRFactorizations.jl README benchmarks add_column! at 0.000635 s against a stdlib qr at 0.0069 s (n=1000, m=128), about 10x per added column. O(n p^3) → O(n p^2) is theoretical. Not quantified at EDI's p.
findings.suggested_action: Keep as the existing Prototype-lite (v1.0.5 catalog §1 item 6). Prototype it with column-append updates, which keeps the current greedy keep-set semantics, and gate on keep-set equality across the test corpus.

clopper-pearson-interval.note: Closed form: two qbeta calls, O(1); nothing can be faster. This run checked binom 1.1-2 (2026-07-07), PropCIs, BlakerCI and exactci 1.4-5, plus a Monte Carlo band search. None offers a faster CP computation; BlakerCI and exactci change the interval (a different estimator), not its speed. The minlike-p vs central-CI mismatch (Fay 2010, R Journal) is a coherence issue that is already recorded (catalog §6 incidental 14), not a speed issue.

exact-binomial-test.note: Re-checked R trunk binom.test (fetched this run): .binom_test_two_sided_pval_minlike has an O(log n) bisection path ('Contributed by Ravi Varadhan', bisect = n >= 1234) and uses pbinom tails. EDI's binom_two_sided_pval (src/zhang_exact_speedups.cpp:22) still sums exp(dbinom) over all n+1 outcomes. The previous low-priority finding stands unchanged; it matters only inside the Zhang CI bisection at large d. The sign test is closed form; its weighted-path O(nm) which() loop is the recorded incidental. DiscreteTests 0.5.3 (2026-11-02) adds sign_test_pv (0.4.0) and is vectorised, but its NEWS reports no speed changes for the binomial/McNemar tests. Nothing faster than O(log n).

noncentral-hypergeometric-enumeration.note: Re-fetched R trunk fisher.test.R: pval.only = TRUE (R-devel NEWS 2026-05-27) skips the CMLE and the CI uniroots. EDI's pval_exact_fisher still calls the full fisher.test with the default conf.int = TRUE for every delta_0. The previous finding stands, with a version-safe addition: conf.int = FALSE already exists in old R (Ripley's 2005 r-help advice) and drops both CI uniroots. Exact CMH: mantelhaen.test (fetched) computes the central convolution once in C (C_d2x2xk); each noncentral evaluation is an O(S) reweight, so nothing faster is needed. Barrett 2017 (Bernoulli devolution, doi 10.1080/03610926.2014.990101) and Kou & Ying (Bernoulli convolution) are simpler reformulations, not faster. Network/FFT methods were already rejected on accuracy. No 2025-2026 arXiv work on a faster 2x2 noncentral hypergeometric computation turned up.

findings.candidate: For p-value-only calls: (a) call EDI's existing zhang_exact_fisher_pval_cpp(n11, n10, n01, n00, delta_0), which uses the same minlike rule with relative tolerance 1e-7 in log space; or (b) the version-safe minimal change: pass conf.int = FALSE to fisher.test, which drops both CI uniroots in every supported R version; or (c) once EDI's minimum R includes it, use fisher.test(..., pval.only = TRUE), new in R-devel, which also skips the CMLE.
findings.claimed_speedup: R-devel NEWS (2026-05-27) says pval.only gives 'substantial speed gains in the case of large counts' but gives no number. By construction it removes the ~3 uniroot searches (tens of O(S) pmf passes) per p-value call. Not measured.
findings.suggested_action: Low priority. closed-form.note: Trivial. build_log_factorials and build_log_choose_table each make a single O(n) pass of cumulative log sums, built once per test, so nothing faster exists. No code commits since 2026-11-16.

exhaustive-enumeration.note: Composition DFS (recurse_jt_distribution) is still exponential in K. Since 2026-11-16, jt_exact_leaf_count_exceeds_limit refuses exact inference above 1e6 allocations, so exact JT p-values are unavailable for 0-10 scales. The already-Adopted polynomial DP (catalog §6 TODO 1) remains the main fix. New this run is a refinement the catalog's options table does not list. Since EDI needs only the two tail masses P(2U<=obs) and P(2U>=obs), not the full PMF, a state (level, treated_so_far, partial 2U) can be retired early. If its reachable range [partial+min_rest, partial+max_rest] lies entirely on one side of obs, its whole mass goes to that tail in closed form. This is the Cheung-Klotz (1997) linked-list / twoUmin-twoUmax bound used in golang.org/x/perf udist.go (BSD-3), and the shortest/longest-path idea of the Mehta-Patel network algorithm. Other methods checked: Sills 2024 q-series polynomial (equivalent to the generating-function DP, no speed claim); EDISON-WMW (a hash DP, slower than a level-count DP); NXV 2026 (a different, model-weighted estimator); Pagano-Tritchler FFT (already rejected for round-off). None beats the DP.

findings.candidate: Implement the already-Adopted level DP over (level k, treated_so_far) -> distribution of partial 2U, but compute only the two tail masses. Precompute for each (k, remaining treated r) the min and max achievable remaining 2U contribution, filled level by level with a greedy or DP. Any node whose full reachable 2U interval lies at or below obs, or at or above obs, has its whole mass added to that tail in closed form: the product of log-choose weights times C(n_rest, r)/C(n, n_T). The node is not expanded. This is Cheung & Klotz (1997) with Klotz's twoUmin/twoUmax bounds, as coded in golang.org/x/perf internal/stats/udist.go, and the network-algorithm tail-pruning idea (Mehta-Patel family). With exact polynomial cost, the 1e6-allocation guard could be replaced by a cell-count guard sized for the DP.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. udist.go notes only that its map-based version spends ~60% of time in hashing, and that slices could roughly double the speed. Theory: the polynomial DP removes the exponential blow-up (catalog: 2.8e12 leaves -> ~4e8 cell updates at K=11, n=200). Tail pruning then cuts the number of expanded partial-2U values per node to the band compatible with obs, which is a large saving when obs is in the tail (small p-values) and little when obs is near the center.
findings.suggested_action: Fold this into the catalog §6 TODO 1 (JT exact null -> polynomial DP), as the 'tail-only with reachable-range bounds' variant. Validate against brute-force enumeration at n<=12 and against the current kernel to 1e-12. Use udist.go (BSD-3, attribution) as a reference implementation or test oracle for tied Mann-Whitney CDFs. Replace the 1e6-allocation refusal with a DP-cell budget.

asymptotic-series-recurrence.note: Rechecked Boost digamma (fetched): it uses a rational approximation on [1,2] and shifts down from [2,10] to reach it, so it does at least as many recurrence steps as EDI's upward shift to x>=8. It is more accurate (<1 eps) but has no timing data. The arXiv listing for 2021-2026 has no fast double-precision digamma/trigamma method; 2111.07686 and 2109.08392 target arbitrary precision. In the NB fits, digamma and trigamma run only once per distinct y per iteration (m_digamma_yptheta tables in fast_negbin_regression.cpp), so they are off the O(n) hot path. A cumulative recurrence over consecutive integer y (ψ(y+1+θ)=ψ(y+θ)+1/(y+θ)) would save little and adds rounding drift, so it is not reported. No faster acceptable option.

closed-form.note: Trivial (O(1) closed form). lgamma(y+1) is already cached per distinct y (m_lgamma_y1), which is the log-factorial lookup idea. The NB fit hot loop calls std::lgamma rather than fast_lgamma for lgamma(y+θ) and lgamma(θ), but only once per distinct y, so the cost is negligible. R 4.5.1 NEWS fixes dnbinom/bd0 at extreme arguments. That is accuracy, matching the existing v1.0.5 TODO-8 near-Poisson item, not speed.

continued-fraction-lentz.note: The previous finding still stands. Every call site passes an integer df (lrt_ci_newton.cpp:53 with df=1; _helper_functions.h:115/162/194), so a = df/2 is an integer or half-integer. DLMF 8.4.10/8.4.14 (re-fetched) give exact finite sums; df=1 reduces to erfc(√(x/2)), and fast_erfc.h already exists. Boost (re-fetched) uses these sums for a<30, calling them 'more stable and more efficient' than the continued fraction, and reports 0 eps on its integer/half-integer tests against 138 eps max for Rmath. The rsx paper (arXiv 2606.06434, 2026) also skips the general regularized-gamma call when df is known. Temme uniform asymptotics (Gil–Segura–Temme arXiv 1306.1754) only matters for large a≈x, which never occurs at EDI's df.

lanczos-stirling.note: No new double-precision lgamma method since the last run. CORE-MATH/glibc and LLVM libc work in 2024–2026 is correctly rounded binary32/half precision; binary64 is a hard-to-round-cases research note. Lanczos g=7 with 9 terms plus a 7-term Stirling series for x>=8 is already minimal O(1). TFP's x>=8 Stirling threshold matches EDI's. The SLEEF and VDT pages found give no lgamma timing. An accuracy aside, as last time: fast_lbeta cancels at large a,b, and TFP log_gamma_difference (Stirling-correction cancellation, Apache-2.0) is a reference for an accurate version. Nothing faster.

power-series.note: This is the x<a+1 branch of fast_gammaq. For integer and half-integer a, which covers every EDI call, the same DLMF finite sums replace this branch too: for df=1, x<1.5 currently takes the series path and computes 1−P plus an lgamma/exp prefactor. The finding now lists this method explicitly; the previous result marked it faster_option_found but its finding named only continued-fraction-lentz. For general a, nothing faster than the standard series was found.

findings.candidate: Add a fast path for integer or half-integer a = df/2 using the exact finite sums: DLMF 8.4.10, Q(n+1,x)=e^{-x}Σ_{k≤n}x^k/k!, and DLMF 8.4.14, Q(n+½,z²)=erfc(z)+e^{-z²}/√π·Σ_{k=1}^{n} z^{2k−1}/(½)_k. df=1 becomes fast_erfc(√(T/2)) and df=2 becomes exp(−T/2). Keep the series/CF path for non-integer a and for a≥30, as Boost does.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. Boost.Math says these sums are 'more stable and more efficient than the continued fraction alternative' for a<30 but gives no timing; its accuracy table reports 0 eps on integer/half-integer cases against Rmath's 138 eps max. For df=1 the change swaps an iterative loop plus lgamma/log/exp for one rational erfc. End-to-end gain is likely negligible because each p-value follows a model refit; the main benefit is accuracy.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look, low priority (unchanged from last run). Add the df=1 → fast_erfc(√(T/2)) and df=2 → exp(−T/2) special cases, then the general integer/half-integer finite sums for a<30. Validate against R::pchisq(lower=FALSE) for df ∈ {1..60} and T ∈ [1e-8, 1e3]. Can be folded into the row-O accuracy TODO.

golub-welsch.note: No code commits since the last research (code_commits_since is empty; the GH rule in _glmm_engine.h:32 and its copies in fast_poisson_glmm.cpp:47, fast_logistic_glmm.cpp, fast_clogit_plus_glmm.cpp, fast_hurdle_poisson_glmm.cpp and fast_weibull_frailty.cpp are unchanged). The previous finding still stands: cache and dedupe (catalog T2, TODO-1). Its cheaper uncached path is Eigen computeFromTridiagonal, or eigenvalues only (Eigen documents about 4n³/3 against 9n³ for compute() with eigenvectors). O(n) methods do not pay off at n_gh = 7–60: Townsend–Trogdon–Olver, the Glaser–Liu–Rokhlin method (GLR) and the new Gil–Segura–Temme (SISC, 2025) and modified-Halley (arXiv 2603.17448) iterative methods. FastGaussQuadrature.jl uses Golub–Welsch for n ≤ 20 and recurrence plus Newton for 21–200. SciPy uses eigenvalues plus Newton for n ≤ 150. Update: the literature says Golub–Welsch weights carry only absolute accuracy, so small tail weights lose relative accuracy (Gil–Segura–Temme give an n = 30 Laguerre example). EDI takes log() of eigenvector-derived weights at n_gh = 60 (non-adaptive Poisson GLMM), so its tail log-weights may be inaccurate. SciPy and NumPy avoid this: eigenvalues, one Newton polish, then weights from 1/(H_{n-1}·H_n') with log normalisation. That is O(n²) after the eigenvalues and needs no eigenvectors. Filed as a combined accuracy/speed finding. lme4 2.0-6 (2026-07-16) symmetrizes its nodes and weights; that point is unchanged.

findings.candidate: Build one shared, cached rule (TODO-1, already Adopt), and build it the SciPy/NumPy way. Take nodes as eigenvalues only of the tridiagonal Jacobi matrix (computeFromTridiagonal with EigenvaluesOnly, or compute(J, EigenvaluesOnly)), apply one Newton step on H_n, and compute weights from the closed form w_k ∝ 1/(H_{n-1}(x_k)·H_n'(x_k)), using normalised Hermite recurrences in log space and normalised to sum 1. Then symmetrise nodes and weights as lme4 2.0-6 does.
findings.claimed_speedup: The rule is built once per fit, so the speed gain is small. For the eigensolve, Eigen documents about 4n³/3 without eigenvectors against about 9n³ with them (≈6.7×), and computeFromTridiagonal skips the reduction as well. The O(n²) Newton/weight pass is cheaper still. Neither source benchmarks this end to end, so the speedup is not quantified. The main gain is accuracy: tail log-weights keep relative accuracy, while Golub–Welsch weights from eigenvector components carry only absolute accuracy, so the smallest weights lose relative accuracy (Gil–Segura–Temme, arXiv 2509.16716). This matters for n_gh = 60, where the outer weights are far below machine epsilon relative to the largest.
findings.suggested_action: When doing TODO-1 (a single cached shared GH rule, deduping all 6 copies), build it from eigenvalues only plus a Newton polish, and take log-weights from the recurrence formula, not from log(v0²). Symmetrise the rule. As a check, compare the log-weights at n = 60 and 100 against a high-precision reference (e.g. Gil–Segura–Temme GHi, or mpmath) before and after the change.

analytic-derivatives.note: The analytic observed information is computed once per fit at O(n·p²), the same cost as forming XᵀWX, so it is optimal. If the Gram precompute is adopted, the Hessian can be read off the same blocks at O(p²), but the total cost is unchanged. TMB/AD (mmrm, glmmTMB) would only add overhead.

closed-form.note: Trivial: an O(1) stack-allocated 2×2 inverse. Nothing is faster.

generalized-least-squares.note: A single GLS solve at fixed VC (the estimate-only replicate path) is O(n·p²+p³). Forming XᵀV⁻¹X is unavoidable once per new X/weights, so nothing is cheaper for one solve. mmrm (Apache-2.0, TMB) does the same whitening-plus-Cholesky GLS per θ. The Wansbeek–Kapteyn closed-form V⁻¹ for incomplete panels is the same quasi-demeaning EDI already uses. Re-checked lme4 2.1-0 (2026-10-23) and glmmTMB 1.1.15: no new LMM algorithm.

laplace-approximation-tmb.note: Fallback only. Laplace and INLA's inner step are exact for a Gaussian LMM, so this method changes no estimate. The glmmTMB 1.1.14/1.1.15 NEWS lists no optimizer speedup (the RTMB back-end is described as speed parity). The FBMS paper (arXiv 2509.00753) reports RTMB slower than lmer in its workflow. The C++ closed-form path remains the fast path.

lbfgs.note: Joint L-BFGS over (β, log σ_e, log σ_b) re-reads all n rows on every NLL+gradient call (O(n·p) × 20–100 evaluations). Clusters have size 1 or 2 and the case weights are per group, so the likelihood depends on the data only through three weighted Gram blocks (singletons' Σw[x y]ᵀ[x y], pairs' Σw[x y]ᵀ[x y], and pairs' Σw s s ᵀ where s is the within-pair sum of [x y]). After a single O(n·p²) pass, each NLL/gradient (or each profiled-λ evaluation) costs O(p²)–O(p³), independent of n. In `fit_null` (CI inversion and parametric bootstrap, inference_continuous_KK_glmm.R:383/:526) X and y are fixed across the δ grid, so a single precompute serves every constrained refit. This complements the already recorded Prototype (profiled 1-D Brent, catalog T7 / v1.0.5 TODO-3) and does not replace it. No newer 1-D random-intercept algorithm was found in lme4 2.0-6/2.1-0 NEWS, glmmTMB 1.1.14/1.1.15 NEWS, mmrm 0.3.19, or LBFGSpp.

sherman-morrison.note: The algebra itself is researched in dense-linear-algebra. How this problem uses it matters for speed: `neg_ll_and_grad` recomputes the per-group sums S_g and Q_g from residuals over all n rows on every optimizer call. Because a_g takes only two values (v_e+v_b, v_e+2v_b), ΣwQ_g and ΣwS_g² are quadratic forms in β over precomputable Grams, so per-call cost drops from O(n·p) to O(p²). The finding is shared with lbfgs.

findings.candidate: Sufficient-statistic (Gram-block) evaluation. With group sizes in {1,2} and per-group weights, the ML likelihood depends on the data only through three weighted (p+1)×(p+1) cross-product blocks of Z=[X y]: singletons Σw z zᵀ, pair rows Σw z zᵀ, and pair sums Σw s sᵀ (s = z_1+z_2). Equivalently, a sum/difference (Helmert) rotation of each pair gives three independent variance strata. Precompute these once in O(n·p²). Then ΣwQ_g and ΣwS_g² are quadratic forms in (β,−1), and each NLL+gradient costs O(p²), each profiled-λ evaluation (GLS β̂(λ) = solve of a weighted sum of the blocks) costs O(p³), and neither depends on n. For numerical stability, keep the triangular factors R_k of each stratum's [X_k y_k] (QR) rather than raw Grams, so the residual sum of squares is ‖R_k[β;−1]‖² without cancellation. In `fit_null` the blocks are invariant in δ (fixing β_T just partitions them), so one precompute serves the whole CI search.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. By operation count, a fit drops from iters·O(n·p) to O(n·p²)+iters·O(p²), roughly min(iters, n/p)-fold. For a δ-grid CI search with K constrained refits it drops from K·iters·O(n·p) to O(n·p²)+K·iters·O(p²). Pichler et al. (arXiv 2502.04990) report the sufficient-statistics advantage growing with n for random-intercept LMMs, but in a Bayesian/Stan setting, not this ML kernel.
findings.suggested_action: Fold into the v1.0.5 TODO-3 profiled-ML prototype: build the three per-stratum R factors (or Grams) once per dataset/weight vector. Evaluate the NLL and gradient (and the profiled λ objective) from them, reuse them across all `fit_null` δ values, and A/B against the current `neg_ll_and_grad` for agreement (≤1e-8 relative) and for timing at n ∈ {50, 500, 5000}, p ∈ {2, 5, 10}.

delta-method.note: Trivial: closed-form gradient times covariance, O(p²) after an O(np) gradient pass. The logistic and fractional-logit paths already use the analytic gradient (gcomp_speedups.cpp compute_gcomp_logistic_post_fit, solved against the LDLT). The FD users (marginal_estimand_delta_se/numerical_gradient_central; ordinal_gcomp_post_fit_cpp) already have the analytic gradient recorded as Adopt (v1.0.5-TODO-8, v1.0.5-TODO-5). Checked for anything new since 2026-11-16: the AD option in Margins.jl/marginaleffects (JAX) gives exact Jacobians, but at EDI's p in the tens the analytic gradient is already exact and cheaper. Nothing new.

finite-differences.note: inference_ordinal_gcomp.R compute_md_gradient makes 2(p+K−1) R→C++ calls, each O(n(p+K)). An analytic gradient would be a single O(nKp) pass, already recorded (catalog §2 v1.0.5-TODO-5, low priority), so nothing new. The fractional-logit FD fires only as a fallback. AD (Margins.jl claims 3-5x over FD; marginaleffects JAX autodiff, experimental) and complex-step/Richardson (numDeriv, pracma) are not cheaper than the already-planned analytic gradient, and the catalog already rejected complex-step. No new 2026 source changes this.

g-computation.note: The plug-in standardization is O(np), or O(n(p+K)) for PO, bounded below by reading X. The cost is dominated by the outcome-model fit. Rivals checked this run (marginaleffects 1.0.0 of 2026-09-03, stdReg2 1.0.7, risks 0.4.3, RISCA 1.0.7, drord) all use the same fit + average + delta/sandwich or bootstrap. Margins.jl (arXiv 2601.07065, Jan 2026) claims a 622x speedup over marginaleffects, but that comes from formula compilation and allocation avoidance in a general-purpose tool. EDI's C++ kernels already do a direct O(np) pass. Per-replicate refits: the linear/quadratic one-step bootstrap (Claeskens, Aerts & Molenberghs 2003) avoids iterative refits, but it approximates the replicate estimator, so it is an estimator change, and it belongs to the resampling problem (J), not here. The 2026 small-sample papers (arXiv 2605.19772, 2509.07369) concern variance accuracy and estimand, not speed (cf. Incidental 16).

sandwich-estimator.note: HC0: LDLT of XᵀWX + O(np²) meat + O(p³) inverse, the standard minimum. sandwich 3.1-2/3.1-3 NEWS (2026) has no algorithmic speedups. clubSandwich 0.7.0 CR2 and the 2025 'more efficient CR2' blog concern CR2 small-sample corrections, which EDI does not use (it uses a CR0-type cluster meat via unordered_map, O(np²)). Nothing faster at EDI sizes.

cholesky-ldlt.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. Here it is a single p x p LDLT solve per scoring iteration (QR fallback). That is O(p^3) against O(n p^2) for forming the information matrix, so the solve is never the bottleneck at EDI's sizes. The previous conclusion stands: LLT is only marginally faster and gives up robustness.

irls.note: Re-checked against what is new since 2026-11-16. (1) Pairs-plus-singletons kernel (fast_gee.cpp gee_pairs_singletons_cpp_impl): each iteration is a single O(n p^2) pass using the closed-form 2x2 V^-1, and it is warm-started from the cached beta and Fisher information (inference_mixin_kk_gee_shared.R:244-251, 493-499). That is optimal per iteration. The newest fast-GEE work targets large clusters: fastFGEE 0.2.2 (CRAN 2026-09-21) and Loewinger et al. arXiv 2506.20437 v3 (2026-06-23), both one-step functional GEE; and Lipsitz et al. 2017 one-step GEE. Their savings come from avoiding O(m^2) pair sums and cluster-sized inversions, which is irrelevant at m <= 2. Lipsitz Table 1 also shows the one-step estimate differs from the iterated one in finite samples, so adopting it would be an estimator change. geeM's speedup over geepack (RJ 2013) is about R-level overhead and does not apply to EDI's C++ kernel. geepack 1.3.13 (2025-10-14) is unchanged. (2) Ordinal LOR GEE (multgee::ordLORgee): multgee 1.9.0 (2023-09-02) is still current. The refman confirms the LOR structure is estimated from response-only marginalized tables (RC-G(1)) and that LORstr='fixed' with LORterm is accepted, so the previous caching finding stands. EDI already passes bstart warm starts.

method-of-moments.note: Closed-form O(n) pass over pair Pearson products. Nothing can be faster. The alternatives found (quasi-least squares, residual pseudo-likelihood for the ICC, Chaganty & Joe 2004) are estimator changes aimed at bias or efficiency, not speed. The phi-scaling fix (alpha = num/((N_pairs-p)*phi)) is still present in fast_gee.cpp:125-130.

findings.candidate: Cache the estimated LOR structure, keyed on (y, pairing m), and pass it back as LORstr='fixed' with LORterm (built with multgee::matrixLOR). According to the multgee reference manual, the structure comes from responses aggregated across clusters into marginalized tables, so covariates do not enter it. It is therefore unchanged across ladder rungs, and across permutation draws whenever y and m are fixed.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. It removes one association-model fit per ordLORgee call; what share of the call that is remains unknown.
findings.suggested_action: Profile one ordLORgee call at typical KK sizes to split the time between LOR estimation and Fisher scoring. If LOR estimation is a material share, prototype the cache and A/B it against current fits for coefficients identical within tolerance.

lbfgs.note: No code commits since the previous result (code_commits_since empty). optimize_likelihood_lbfgs still uses LBFGSpp with backtracking strong-Wolfe, max_linesearch 100, past=1. Checked for anything new since 2026-11-16. LBFGSpp's GitHub page lists no new releases and no performance claims. No 2025–26 paper compares the line-search choice by evaluation count. arXiv 2405.10897 reports the same number of evaluations as L-BFGS-B's Moré–Thuente search. At EDI's small p (≈2–50), full BFGS or ucminf (BFGS with trust-region-monitored line search) would not reduce evaluations in any benchmarked way. The real alternative for concave fits is Newton, already catalogued (catalog §1 TODO-7 and §2 TODO-1/2). The marqLevAlg R Journal comparison (17–18 parameters) shows L-BFGS-B taking 244–823 iterations against 6–24 for Marquardt–Levenberg on a hard joint model, with similar wall-clock. That supports the existing Newton-default items rather than a new L-BFGS change.

newton-raphson.note: The code is unchanged: FullPivLU at _helper_functions_core.h:1471, no descent-direction check, and warm_start_hessian is still (void)-ignored at :1441. The previous finding still stands: a gradient-regularized Newton step (Gratton–Jerad–Toint AN2C, arXiv 2302.10065) as the τI rule for catalog §1 TODO-9. New since the last run: (i) the same authors' arXiv 2505.04807 (DOI 10.1016/j.ejco.2026.100128) extends AN2C to local Lipschitz smoothness and reports it competitive, without numbers on the abstract page; (ii) Mishchenko's regularized Newton (SIAM J. Optim. 33(3), 2023) gives the λ=√(H‖g‖) rule global convergence; (iii) the marqLevAlg R Journal 2021 paper reports Levenberg–Marquardt-damped Newton converging in 31/35 Moré test problems and reaching the same optimum regardless of scaling where BFGS and L-BFGS-B did not. arXiv 2502.04799 and 2601.01575 target large problems (CUTEst n≥100) using CG/MINRES, which is irrelevant at EDI's dense small p. None shows a wall-clock win on well-behaved concave fits. The benefit is robustness: fewer wasted halving cascades and fewer L-BFGS hand-offs.

findings.candidate: A gradient-regularized (Levenberg–Marquardt-type) Newton step: solve (H + λ_k I) s = −g with λ_k ∝ sqrt(‖g_k‖), using the AN2C / Mishchenko rule, and add a [−λ_min(H)]_+ shift when LLT/LDLT detects indefiniteness. Factor with LLT/LDLT instead of FullPivLU. Keep step-halving and the L-BFGS fallback as the outer safety net. This gives a concrete, parameter-free τ for catalog §1 TODO-9.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified relative to EDI's loop. On 119 small OPM/CUTEst problems (2–49 variables), Gratton–Jerad–Toint (arXiv 2302.10065) report parity with trust region and AR2 in iteration-profile area (AN2CE 0.91, TR2M 0.91), not a win. In the marqLevAlg R Journal paper, LM-damped Newton took 6–24 iterations against 52–502 for BFGS and 244–823 for L-BFGS-B on a 17–18-parameter joint model, with similar wall-clock, and it converged consistently where the others depended on scaling. The expected gain is robustness: fewer wasted halving cascades (~14 evaluations each) and fewer L-BFGS hand-offs.
findings.suggested_action: When prototyping catalog §1 TODO-9, use the √‖g‖ regularization with an LLT/LDLT factorization and the indefiniteness shift. Either honour or remove warm_start_hessian. Measure halving cascades, L-BFGS hand-offs and wall-clock on NB, beta and stereotype in the A/B harness.

closed-form.note: Trivial: O(1) link cdf/pdf policies. Aside: for a probit random intercept with m_g<=2, the pair likelihood is a bivariate normal CDF with rho=sigma^2/(1+sigma^2), which is quadrature-free. This is my derivation and unsourced. It would only matter for the engine's ProbitLink users (ordinal CLMM, another problem), not the logistic/Poisson kernels here.

gauss-hermite-quadrature.note: Both previous findings still stand. No code commits since the last run, and re-reading fast_poisson_glmm.cpp confirms the target is still there: operator() :199-200 and hessian :258-259 compute exp(eta+b_k) over all n at each of the 60 nodes, and :276-283 runs one weighted_crossprod per node. The cluster-total collapse is re-reported. On AGQ: Stringer 2310.01589 is still v2 (Nov 2024) with no journal DOI. Rizopoulos 2012 is confirmed at doi 10.1016/j.csda.2011.09.007 (RePEc copy). New supporting evidence: Stringer, Bilodeau & Tang arXiv 2202.07864 (v2, Jan 2025) prove that MLEs from non-adaptive quadrature are inconsistent under weak conditions, which strengthens the accuracy case for AGQ, not the speed case. arXiv 2410.08492 (exact-MLE preprint) gives no speed comparison. The arXiv API listing has no 2025-26 paper on faster GLMM quadrature. Sparse grids and QMC only pay off in higher dimensions, not for a 1-D random intercept.

log-sum-exp.note: Trivial: O(K) per group, max-shift fused with the weights. Nothing faster.

louis-identity.note: Still stands for the Poisson GLMM Hessian only: the beta-beta block becomes one weighted crossprod with weights w*e^eta*E_g[e^b] instead of 60 per-node crossprods (fast_poisson_glmm.cpp:276-283, unchanged). The logistic and clogit+GLMM Louis Hessians are unchanged. The searches turned up nothing faster than the analytic Louis identity for GHQ observed information (Liu & Chalmers 2021 call it efficient; the R-VGAL alternative is Monte Carlo).

soft-barrier-penalty.note: Trivial, O(1). Chung et al. 2013 / blme penalties change the estimator, not the speed. No new evidence.

findings.candidate: Cluster-total (sufficient-statistic) collapse for the log link. Per group, form S_g=sum w*y, log Lambda_g=LSE(log w+eta) and A_g=sum w(y*eta-log y!). Each node term is log w_k+A_g+b_k*S_g-exp(b_k+log Lambda_g), which costs O(G*K). The beta-gradient is one GEMV X'[w(y-e^eta*E_g[e^b])]. The Louis beta-beta block is one weighted crossprod with weights w*e^eta*E_g[e^b], and the cross/E[GG'] terms come from u_g=X_g'wy, v_g=X_g'we^eta and posterior moments of e^b and b. This is the same quadrature-approximated likelihood algebraically, with only the summation order changed. The hurdle kernel already shares e^eta*e^b_k.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source; this is a derivation from the code. The n-dependent work drops from O(n*K*p) to O(n*p)+O(G*K) per evaluation. Expect roughly 3-10x on gradient+Hessian at K=60, p=5-20, G of about n/2. Must be measured.
findings.suggested_action: Add a v1.0.5 catalog section 4 Adopt item for fast_poisson_glmm.cpp (cluster-total form for operator(), hessian and the :515/:545 exports). Gate: the existing tests plus an all.equal(tol 1e-10) A/B on the R8 grid, then benchmark at n=100-1000.

findings.candidate: Adaptive GH with fewer nodes, by one of two routes. (a) The exact AQ gradient via implicit differentiation of the per-group mode, keeping L-BFGS plus one Newton polish (Stringer arXiv 2310.01589 v2, no journal DOI). (b) Pseudo-adaptive GH: nodes centred and scaled once from an initial fit and then frozen, so the cheap fixed-node analytic gradient still applies (Rizopoulos 2012, CSDA 56(3):491-501, doi 10.1016/j.csda.2011.09.007).
findings.claimed_speedup: Stringer: faster than finite-difference (GLMMadaptive) and derivative-free (lme4) approaches. The abstract does not quantify the gain; the paper's text reports about 2-4x versus those packages, not versus EDI. Rizopoulos: 'considerably faster than the standard Gauss-Hermite rule', not quantified on the abstract page. Versus EDI's 20 fixed nodes at m_g<=2, catalog T1 estimates 1.2-1.6x.
findings.suggested_action: Keep under v1.1.0 performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md TODO-153. Add arXiv 2202.07864 as the accuracy argument and the Rizopoulos DOI as the frozen-mode route. Prioritise the logistic/clogit 20-node kernels and the hurdle K=7 accuracy item (v1.0.5 catalog TODO 5); the Poisson kernel is lower priority once the cluster-total rewrite lands.

weighted-gram-accumulation.note: The previous conclusions still stand for weighted_crossprod (the col-major branch uses Eigen's vectorised dot on w∘x_j), symmetric_crossprod (DSYRK; nothing better at p ≲ 50) and the √w∘X + DSYRK / Eigen rankUpdate option, which remains Keep-tracked under performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md TODO-155. I found no new benchmark at EDI's sizes for those. The new item this run comes from reading the code: score_weighted_crossprod_colwise_assign (_helper_functions_core.h:601), the fused score + X'WX kernel on the logistic and probit IRLS hot path (fast_logistic_regression.cpp:215, fast_probit_regression.cpp:186), uses plain scalar loops `acc += xj[i]*w[i]*xk[i]` with one accumulator and no EDI_SIMD_REDUCTION. EDI builds without -ffast-math (Makevars line 6), and compilers do not reassociate an FP reduction without that permission, so these loops stay scalar and latency-bound. They also re-stream x_j, w and x_k for every one of the p(p+1)/2 pairs. Unlike weighted_crossprod's Eigen dot path, this kernel gets neither SIMD nor multiple accumulators. A register-blocked, SIMD tile kernel (as in tabmat's dense sandwich), or simply EDI_SIMD_REDUCTION or Eigen dot, would remove that. See the finding. Other checks this run: OpenBLAS 0.3.29–0.3.34 has no DSYRK speedups, but 0.3.32 (2026-03) fixed non-serialized concurrent calls into parallel SYRK, which matters for robustness if symmetric_crossprod runs inside OpenMP threads on older OpenBLAS. fastglm 0.1.4 (2026-11-11) has no cross-product changes. RcppEigen on CRAN is still 0.3.4.0.2.

findings.candidate: (a) Minimal: annotate both inner loops with EDI_SIMD_REDUCTION(+:acc,score_acc), or form w∘x_j once per j and use Eigen's dot, as the col-major weighted_crossprod already does. Eigen's packet reduction uses SIMD lanes and several accumulators. (b) Fuller: a register-blocked tile kernel like tabmat's dense sandwich (dense_helpers.hpp). It packs a k-block of rows, scales one panel by w, computes 4×4 output tiles with up to 16 SIMD FMA accumulators over the lower triangle only, and mirrors at the end. That cuts loads per FMA by about 4× and vectorises. The score X'r can be fused as an extra column. Run the k-blocks in fixed serial order (tabmat's column/row-parallel mode), not its atomic k-parallel mode, to stay deterministic.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source at EDI's sizes. The basis is mechanism, not a benchmark: SIMD width (4 doubles with AVX2, 8 with AVX-512) plus multiple accumulators that break the add-latency chain. glum/tabmat describe their dense sandwich as 'parallelized, cache-friendly, SIMD-optimized' but publish no standalone dense number.
findings.suggested_action: Fold into performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md TODO-155 as a cheap first step before the √w∘X + DSYRK option. Check vectorisation with -fopt-info-vec-missed on _helper_functions_core.h users (targeted compile of fast_logistic_regression.cpp only). Then microbenchmark score_weighted_crossprod_colwise_assign against an EDI_SIMD_REDUCTION version and an Eigen-dot version at n ∈ {100, 500, 2000}, p ∈ {2, 5, 10, 20}, and confirm the β agreement tolerance in the logistic and probit tests.

best-improvement-swap.note: I checked for anything new since the 2026-11-16 seed. No code commits touched these files. The best-improvement rule defines the design's allocation distribution: first-improvement, Kernighan-Lin, tabu and simulated annealing reach different local optima, so they are design changes (the Aloise et al. 2025 EJOR study, DOI 10.1016/j.ejor.2025.04.019, finds no general winner even on speed). The newer allocation literature (pair-switching rerandomization arXiv 2103.13051; Metropolis-Hastings PSRSRR arXiv 2602.07613; Langevin-gradient rerandomization doi 10.1007/s11222-026-11029-x; discrepancy designs arXiv 2608.18057) proposes different designs, not a faster exact best-swap search. GreedyExperimentalDesign 1.6.1 (CRAN, 2026-04-30) adds a GPU full-greedy loop (wgpu, apparently 4-byte float argmin) with an O(p) incremental update. EDI already has that incremental update, and a GPU float path would break EDI's accuracy, determinism and dependency constraints. The exact speedups that keep the same optimum (Gram G = M'M for O(1) per pair, routing Mahalanobis through the pruned D engine with P = 4G) are already tracked (catalog §8 P2, small_kernel_hoists_batch.md Item A). The pruned scan's per-pair delta A_i + B_j − 2P_ij is a biased bichromatic MIPS / closest-pair problem; no exact subquadratic method pays off at n in the hundreds to low thousands. From reading the code, not the literature, and still open: in DOptimalPruneObjective the prune offset is 2·max_P (global). A per-treated-row max_j P_ij would be a tighter bound that is still valid.

fisher-yates-shuffle.note: The previous finding still stands: batched ranged random integer generation (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, SP&E 55(1), DOI 10.1002/spe.3369; MIT reference code at lemire/batched_random). I found no newer shuffle algorithm. dqrng's vignette confirms that partial Fisher-Yates is preferred and Floyd's algorithm is not faster. Randompack (arXiv 2605.05099, MIT, May 2026) is a portable reproducible RNG library with permutations, relevant to the cross-platform determinism goal rather than speed. Within this problem the shuffle is O(n) once per draw, negligible next to the O(n_T n_C) per-round swap search, so the win here is marginal; it is low confidence.

findings.candidate: Batched ranged random integer generation (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire): several unbiased bounded indices from one random word, so fewer RNG calls per shuffle. Alternatively, a partial shuffle of only min(n_T, n−n_T) positions.
findings.claimed_speedup: The paper reports 1.4–2.6× on whole shuffles with 64-bit PCG/Lehmer generators. It was not measured with MT19937 or 32-bit words. In this problem the shuffle is a negligible share of the per-draw cost, since the swap search dominates, so the end-to-end gain is not quantified and is likely near 1×.
findings.suggested_action: Keep it as a recorded option in catalog P2. Adopt it only together with another planned RNG-stream change, so seeds are refreshed once. Do not prioritise it for this problem.

hash-map-grouping.note: Trivial (expected O(n), one pass). Checked against the 2026 sources: the hash-vs-sort study (arXiv 2411.13245) finds hashing is the better choice for small inputs and few groups, which is EDI's setting. absl/Swiss-table flat maps beat std::unordered_map by a constant factor, but sample_mode, find_discordant_pairs and compute_survival_strata_ids run once per call, outside any replicate loop, so the gain is immaterial. collapse::fmode uses the same hash-plus-first-tie algorithm. No code commits since the last research.

linear-scan.note: compute_matching_grouping_cpp is O(n), the lower bound, so nothing to change there. Correction to the previous note, which said kk_pair_and_reservoir_bootstrap_weights runs 'once per call, outside the replicate loop': the code shows it is called from compute_estimate_with_bootstrap_weights (inference_mixin_kk_passthrough.R:222,233) and from fit_weighted_combined in the KK OLS, robust, quantile, cond-logit and compound classes, all with per-replicate row_weights. Its O(n·#pairs) = O(n²) vapply/which therefore runs in every bootstrap replicate. The same is true of build_combined_cpoisson_data (catalog: per replicate, Incidental). A hashing rowsum/tapply pass makes both O(n). See the finding.

sort-and-sweep.note: These steps are one-time O(n log n) layout and level coding (GLMM data constructors, init_levels, get_levels/map_y_to_1K), dominated by the fits that follow. libc++ added an LSD-radix path to std::stable_sort in 2025, but it applies only to the default comparator on arithmetic types, not to EDI's index sort with a custom comparator, and R builds usually use libstdc++. A counting sort on dense group ids (O(n+G)) remains immaterial, as the catalog already records. collapse qF/radixorder use the same sort-or-hash choice. Nothing new since 2026-11-16.

findings.candidate: A single grouped pass. Take `pw = rowsum(row_weights[ok], m_vec[ok]) / rowsum(rep(1, sum(ok)), m_vec[ok])` with ok = pair rows with non-NA weight; rowsum uses hashing, and reorder=TRUE gives groups ordered by sort(unique()), the same as pair_ids. Alternatively, precompute the pair-row index once (match/split, or a cached .complete_pair_index_matrix) and index it per replicate. For build_combined_cpoisson_data, cache the pair extraction (it depends only on m, w and X_fit) instead of rebuilding it per replicate.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. Asymptotically O(n²) → O(n) per replicate, which also removes about n/2 R-level closure calls per replicate.
findings.suggested_action: Replace the vapply/which loop in kk_pair_and_reservoir_bootstrap_weights with a rowsum-based (or cached index) aggregation. Cache the pair extraction in build_combined_cpoisson_data across replicates. Test that the results equal the old ones to 1e-12.

selection-algorithm.note: Unchanged from the 2026-11-16 result (no code commits since). For n_T·n_C ≤ 4096, hl_from_groups/hl_signed_rank/median_in_place materialize the differences and run std::nth_element (introselect, O(N)); above that they hand off to sort plus value-space bisection. This search found no new head-to-head benchmark at small N. Floyd–Rivest (miniselect, BSL-1.0) still has only anecdotal or asymptotic advantages, and one analysis says it reduces to the same algorithm at small N. Any gain is a constant factor on a step dominated by materializing the differences. Rfast and matrixStats offer nothing faster for one vector.

streaming-moments.note: This method is marked trivial, but these two entries are not O(n): estimate_hl_ssq_rank_sum and estimate_hl_ssq_signed_rank loop over all O(n_T n_C) or O(m²) pairs. Exact O(n) closed forms from centered per-group moments exist and are already tracked as Adopt, low priority (catalog Incidental 5). The finding is re-reported and still stands. Newly checked: Reichel, arXiv 2511.08223 (v2, 2025-12-08), restates the linear-time scalar-sum rewrite of all-pairs squared differences. Callers are legacy IVWC only. The SE scale bug F7/I2 is separate and is about correctness.

value-space-bisection-selection.note: Unchanged. Checked for anything new since 2026-11-16: no 2025–2026 arXiv paper on selection in X+Y or sorted matrices. Searches return only Kaplan et al. 2018 (soft heaps), de Berg–Thite 2008 and Serang 2021 (top-k, not the median). DescTools NEWS shows only a C++ Monahan port (0.99.52), a two-sample version (0.99.53) and long-long indexing (0.99.54), with no benchmark against bisection. robslopes 1.1.4 (R Journal RJ-2023-012) is randomized (Matoušek), and its 10^3× speedups are measured against brute-force O(n²) code, not against an O(n·L) bisection. Monahan and Johnson–Mizoguchi selection were already rejected in the catalog (§6 options table), and no new evidence overturns that. The levers remain wilcox_hl_kernel_hoisting.md TODO-3 (tie-safe early stop) and TODO-4 (warm bracket).

walsh-average-enumeration.note: Unchanged. These are the stats::wilcox.test(conf.int) paths: exact sorted Walsh averages for m<50, otherwise a normal approximation with uniroot. Both are cheap at EDI sizes, and the point estimate already uses the C++ kernel. NAG g07eaf/g07ebf and DescTools use Monahan 1984, which the catalog already covers. npsm::hodges_lehmann.ci just wraps wilcox.test. coin 1.4-6 (2026-09-30) offers no HL estimator. The weighted HL branch was flagged as dead code last run; no change since. The open item is the SE scale (F7/I2), a correctness bug, not a speed one.

findings.candidate: Exact closed forms from per-group sums of centered data. Pairwise differences: N/(N−1)·(var_pop(T)+var_pop(C)) with N=n_T n_C. Walsh averages: the sum is (m+1)S/2 and the sum of squares is ((m+2)Q+S²)/4, with S=Σd and Q=Σd² over centered d, divided by M=m(m+1)/2. Centering also avoids the cancellation that the naive sum/sum² formula suffers.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by a source. Algebraically O(n_T n_C)→O(n_T+n_C) and O(m²)→O(m). arXiv 2511.08223 states the linear-time scalar-sum rewrite of all-pairs squared differences.
findings.suggested_action: No new decision needed. When catalog Incidental 5 (TODO 5) is picked up, replace both loops with the centered O(n) forms, and test them against the loop to 1e-12 relative, including a fixture with a large offset.

icm-npmle.note: The point fit (ic_sp: ICM + Newton) is unchanged. icenReg NEWS has no change, and no faster semiparametric-PH fitter was found. New: icsp2 0.2.0 (2026-06-22; LGPL (>= 2, < 3); Gravestock, with icenReg's author as contributor) is a fork of ic_sp with analytical derivatives. It adds vcov.ic_sp2, a profile-likelihood covariance (Murphy & van der Vaart 2000; Zeng, Mao & Lin 2016). Each profile refit is warm-started from the fitted baseline with beta fixed. It needs k + k(k+1)/2 refits ('oim' types) or k refits ('opg_fixed'), against 200 bootstrap refits. That is 2 refits for a single treatment coefficient. This catalog option was previously listed but blocked because it 'requires a profile maximiser'; icsp2 provides one. Filed as a finding: it is an SE-method change, not a point-estimate change.

turnbull-em.note: Both previous findings still stand: (1) go straight to icenReg::ic_np (EMICM in C++, weights=), and (2) stop re-solving the pooled NPMLE per draw (ictest icFIT= / wlr_trafo scores). Checked what is new since then. icenReg is still 2.0.16 (2024-01-13), and its NEWS has no new ic_np change. interval is still 1.1-1.0 (2023). arXiv/OpenAlex 2025–2026 show no faster univariate NPMLE algorithm; 2511.01103 uses ICM, and 2411.19878 is log-concave only. Two new items. First, SQUAREM (Du & Varadhan, JSS 2020, doi 10.18637/jss.v092.i07): on interval censoring it is about 17× fewer EM evaluations than EM and 'very competitive' with EM-ICM, with more variable CPU time. It is not better than ic_np's C++ EMICM, and icfit exposes no fixed-point map to wrap, so it adds no new finding. Second, longevity 1.3.1 (GPL-3, R Journal 2025, doi 10.32614/RJ-2025-034) has a C++ Turnbull EM with weights. It is plain EM, so it is a reference implementation, not a faster algorithm. The Waller et al. 2025/2026 preprint (EM + Pan ICM for left-truncated data) gives no quantified speed and covers a broader setting.

findings.candidate: Profile-likelihood covariance for beta, as in icsp2::vcov.ic_sp2 (types oim_curvature, oim_fixed or opg_fixed). The baseline is re-fitted with beta held fixed at perturbed values (profile_fit, warm-started from the fitted baseline), and the information is a finite difference of profile log-likelihoods. Either use icsp2 (LGPL, GitHub/r-universe only, not on CRAN), or port its roughly 100-line vcov/profile_fit logic around icenReg's fitter.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not benchmarked by the source. The refit count comes from the code: for k coefficients, oim needs k + k(k+1)/2 warm-started profile refits and opg needs k, against 200 cold bootstrap refits. For EDI's single treatment coefficient that is 2 refits instead of 200, so roughly 100× fewer fits, and each profile refit is cheaper because beta is fixed and the baseline is warm-started. This is theoretical, not measured.
findings.suggested_action: Add icsp2's profile-likelihood vcov to the catalog's ic_sp SE options row as an available implementation, which removes the 'requires a profile maximiser' obstacle. Prototype it with A/B against bs_samples=200 SEs on fixtures. If accepted, compute SEs with it and keep bootstrap as an option.

findings.candidate: icenReg::ic_np: EMICM in C++ (RcppEigen), with a weights= argument since 2.0.8; icenReg is already an EDI dependency. Skip the intermediate icfit(initfit='initEMICM') step. (Re-reported from the previous result; still stands. icenReg 2.0.16 has had no change since then.) SQUAREM-accelerated EM, which this run found, is an alternative. It is about 17× fewer EM evaluations and competitive with EM-ICM, but it is not better than ic_np's C++ EMICM.
findings.claimed_speedup: icenReg JSS paper, Table 1, from the previous run: ic_np 0.001 s at n=100 and 0.003 s at n=1,000, against Icens::EMICM 0.106 s and 8.3 s. The gain over interval::icfit's EM is not quantified directly. Du & Varadhan (2020) report that SQUAREM averages about 17× fewer EM evaluations than plain EM on interval censoring.
findings.suggested_action: Unchanged from the previous result: prototype icenReg::ic_np first under v1.0.5 TODO-28 (release_v1_1_0.md TODO-50), with an A/B harness on median and RMST, and deprioritize initEMICM.

findings.suggested_action: Implement within v1.0.5 TODO-11. If it slips, ship the interim icFIT= plus method='pclt' change first.

jackknife.note: [delete-one jackknife: approximate_jackknife_distribution_beta_hat_T_private / build_jackknife_deletion_draws] No commits since 2026-11-16, and EDI still has no closed-form path: the least-squares classes (average_diff, simple_mean_diff_pooled_var, continuous_lin) go through the generic refit loop. The previous finding still stands. It is the exact least-squares delete-one-unit/cluster identity β^(g) = (X'X − X_g'X_g)⁻¹(X'y − X_g'y_g) (MacKinnon, Nielsen & Webb 2023, Eq. 15; arXiv 2301.04527), now cited with its published DOI 10.1002/jae.2969. New this run: the same authors' linearized delete-one-cluster jackknife for nonlinear M-estimators, b^(g) = (J − J_g)⁻¹(s − s_g) (Econometric Reviews 2025, arXiv 2406.00650, Eq. 17–18). It reports about 40× less cost than exact CV3 in one empirical example, with tests and CIs 'usually very similar' to the exact jackknife. This is an estimator change (approximate replicates), filed as an opt-in finding. It partly overturns the catalog's reason for rejecting one-step deletion ('R6 overhead per replicate probably dominates'), because it builds no per-replicate objects at all. It still needs per-unit score and information contributions, the same obstacle the catalog records for the infinitesimal jackknife. The V-fold jackknife (arXiv 2607.22493, 2026) gives a citation for the catalog's grouped-jackknife row, which currently says [cite needed]. It is an estimator change with no new speed evidence, so it is not a finding. | [Quenouille–Tukey bias/variance: compute_jackknife_summary] Closed-form moments, O(n_units) after the replicates exist. Nothing faster can exist; I17 (unequal-unit weighting) is unchanged. | [weighted delete-one jackknife, Bayesian BCa: approximate_bayesian_jackknife_distribution_beta_hat_T] The exact closed form above also covers weighted least squares (zero weight on the deleted unit, then a rescale), and the linearized form covers weighted M-estimators. No other new 2025–2026 method was found. The serial vapply is a parallelisation item (I13), not an algorithm change.

findings.candidate: Exact closed-form delete-one-unit/cluster replicates for least-squares estimators: β^(g) = (X'X − X_g'X_g)⁻¹(X'y − X_g'y_g). The per-unit cross-products are formed once in O(n·k²), followed by G k×k solves (MacKinnon, Nielsen & Webb 2023, Eq. 15, proved via Woodbury). For a mean difference this reduces to O(n) arm-sum updates. The weighted (Bayesian-BCa) variant is the same identity with weights. Keep the refit loop for nonlinear fits.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified against naive re-estimation. The source benchmarks only against other CV3 algorithms: at N = 2^20 its jackknife formula is about 12× (k = 20) to 26× (k = 40) faster than the score method for small clusters (arXiv 2301.04527, Section 4, Figure 1). Against EDI, the saving is the entire refit loop: n_units R6 fits become O(n·k² + G·k³).
findings.suggested_action: Re-reported from the 2026-11-16 seeded result; still not implemented. Prototype an exact closed-form jackknife fast path for mean difference, OLS/Lin and WLS behind a tolerance test against the refit jackknife, and add the option to the catalog's NEW-jackknife-influence table.

findings.candidate: Linearized delete-one-unit/cluster jackknife (CV3L): from the full fit, form per-unit score s_g and information J_g contributions and their totals. The replicate shift is b^(g) = (J − J_g)⁻¹(s − s_g), so G k×k solves replace G nonlinear refits (MacKinnon, Nielsen & Webb, Econometric Reviews 2025, Eq. 17–18). This is the exact-downdate analogue of the catalog's one-step Newton row, but it builds no per-replicate objects at all. Offer it as an opt-in option for â (v1.0.6-TODO-7 area) and jackknife SE, with the exact refit staying the default.
findings.claimed_speedup: About 40× cheaper than exact CV3 in the paper's empirical (tuition-fee) example (arXiv 2406.00650v2, Section 7.2); not otherwise quantified.
findings.suggested_action: Add a CV3L row to the catalog's NEW-jackknife-influence table, citing DOI 10.1080/07474938.2025.2515161. If v1.0.6-TODO-7 adds per-unit score and information hooks, prototype the linearized jackknife on the same hooks as an opt-in option, A/B against the exact jackknife.

greenwood-variance.note: The C++ get_restricted_mean_se_for_group_at_tau does one sort plus suffix sums, O(n log n), and stays Keep. FastSurvival 2.0.0 (CRAN, 2026-11-16) uses the same Var = Σ A_i² d_i/(n_i(n_i−d_i)) single-scan form, which confirms nothing faster exists for one evaluation. The R weighted_restricted_mean_se_diff is unchanged at commit 8b718ae1: it builds n_j and d_j with vapply(ut, sum(wt[y>=t])), which is O(n·D) per Bayesian-bootstrap replicate. The previous finding stands: sort once and take a reverse cumsum for O(n log n), same formula. No new literature (Aalen-type or improved-Greenwood variants) would keep the estimator.

kaplan-meier-product-limit.note: For a single evaluation, the C++ sort plus product-limit sweep is optimal, so km_stat_inline, rmst_from_km and get_survival_stat_for_group stay Keep. The BRT presort is already Adopt in the catalog. Two items remain. (1) weighted_km_median still recomputes sum(row_weights[i:n]) at every distinct time (v1.0.5 TODO-6, still unimplemented at 8b718ae1). (2) New since last run: the FastSurvival 2.0.0 speed vignette quantifies the per-call survfit overhead that the previous note left unquantified. Its single-pass C++ RMST and KM routines are about 30× faster than survfit/survRM2 at n=500 (presorted). This bears on weighted_survival_stat_for_group, which calls survival::survfit(weights=) once per Bayesian-bootstrap replicate. km_median_arm_bounds (survfit + Brookmeyer-Crowley) runs once per fit and is memoised, so it is not hot and stays Keep.

mover-interval.note: Closed form from two intervals, O(1); nothing faster. Tang 2021 (MOVER under stratified sampling, doi 10.1002/sim.9230) and McGrath et al. arXiv 2503.03065 v2 (2026) concern interval quality and SE estimation, not speed. FastSurvival's medsurv_fast uses a different estimator (kernel-smoothed-hazard delta-method SE), so it would be an estimator change, not a speedup.

findings.candidate: Sort the arm once, aggregate weighted events and totals per distinct time (rowsum), and take n_j as a reverse cumulative sum. Then apply the same cumprod / reverse-cumsum A(t_j) / Σ A² d/(n(n−d)) formula. Ideally do this in the same C++ single scan that FastSurvival's rmst_fast uses for the unweighted case, with weights added.
findings.claimed_speedup: Complexity O(n·D) → O(n log n) per arm per replicate. No source quantifies the weighted case. FastSurvival's vignette reports about 30× for an unweighted single-pass C++ RMST+Greenwood against survRM2::rmst2 at n=500, but that measures a different baseline.
findings.suggested_action: Adopt: fold into v1.0.5 TODO-6 (the same reverse-cumsum fix as the weighted KM median) and change the inventory verdict from 'Not yet audited' to Adopt.

findings.candidate: Add a weights argument to the existing C++ km_stat_inline / rmst_from_km sweep: weighted d_j and reverse-cumsum n_j over tie groups, the survfit quantile midpoint convention (which km_stat_inline already implements), and RMST by step areas. Call it for both the weighted median and the weighted RMST per replicate. As a minimum, fix weighted_km_median with a reverse cumsum (TODO-6).
findings.claimed_speedup: weighted_km_median: O(n·D) → O(n log n), not quantified by any source. Replacing per-replicate survfit: FastSurvival's speed-comparison vignette reports about 30× for single-pass C++ KM/RMST over survfit+summary and survRM2::rmst2 at n=500, 1,000 microbenchmark reps, presorted input. That is the source's own claim; it is unweighted and was not measured on EDI.
findings.suggested_action: Keep v1.0.5 TODO-6 open (still unimplemented). Widen its scope to a weighted C++ KM sweep shared by weighted_km_median, weighted_survival_stat_for_group and weighted_restricted_mean_se_diff, so all three per-replicate paths go through one routine.

brute-force-distance.note: The weighted Euclidean scan over the reservoir is O(|R|d), one query per arrival, and the weights change with each KK21 refit, so a tree built once cannot be reused. The scikit-learn guide (re-fetched) says brute force wins when there are very few queries or N is below about 30, and its 'auto' rule picks brute force for D>15. Searching tree versus SIMD brute-force benchmarks and FNN/RANN (both L2/kd/cover tree, and they need a fixed metric) found nothing new since 2026-11-16. The scan is already the minimum exact cost.

mahalanobis-quadratic-forms.note: A GEMM rowsum((D·S⁻¹)∘D) costs O(|R|p²), the same order as Cholesky whitening. The covariance changes every arrival, so cached or incremental reservoir distances are invalidated each time. Rank-one Cholesky updates (O(p²) per arrival instead of O(p³)) only touch the S⁻¹/solve part, which kk14_incremental_covariance.md TODO-3 already tracks. The searches found no exact dynamic-metric nearest-neighbour structure newer than the approximate one already rejected (Qin et al. 2023). mvnfast's maha and Rfast::mahala use the same brute-force algorithm and give only constant-factor gains over stats::mahalanobis, and EDI already does this in C++. Keep holds.

monte-carlo-pair-sampling.note: O(Bd) with B=500 per arrival, followed by stats::quantile on B values. Exact enumeration when t(t−1)/2 ≤ B is already a tracked Prototype (catalog §7, v1.0.5 TODO-35). It changes the design draws for a given seed, so it is a design-rule change, not a speedup. Streaming quantile sketches (KLL, t-digest) are approximate and pointless at B=500, since sorting is exact and cheap. The incomplete-U-statistic literature turned up no faster exact estimator. The rejection step that keeps pairs distinct costs O(1) expected per draw.

alternating-irls-theta.note: The previous finding still stands. At 8b718ae1, kk21_weights.cpp (~L553-564 and ~L1028-1039) still evaluates digamma/trigamma(y_i+θ) per observation in the θ Newton step. glmGamPoi 1.24.0 (GPL-3) still uses the count frequency table (Anscombe 1950) for its overdispersion MLE. It skips the table when more than half the counts are unique. New since the last run: fastglm 0.1.4 (CRAN, 2026-11-11) added fastglm_nb, which uses the same alternation (β IRLS with θ fixed, then a 1-D θ MLE with μ fixed). So it confirms EDI's design and is not a faster algorithm. No arXiv paper on faster NB θ MLE turned up.

closed-form.note: Trivial: closed-form simple-regression t, one O(np) pass, so nothing can be faster. The accuracy note from the last run (centered two-pass sums) still applies. No code commits since.

forward-stepwise-selection.note: The previous findings still stand: score entry from one reduced fit for the beta/NB/ordinal stepwise paths that still refit (v1.2.0-TODO-23), with statmod::glm.scoretest (1.5.2, GPL≥2) and SAS PROC LOGISTIC score-chi-square entry as references. The FWL/Gram-Schmidt continuous path is already O(np²) and optimal. Nothing new: arXiv API ("forward stepwise" AND "score test") returned 0 results; the latest relevant paper is still QR-updating arXiv 2412.05905v3 (Mar 2026), which has no quantified gain. greybox::stepwise (partial correlations) and FWDselect (R Journal 2016) are the same or slower greedy schemes. Rfast::score.glms gives vectorized score tests against an intercept-only null, so it applies only to step 1.

irls.note: Rechecked fastglm 0.1.4 (2026-11-11). It runs the same IRLS (Cholesky) with step-halving, so it is no faster per iteration. Rfast::logistic_only fits many univariate logistic regressions by C++ Newton, the same per-covariate structure as EDI. The beta φ grid → Brent/Newton option is already catalog P4 / v1.0.5 TODO 4, so it is not re-reported.

newton-raphson.note: Weibull AFT univariate and reduced fits use damped Newton on the analytic Hessian, the fastest-converging choice at p ≤ ~10. The 2026 search found only tutorials: survreg converges in 3-5 Newton iterations, and lgspline uses Brent for scale plus Newton for β, which is not faster. Nothing new.

univariate-screening-fits.note: With the Wald |t| statistic EDI uses, p independent 2-parameter fits are already minimal, and warm-starting stays the recorded low-priority Prototype. New this run: Rfast::score.glms (GPL≥2) computes per-covariate score tests against the intercept-only null in closed form, with no fitting at all for Poisson/logistic. That removes the Newton iterations, but it changes the importance statistic (score instead of Wald t), so it is an estimator change and reported as such. BanditSIS (arXiv 2509.16085) cuts screening cost for Pearson correlations by subsampling, so it is randomized and approximate, and the gain only matters at large n. The MC threshold is unchanged.

findings.candidate: Compute the θ score and information sums over the distinct-y frequency table, so D ≪ n special-function calls. This is Anscombe's (1950) trick, used by glmGamPoi's overdispersion MLE, and the same pattern is already in fast_zinb.cpp and fast_hurdle_negbin.cpp.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified at EDI sizes. glmGamPoi's 6-13× is for its whole single-cell pipeline. Here the gain is bounded by the special-function share of each outer iteration.
findings.suggested_action: Profile univariate_negbin_tstat on a KK21 count fixture. Only if the θ-step special functions are a visible share, reuse the distinct-y helper from fast_zinb.cpp.

findings.candidate: One reduced fit per step, then a Rao score z for each candidate, as kk21_stepwise_logistic_weights_cpp already does. statmod::glm.scoretest (matrix x2, needs only the null fit, NB dispersion held fixed) and SAS PROC LOGISTIC's score-chi-square entry (cumulative logit, thresholds as nuisance parameters) are the references.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified in the sources. The catalog's theoretical estimate is about p/2× fewer fits.
findings.suggested_action: No re-decision needed. When implementing v1.2.0-TODO-23, A/B against statmod::glm.scoretest and run the existing KK21 weight-comparison A/B.

findings.candidate: Null-model score statistics: fit the intercept-only model once (closed form: μ = ȳ), then compute each covariate's score z in one O(n) pass, as Rfast::score.glms does for Poisson/logistic.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. The Rfast docs say only that it is 'much faster' than fitting models. It removes all per-covariate iterations: O(np) instead of O(p·iter·n).
findings.suggested_action: Record as a rejected or optional option in catalog §12 (estimator change). Consider it only if a profile shows the univariate fits dominate KK21 design time and the owner accepts a score-based importance measure.

bisection.note: pval_invert_ci_cpp is still pure bisection: no code commits since the last research, and lrt_ci_newton.cpp / inference_ext_ci_inversion.R:137,190 are unchanged. The previous Chandrupatla/ITP finding stands. I re-fetched degenerateconic.com and got the same counts: bisection 574, Brent 260, TOMS748 273, ITP 303, Chandrupatla 178. Chandrupatla's DOI is now confirmed (10.1016/s0965-9978(96)00051-8). New since the last run: modAB, a modified Anderson–Björck bracketing method (Ganchovski et al., Algorithms 2026 19(5):332; MIT code). Its authors self-report a mean of 13.5 evaluations against Brent's 17.2 on 101 functions, with a worst case of 56 against 142. I added it as a third candidate in the finding. Gaussian-refit rows: the closed form adopted under v1.1.0-TODO-50 is still not landed, and there is no new candidate.

brent-root.note: The inventory row is still mislabelled. inference_incidence_log_binomial.R:392 calls invert_gradient_ci_uniroot, which calls pval_invert_ci_cpp (bisection, inference_ext_ci_inversion.R:150-195), so the earlier finding stands. The real uniroot use (invert_ci_to_find_two_sided_pval_for_treatment_effect) works on a closed-form CI, and its closed form 2Φ(−|z|) is already recorded. A better root finder gains nothing there.

safeguarded-newton-root.note: I checked for new endpoint methods. arXiv 2404.02774 (profile likelihood via constrained optimisation / ODEs, 2024) makes no speed claim and is aimed at continuous families of limits. The RVM paper (Fischer & Lewis 2021, doi 10.1007/s11222-021-10012-y) is unchanged. logistf still uses Venzon–Moolgavkar. I found no 2025–2026 safeguarded-Newton benchmark. The cataloged signed-root Newton (v1.0.5 audit TODO 4) remains the improvement to make.

warm-start-continuation.note: New sources only confirm that warm starts help. The IceCube thesis (arXiv 2609.12941) reports a 3.6× median cut in likelihood evaluations from neighbour warm starts in profile fits. aquakin uses a continuation sweep with a cold anchor. Both are path-dependent chaining, the option row 5 rejects. The deterministic tangent predictor (v1.0.5 TODO-5, catalog NEW-ci-refit-warm-start) is still the path-independent choice, and nothing newer turned up. The code still disables warm starts for *_ci keys (std_mod_cache.R:122).

findings.candidate: When brent_ci_inversion.md TODO-2 is implemented, use Chandrupatla's hybrid quadratic/bisection method (Chandrupatla 1997, doi 10.1016/s0965-9978(96)00051-8; the solver in SciPy's elementwise find_root) or ITP with n0=0/1 (Oliveira & Takahashi 2021, doi 10.1145/3423597; CRAN itp, GPL≥2) instead of textbook Brent. A new 2026 option to benchmark as well: modAB, a modified Anderson–Björck method (Ganchovski et al., Algorithms 19(5):332, 2026; MIT-licensed C/C++ code).
findings.claimed_speedup: degenerateconic.com, 15 functions at tol 1e-15: bisection 574 evaluations in total, Brent 260, TOMS748 273, ITP 303, Chandrupatla 178. On the flat roots x³ and sin((x−7.14)³), Brent needs 40/46 against bisection's 17/18, while Chandrupatla needs 17/18. The modAB README self-reports a mean of 13.5 evaluations against Brent's 17.2 (max 56 against 142) on 101 functions. None of these benchmark EDI's p(δ), so the gain for EDI is not quantified.
findings.suggested_action: Add Chandrupatla, ITP and modAB to the catalog's row-M options table. Before implementing brent_ci_inversion.md TODO-2, run an evaluation-count test on the score, gradient, Bartlett and count-LR p(δ), including a flat or jumpy case, and pick the solver from that. Keep bisection as the fallback.

findings.claimed_speedup: Roughly 2–3× fewer evaluations on smooth functions (bisection 574 vs Brent 260 vs Chandrupatla 178 in total, degenerateconic.com). Not quantified for log-binomial refits.
