closed-form.note: Trivial: LR = 2(nll0-nll1) and gradient statistic are O(1) closed forms plus one chi-square tail; nothing faster. The only p^3 step is the Schur complement in the score test (constant factor, v1.1.0-TODO-155). No commits since the previous result.

irls.note: Checked fastglm 0.1.4 (CRAN, 2026-11-11, new since last result): it is C++ IRLS with a Cholesky solve and step-halving, the same algorithm class as EDI's C++ Newton/IRLS. Its benchmark vignette's ~3-8x gain over glm.fit is a gain of C++ over R, which EDI already has. Refits are already warm-started. No newer arXiv IRLS method keeps the estimator and wins at EDI's sizes.

multistart.note: Previous finding re-confirmed from the clm article (fetched this run; Pratt 1981 / Burridge 1981): the basic cumulative-link log-likelihood, cloglog included, is concave with a unique global optimum, and fixing beta_T keeps it concave. The cloglog fit_null (inference_ordinal_cloglog.R:240-262) still always runs 2 starts, so a certified single start (with the second start only on failure) halves cloglog null-refit cost. Stereotype is nonconcave, so its multistart stays; Hess & Bunch 2025/2026 (arXiv 2506.02722) found no single method recovers every optimum, which supports keeping it there.

newton-raphson.note: The constrained C++ Newton refits with fixed_idx and warm starts are the standard optimal approach for concave GLM likelihoods. Trust-region profile-interval algorithms (Fischer & Lewis 2021, Venzon-Moolgavkar) target the CI endpoint search (row M, brent_ci_inversion.md), not the per-delta refit. fastglm_ordinal (2026) also uses observed-information Newton with an expected-information certificate, the same as EDI. Nothing new since the last result.

parametric-bootstrap.note: Monte Carlo Bartlett factor, recomputed per delta. New items checked: Hanada & Sugimoto 2025/2026 (Biometrics, arXiv 2508.08758) give an analytic 'simplified Bartlett correction', but it is specific to random-effects meta-analysis, so for EDI it would be an estimator change. pbkrtest 0.5.5 PBmodcomp computes the same mean-of-LR Bartlett factor (nsim = 1000 default); its seqPBmodcomp early stop applies to tail p-values, not means. I found no variance-reduction or cheaper estimator of E[LR|H0]. The catalog's own option (one factor per CI, v1.0.5 TODO-3) still covers the space.

ridge-regularization.note: Escalating ridge on the (p-1)x(p-1) nuisance block runs once per score test, at most 8 small solves. Searches on Tikhonov / diagonal loading for score tests and on nearPD / modified Cholesky turned up nothing faster with the same answer. Its calibration remains a robustness question, not a speed one.

schur-complement.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. Here it runs once per test, not per replicate. The only gain is one LDLT solve in place of the full inverse (constant factor, v1.1.0-TODO-155).

findings.candidate: Run one constrained Newton refit with a convergence certificate (max |gradient| below tolerance and a positive-definite Hessian, as ordinal::clm's regularized Newton with step-halving uses), and run the second start only when the certificate fails. This is justified because the basic cumulative-link log-likelihood (cloglog included) is concave with a unique global optimum (Pratt 1981; Burridge 1981), and fixing beta_T restricts it to an affine subspace, which keeps it concave.
findings.claimed_speedup: not quantified by the source; about 2x fewer cloglog null refits by construction when the first start converges
findings.suggested_action: Resolve the cloglog 'Investigate' verdict: make the second start conditional on the first refit failing a gradient-norm certificate, then A/B the LR p-values and CIs on the existing cloglog fixtures.

closed-form.note: Trivial (closed form, O(1) per element). logit/inv_logit/sample_mode and the ordinal link cdf/pdf/pdf' are one pass of arithmetic, so nothing is faster. Checked since 2026-11-16: no commits touched these files. Eigen gained vectorized double erf/erfc (commit 5133c836, Nov 2024; generic_fast_erfc packet path), which could in principle SIMD-batch the probit erfc. But EDI's ordinal helpers evaluate per observation inside a link switch, RcppEigen still bundles Eigen 3.4.0, and the packet traits are gated on EIGEN_FAST_MATH on SSE/AVX512/NEON, so there is no drop-in win. Robustness note, not speed: the cloglog clamp z<-37 -> F=0 floors F where F≈e^z≈1e-16, so log F is lost for extreme negative z.

power-series.note: fast_log1pexp / log1pexp_array_fast cost one exp, one divide and a 10-term Taylor Horner in s²=(z/(2+z))², with s≤1/3. The exp dominates. Re-checked fdlibm e_log.c this run: the same s=f/(2+f) reduction with a 7-coefficient minimax polynomial (Lg1..Lg7) has error ≤2^-58.45. So a refit minimax polynomial reaches better accuracy than the current 5e-12 with about 3 fewer FMAs, or reaches 5e-12 with fewer still. The saving is marginal and the finding is re-reported mainly for accuracy and to supply the catalog P11 citation. Estrin evaluation (Boost.Math docs, SLEEF discussion #415) would cut latency but not throughput, and is less accurate. In an Eigen array loop, throughput is what matters, so Horner stays. Nothing newer turned up on arXiv.

rational-approximation.note: fast_atan is Cephes range reduction plus a 5/5 rational at about 1 ulp. VDT's fast_atan (LGPL-3, Cephes-derived) reports 11 ns scalar and 8.3 ns AVX versus 19.7 ns libm on an i7-3930K. That is the same construction as EDI's, so there is no algorithmic gain, and the AVX gain needs batched calls, which the per-observation cauchit loop does not do. Cephes erfc for probit is likewise standard. Arm optimized-routines erfc (table plus series, about 1.2-1.7 ULP) is a SIMD design, not faster per scalar call at full precision.

stable-branch-evaluation.note: plogis_safe/array, log1pexp_safe/array and fast_log1p_arr (Goldberg) cost one exp plus a log or divide per element: closed form, nothing faster that is exact. R's nmath log1pexp uses cutoffs at 18/33.3 (log1p(exp x), x+exp(-x), x), and LogExpFunctions.jl follows Mächler 2012. Neither is faster. Boost.Math's log1p docs warn that Goldberg's log(u)·z/(u−1) identity 'fails quite spectacularly' under aggressive compiler optimizations. EDI's configure adds -O3/-march=native but not -ffast-math, so it is safe as built; keep it that way. log_one_minus_exp_neg_hp (fast_hurdle_poisson_glmm.cpp:76) is still not the Mächler log1mexp switch: it uses log1p(-e^{-λ}) for λ≥1e-10, which loses relative precision for λ≲ln2. The fix costs the same and is already recorded as an incidental accuracy fix, not a speed issue.

findings.candidate: Minimax (Remez/fpminimax) polynomial in s² on [0,1/9], the fdlibm e_log.c construction: s=f/(2+f) with a 7-coefficient even polynomial (Lg1..Lg7) whose error is bounded by 2^-58.45. Same evaluation scheme, with fitted coefficients in place of the 1/(2k+1) Taylor ones.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by the source. It saves about 3 FMAs per element (7 vs 10 terms) at much better accuracy. The exp call dominates, so the speed gain is marginal; this is mainly an accuracy-at-equal-or-lower-cost option.
findings.suggested_action: Fill the '[cite needed]' in catalog P11 with fdlibm e_log.c. Optionally refit the Horner coefficients as a minimax polynomial in s² on [0,1/9] (Sollya fpminimax), with fewer terms at equal or better error. No urgent speed-driven change.

logrank-sweep.note: The single evaluation is already optimal: one O(n log n) sort plus a fused O(n) sweep in C++. FastSurvival 2.0.0 (CRAN, 2026-11-16) uses the same design, presorting once and doing a single C++ pass. The gap is in the randomization p-value path. InferenceSurvivalLogRank and InferenceSurvivalGehanWilcox have no compute_fast_randomization_distr, so every permutation draw re-runs fast_logrank_stats_cpp / fast_gehan_wilcox_stats_cpp, including a full re-sort. At delta=0 the pooled (y, dead) order, the pooled Nelson-Aalen / pooled KM weights and therefore the null martingale residuals are label-invariant. The statistic is linear in w, so it can be computed once and evaluated per draw in O(n), the coin linear-rank-statistic formulation. This applies to the right-censored permutation path; the catalog only records the interval-censored analogue (v1.0.5 audit TODO-11). See finding 1.

martingale-residuals.note: Trivial: a closed form from the null fit, O(n) after the sort. Replacing coxph(~1, weights) with a C++ weighted sweep is already recorded as implementation-only (Keep). No new evidence since 2026-11-16. Their label-invariance under permutation is what finding 1 relies on, but that changes logrank-sweep, not this method.

sort-and-sweep.note: For a single evaluation, std::sort with record_less is fine at EDI's sizes. Radix and pdqsort swaps are constant-factor and were already rejected in the catalog. The 2026 sources found (a CppCon 2026 abstract, djbsort docs) are for int keys and give no evidence for (time, dead, w) records near n~1000. The sort that matters is the one repeated per permutation draw. At delta=0 it can be hoisted entirely: sort once and reuse the order for all r draws (finding 1). At delta!=0, BRT presort + merge is already tracked (catalog NEW-resample-presort).

turnbull-em.note: The interval-censored path calls interval::ictest(scores='logrank1') per observed statistic and again on every randomization draw, because the fast path returns NULL. Each call re-solves the label-invariant pooled NPMLE. Three options, already catalogued as Adopt and still unimplemented at commit 8b718ae: (a) reuse the pooled NPMLE and scores across draws (catalog TODO-11 / §10 TODO-5; ictest documents icFIT as 'for increased computation speed'); (b) EMICM via icenReg::ic_np (C++ EMICM, weights= argument) or icfit(initfit='initEMICM'); (c) the constrained Newton method (npsurv CNM/HCNM, Wang & Taylor 2013), which the authors claim is the best choice at any data size. SQUAREM is listed only as a lesser alternative: about 15-17x fewer EM evaluations than plain EM, competitive with EM-ICM. This re-reports the standing option with sources, fixing the previous run's faster_option_found that had no finding.

findings.candidate: Use a linear-rank-statistic fast path at delta=0. Sort the pooled (y, dead) once. In one sweep, compute the pooled null martingale residuals m_i = dead_i - Lambda_NA(t_i) (for Peto-Prentice, the pooled-KM-weighted residuals). These do not depend on w. The estimate is mean(m|w=1) - mean(m|w=0) = S_T·n/(n_T·n_C), using sum(m)=0, and the log-rank score equals S_T = sum_{w_i=1} m_i. For each draw, evaluate it as an O(n) dot product, or for all draws at once as one t(W) %*% m product over the permutation matrix. At delta!=0 (log-shift sharp null), fall back to the per-arm presort + merge already tracked (NEW-resample-presort). This is how coin computes logrank_test: scores are computed once from the pooled data and the conditional null permutes only the group labels.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by a source for this exact path. Theoretical: removes r sorts and r R-level calls, from O(r·n log n + r·overhead) to O(n log n + r·n). FastSurvival's speed vignette reports about 25x over survival::survdiff at n=500 from presorting once plus a single C++ pass. That figure is mostly overhead removal, an analogous but not identical comparison.
findings.suggested_action: Add a catalog row (§10, NEW-survival-sort-sweep) and a TODO for a compute_fast_randomization_distr on InferenceSurvivalLogRank and InferenceSurvivalGehanWilcox (right-censored, delta=0). Build it as fixed pooled residual scores plus one W'm product, with fallback to the existing path when delta!=0 or general censoring applies. It mirrors the interval-censored v1.0.5 audit TODO-11, so implement both together.

findings.candidate: (1) Solve the pooled NPMLE once. It is label-invariant at delta=0, so compute the scores once (ictest(icFIT=) / wlr_trafo) and evaluate each draw as a linear statistic. This gives r times fewer NPMLE solves and is catalog Adopt (v1.0.5 audit TODO-11, §10 TODO-5), still unimplemented. (2) Speed up the single solve: start with icfit(initfit='initEMICM'), or use icenReg::ic_np (an efficient C++ EMICM with weights=, Anderson-Bergman 2017), or the constrained Newton method (npsurv CNM/HCNM, Wang & Taylor 2013).
findings.claimed_speedup: (1) r-fold, about 500x at r=501, fewer NPMLE solves (theoretical, from the catalog). (2) Anderson-Bergman's JCGS abstract (as reported by search; the publisher page returned 403) says the efficient EMICM is 'significantly faster than other EMICM implementations and competing algorithms'. Wang & Taylor say HCNM is 'the best choice for data sets of any size'. Du & Varadhan report SQUAREM using about 15-17x fewer EM evaluations than plain EM, competitive with EM-ICM. No source benchmarks these at EDI's n.
findings.suggested_action: Implement v1.0.5 audit TODO-11 first: pooled NPMLE once plus a linear statistic per draw, in the same change as finding 1. Then A/B ic_np (or npsurv CNM) against icfit for the single pooled solve, compared on the ictest statistic. Cite the Wang & Taylor 2013 DOI 10.1007/s11222-012-9341-9 in the catalog's (f) Turnbull table, which lacks the CNM option.

pairs-of-pairs-variance.note: Per-replicate BRS λ² is O(n), the lower bound. Using it would avoid the one-off O(m^3) blossom pairing (row G, not this problem's entries), but it is an estimator change, not a speedup. Also new: Bai et al. arXiv 2503.10851 (paired-strata design-based estimator) and Chen & Li arXiv 2602.18383. Neither offers a faster way to get the same estimate.

random-forest-imputation.note: [full re-imputation per arrival] The previous finding still stands. missRanger 2.6.1 (CRAN, 2024-12-07; NEWS re-read) has keep_forests = TRUE with predict(imp, newdata, iter = 4), so a new arrival can be imputed without refitting. New since the last result: missForestPredict 1.0.1 (CRAN 2025-05-24, GPL ≥ 2, ranger-based) saves the models from every iteration. It imputes new rows with the same sequence of models, and re-imputing the training set reproduces the original imputation exactly. It also offers initialization = 'custom' with x_init, a warm start for the periodic refits, which missRanger lacks (refman checked). mixgb 2.2.3 (2026-01) offers impute_new() from saved XGBoost imputers, but it is a different estimator (boosting). Mondrian (online) forests grow incrementally but are a different forest, and nothing was found on using them for imputation. Every per-arrival option is an estimator change, because past rows' imputations stop drifting. | [random-forest chained imputation (missRanger / missForest)] Fixed designs run this once, and missRanger with ranger is still the fastest chained-RF single imputer. No 2025–26 benchmark (IMAGIC-500, missForestPredict paper, arXiv 2401.09602) shows a faster same-estimator alternative. Update: missForest 1.6 (2025-10-13) made ranger its default backend and added num.threads, so EDI's missForest fallback, which already passes num.threads, is now ranger-speed rather than randomForest-speed. Its output differs from pre-1.6 versions, which is a reproducibility note and not a speedup. Fewer trees or iterations remain estimator changes.

findings.candidate: Re-report of the previous finding, which still stands. Call missRanger(..., keep_forests = TRUE, data_only = FALSE) once, or every k arrivals. Impute each new arrival with predict(imp, newdata = x_new) from the stored forests, using iter = 4 for rows with several missing values. Refit only every k arrivals, or when columns or factor levels change. missRanger ≥ 2.6.0 is already an EDI import, so there is no new dependency.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by the sources. Structurally, about k times fewer forest fits per arrival, with only a predict for the new row in between. The mixgb new-data vignette says reusing saved imputers 'is considerably faster, as it avoids retraining the imputation models' (qualitative).
findings.suggested_action: Keep as the concrete, dependency-free implementation of catalog §12(e) 'stored forest, refit every k' for v1.0.5-TODO-9, and cite the missRanger 2.6.0 NEWS in that row.

findings.candidate: missForestPredict (Albu et al.; CRAN 1.0.1, GPL ≥ 2, ranger backend). missForest(..., save_models = TRUE, initialization = 'custom', x_init = previous completed X) warm-starts each periodic refit from the last imputation, which should cut chained iterations to convergence. missForestPredict(obj, newdata) imputes a single arrival with the saved per-iteration models. Re-imputing the training set reproduces the original imputation exactly, which gives a deterministic, auditable path.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. The paper claims only 'competitive results … within short computation times'. The iteration savings from a warm start are an inference; the mice literature reports that most of the cost is burn-in iterations.
findings.suggested_action: Note missForestPredict (DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2407.03379) in catalog §12(e) as the alternative offering warm starts and exact training replay. Benchmark iterations to convergence, warm versus cold, at n ≈ 100–500 inside the v1.0.5-TODO-9 prototype.

boundary-reduced-refit.note: Both entries, fit_zinb_zi_boundary_fallback and fit_zip_reduced_fallback, cost one extra L-BFGS fit and run only on the boundary path. The way to remove them is the α=1/θ L-BFGS-B reparametrization already tracked in catalog §3 TODO 4, and that is a robustness change, not a speedup. Checked for new work since 2026-11-16 (the previous run): an arXiv listing on ZINB boundaries, a web search on the α=1/θ Poisson limit, and the CRAN pages of pscl (1.5.9, 2024) and glmmTMB (1.1.15.2, 2026-09-29). glmmTMB's approach to a dispersion or zero-inflation parameter at the boundary is to flag it and suggest the reduced model (per the troubleshooting-vignette search result), which is the same thing EDI does automatically. No new method found, and no code commits since.

convergence-certification.note: No code commits since the previous run. newton_stalled_at_optimum runs one Hessian evaluation and a values-only eigensolve, and only on the line-search-failure exit. ordinal_newton_decrement_ok is one LDLT, O(p³/3), run only when the covariates look badly scaled. The Poisson-limit and limit-score certificates cost 2–3 objective evaluations. The gradient-norm acceptance threshold and the column scale heuristic are O(1) and O(np). This run's searches on the Newton decrement (affine-invariant stopping test; the decrement squared equals the gap to the quadratic model's minimum), on scaled and relative gradient tests, and the CRAN Optimization task view (only optimflex's AND-combined criteria are new) turned up nothing cheaper that keeps the same certificate. Swapping the eigenvalue-based scaling for a Newton decrement in newton_stalled_at_optimum would change which fits get accepted (a policy change, as noted before), and the cost on that rare path is negligible either way.

separation-detection.note: bootstrap_estimates_extreme is an O(B) scan plus one quantile per bootstrap distribution, so nothing faster is possible. New since the previous run: detectseparation 0.4.0 (2026-04-19, GPL-3) and brglm2 1.1.1 (2026-10-07) on CRAN. arXiv 2610.08100 (2026-10-06) shows that a single linear program decides whether a finite MLE exists (overlap) across cumulative-link, adjacent-category, sequential and stereotype models. Eck & Geyer (EJS 2021, doi 10.1214/21-EJS1815) detect nonexistence after the fit from null eigenvectors of the Fisher information, faster than LP. Both are exact per-fit existence checks that would cost more per replicate than the current heuristic, so neither is a speedup. They could be a robustness upgrade (an exact check on the observed fit) and are noted under implementations and proposed terms, not as findings.

cholesky-ldlt.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. Here it is only fast_gaussian_lmm make_start: OLS by normal-equation LDLT, run once per fit. Per the Eigen benchmark fetched this run, LLT/LDLT on normal equations is already the fastest dense least-squares solve, and it is negligible next to the LMM optimization.

closed-form.note: Trivial: the iter-0 information X'diag(w)X and the NB observed Hessian are single-pass O(np²) closed forms. The weighted_crossprod reuse and the per-row heap temporaries in negbin_smart_hessian are constant-factor notes the catalog already records (Incidental 13). Nothing faster.

irls.note: Only the GEE independence-GLM starting β. geeasy/geepack-style GEE also starts from an ordinary glm fit (geeasy geelm source). Canonical-link IRLS is Newton with quadratic convergence, so a cheaper start would not reduce total work: the GLM start is itself one cold fit of ~5–8 iterations. No new 2026 source changes this. Checked fastglm 0.1.4 (2026-11-11 CRAN), which offers warm.start only across sequential batch fits.

method-of-moments.note: The Pearson moment θ start (NB and truncated NB) and the marginal-cumulative-proportion thresholds are closed forms, O(np) and O(nK), run once per fit. MASS theta.mm and theta.md are the same moment-type estimators. I found no truncation-corrected moment start that is clearly better: the searches turned up only generic ZTNB moment inversion and ptmixed's capped moment start. ordinal::clm documents its starts as polr-inspired, the same idea EDI uses. Nothing faster.

multistart.note: The hurdle-NB deterministic start grid (≤3 β × 4 θ) is the right design, and Knitro-style deterministic multistart is the same idea. MLSL, basin hopping, GenSA and DEoptim are stochastic and costlier, and they break the determinism guarantee. One small implementation finding: make_truncated_negbin_candidate_starts factorizes the same X_pos with ColPivHouseholderQR twice, once for the log1p response and once for the log response. A single factorization solved for both right-hand sides gives identical starts. See finding 2.

ols-on-transformed-response.note: glm mustart-style starts cost one O(np²) least-squares solve each. Rival software uses the same (glm family initialize, statsmodels starting_mu, pscl zeroinfl default glm.fit starts). One related point is about robustness, not speed: the Weibull start ignores censoring, unlike survreg (intercept-only pre-fit, then the full model) or a Buckley-James/Gehan seed. The catalog already records this (O14 'Ignores censoring for Weibull'), and the fix would cost more per start. The speed of the least-squares solve itself is covered under qr-decomposition.

qr-decomposition.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra, but how this problem uses it matters. The start-value solves (safe_ols_solve, try_safe_ols_solve, robust_ols_solve) only need an approximate β, not rank-revealing accuracy. Eigen's benchmark (re-fetched) puts ColPivHouseholderQR ~5.3x slower than LLT on normal equations at 10000x8 and 10000x100, including forming AᵀA. The previous finding stands (finding 1). Finding 2 adds the duplicate QR in the hurdle start grid.

warm-start-continuation.note: Starting nonconcave joint survival models from marginal Weibull/survreg pilot fits matches standard practice: frailtypack fits three independent Weibull models for illness-death starts, and the Lindley frailty paper starts from a Cox fit. Warm starts across replicates and CI steps are already in place (warm_start_dispatch_policy, chain_warm_start in rand, gated on concavity). Supporting evidence: arXiv 1101.6037 reports warm-started logistic Newton falling from ~13 to <4 iterations, and aquakin warm-starts profile-likelihood sweeps from an anchor multistart. No faster acceptable alternative: the one-step/linearized bootstrap changes the estimator.

findings.candidate: Normal equations (symmetric_crossprod, then LLT/LDLT, as fast_ols_internal already does). Fall back to the current ColPivHouseholderQR when the factorization fails, β is non-finite, or a cheap pivot-ratio check flags near-singularity. A start value does not need QR-level accuracy.
findings.claimed_speedup: Eigen dense decomposition benchmark (float, one thread): at 10000x8, ColPivHouseholderQR 36.05 ms vs LLT 6.79 ms including forming AᵀA (~5.3x). At 10000x100, 163 vs 30 ms (~5.4x). EDI's sizes (n in the hundreds to low thousands, p≈2–20) are not benchmarked, and the start is one of several O(np²) passes per fit, so the whole-fit saving is not quantified.
findings.suggested_action: Unchanged from the previous run. Fold into performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md TODO-155: micro-benchmark try_safe_ols_solve (ColPivQR) against crossprod+LLT with a QR fallback at n∈{100,500,2000}, p∈{2,5,10}, and measure the start's share of a cold-started fit before switching.

findings.candidate: Factorize X_pos once and solve for a two-column right-hand side [log1p(y), log(max(y,1))]. Keep the existing per-column finiteness and usability checks.
findings.claimed_speedup: Saves one of two O(np²) QR factorizations in the start-grid construction (~2x on that step). The factorization dominates a solve per the Eigen benchmark. Whole-fit impact is small, not quantified. Applies on every cold hurdle-NB fit, including cold-started resampling replicates.
findings.suggested_action: Trivial refactor. Add a try_safe_ols_solve overload taking a MatrixXd RHS, use it in make_truncated_negbin_candidate_starts, and check that the hurdle-NB fixtures are bit-identical.

bisection.note: Earlier findings still stand: Glazer–Stark fixed-sample inversion (arXiv 2405.05238 v3, still unpublished), Xu's rational breakpoints (2512.14024, still v1) and ITP with n0=0 (itp 1.2.2 on CRAN, GPL>=2). The Xu finding is now strengthened by Zhu & Liu, Biometrics 2024 (doi 10.1093/biomtc/ujae052, arXiv 2502.18666). For the studentized t, they solve one quadratic per randomization draw and sweep the jump points. Their reported runtime is about 23 s versus about 4 h for a grid at n=100 with 10^4 draws. New this run (code read): in the Zhang quantile CI, the reservoir component regresses ty−δ·w_perm on a design that contains w_perm. By quantile-regression shift equivariance, T_b(δ)=T_b(0)−δ exactly. So that component needs one set of B rq fits, not B fits per bisection step. This is also a correctness issue: p_R(δ) does not go to 0. Checked but no finding: Yu–Banerjee–Ritov sequential-test bisection (arXiv 2508.17591, v2 Oct 2026). It is in effect EDI's bisection plus SMC, now with theory. It applies only to fresh-noise p(δ), and CRN paths make p deterministic.

breakpoint-inversion.note: Same O(B log B) sweep as Xu 2025, Zhu–Liu 2024 and Nguyen/CIPerm (one permutation set; sorted w = (t0−t_b)/[k(1/n+1/m)]). That is the method EDI already uses for affine statistics, and at B ≤ low thousands the O(B²) probe counting is not a bottleneck. Nothing faster for the same exact answer. Extending its reach (studentized pivots, the quantile reservoir component) is filed under the bisection findings.

brent-root.note: Only 3 candidate p evaluations in the usual case, and stats::optimize runs only when all three fail. Checked: no new derivative-free 1-D maximiser for a piecewise-smooth minlike p, and the exact2x2 (GPL-3, v1.7.0) validation notes say interval-finding algorithms for such p carry no assurance. The lmi reanalysis says Brent beats TOMS748 on smooth functions; nothing helps with jumps. The concern remains correctness (local maximum), not speed.

exponential-bracketing.note: Wald-seeded doubling costs ≤7 evaluations and matches Glazer–Stark and uniroot extendInt. Nothing new since the last review; nothing faster.

findings.candidate: The response shift −δ·w_perm is a linear function of the design (w_perm is its trt column). Quantile-regression shift equivariance, β̂(y+Xγ, X) = β̂(y, X)+γ, therefore gives T_b(δ) = T_b(0) − δ and T_obs(δ) = T_obs(0) − δ exactly. Draw the permutations once (CRN), fit B rq models once, and p_R(δ) = mean(|T_b(0)−δ| ≥ |T_obs(0)−δ|) becomes a closed-form step function with breakpoints (T_b(0)+T_obs(0))/2. This reuses closed_form_ci_from_affine_null_draws with c_b = 1. The same algebra also shows a validity issue. As δ→+∞, p_R → Pr(T_b ≤ T_obs), and as δ→−∞, p_R → Pr(T_b ≥ T_obs); one of these is ≳ 0.5, so p_R never falls below α on that side. When m = 0 (Bernoulli; all subjects in the reservoir) the combined p equals p_R, so bisection ends at the bracket edge. The standard test would subtract δ·w_obs before permuting, and that form is not affine.
findings.claimed_speedup: Derived from the code, not measured. The reservoir component falls from about (number of bisection steps, 10–50) × nsim_rand rq fits per bound to nsim_rand fits in total, roughly 20–100× on that component. The matched-pairs component (sign flips with intercept rq) is unchanged.
findings.suggested_action: Investigate first as a possible validity bug (the reservoir p-value does not vanish for large |δ|; check the m=0 Bernoulli path with a unit test). Then either fix the null adjustment to the observed w, or, if the current form is intended, replace the per-δ refits with the one-shot affine breakpoint inversion.

findings.candidate: Exact jump-point inversion for studentized statistics. Each draw's pivot equation t(z_π, Y+δθ) = t_obs reduces to a quadratic in δ with explicit roots (Zhu & Liu 2024; Xu 2025 generalizes this to rational statistics). Sort the ≤ 2B roots and sweep ±1/B steps to get the exact p-curve.
findings.claimed_speedup: Zhu & Liu (Biometrics rejoinder) report about 23 s per two-sided interval versus about 4 h for grid inversion (n=100, 10^4 MC draws), about 0.3 s at n=8 exhaustively, and about 146 s at n=10,000. Xu claims an order of magnitude over grid search without timings. Neither compares against bisection, so versus EDI the gain is about (10–20 evaluations × B refits) → B coefficient extractions.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look (updated): when checking whether the studentized BRT pivots are rational in δ, use Zhu & Liu's explicit quadratic roots as the template. If they are, prototype quadratic breakpoints in closed_form_ci_from_affine_null_draws.

findings.candidate: Keep the fixed-sample (CRN) bisection, made conservative as in Glazer & Stark: p = (1+#)/(1+N), with the endpoint taken on the rejecting side. This argues against prioritizing Robbins–Monro.
findings.claimed_speedup: Glazer & Stark (lizard data, n=30, N=6000): 0.33 s versus 0.47 s for Garthwaite (about 1.4×), and conservative rather than approximate. Not measured for non-affine refit statistics.
findings.suggested_action: Re-check the premise of garthwaite_buckland_ci_search.md (v1.2.0-TODO-21) against Glazer & Stark 2025. Narrow it to refit-heavy, non-affine statistics or downgrade it.

findings.candidate: Glazer–Stark fixed-sample inversion: one sign-flip/permutation matrix per CI search, with the conservative p. Their Theorem 1 gives coverage ≥ 1−α, and bisection then runs on a deterministic function (catalog TODO-6a).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for quantile regression. The number of evaluations stays about the same, but steps spent resolving MC noise are removed and the search can stop once the bracket holds a single jump.
findings.suggested_action: Use Glazer & Stark as the reference when prototyping catalog TODO-6a, together with the reservoir-equivariance finding above.

findings.candidate: ITP with n0=0 (Oliveira & Takahashi 2021). It never needs more evaluations than bisection and converges superlinearly when the crossing lies inside a smooth piece.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for this problem. Expected about 20 → 8–10 evaluations per bound when the crossing is smooth, and never worse. Each evaluation costs only O(d+S), so the gain is small.
findings.suggested_action: Correct the 'step function' rationale in the inventory. Optionally record ITP (n0=0) in the options table; low priority.

alternating-irls-theta.note: Only robust_negbinreg (the KK21 fallback path) uses MASS::glm.nb. The earlier finding stands, and it now has a timing. The fastglm benchmarks vignette (fastglm 0.1.4, CRAN 2026-11-11) reports median times of 1.62 ms for fastglm_nb vs 7.71 ms for glm.nb at n=1000, p≈4 (about 4.8x), and about 4.8x again at n=10^4. The convergence vignette reports 200/200 vs 165/200 converged at n=200, p=9. fastglm_nb uses the same alternation, with IRLS for beta and an inner Brent maximization for theta (NEWS 0.1.0), so it fits the same MLE. The other option is EDI's own C++ fast_neg_bin_cpp, which needs no new dependency.

analytic-derivatives.note: These are closed-form O(np) / O(np^2) passes. The negative log-likelihood and gradient already cache lgamma/digamma per distinct y, which is the lower bound up to constants. AD (TMB/RTMB) gives the same derivatives with tape overhead; no NB benchmark was found showing AD beating hand-coded formulas. Settanni et al. (arXiv 2407.05824 v2, 2026) argue that the published score/information expressions for the NB dispersion are inconsistent. That is a pointer for checking correctness, not a speedup. EDI's derivatives are already checked against the likelihood.

lbfgs.note: I checked for new evidence since 2026-11-16. LBFGSpp (MIT) states no performance claims. No source compares joint L-BFGS on (beta, log theta) head-to-head with IRLS/theta alternation at n≈50–500, p≤10. The fastglm timings compare against glm.nb in R, not against a C++ joint quasi-Newton. Fisher scoring/alternation (catalog O6, v1.0.5-TODO-5) and the alpha=1/theta L-BFGS-B parametrization (P3) are already Prototype. The fast alternatives that did turn up (a pre-trained transformer in arXiv 2508.04111; moment theta, about 1000x faster) are estimator changes and are rejected under catalog O6.

newton-raphson.note: The joint Newton on (beta, log theta) is an optional path. Searches for trust-region/damped Newton NB variants found nothing new. statsmodels NB also defaults to Newton or BFGS on the joint vector. Kenne Pagui et al. 2022 (arXiv 2011.02784) use alternating scoring with bias reduction, which changes the estimator. Nothing new beyond catalog O6.

truncated-series-summation.note: This is dead code with no R caller. The recurrence-based pmf series is already O(1) per term. Yu, Dousti Mousavi & Yang (arXiv 2306.04798, Statistical Papers 2024) is an equivalent reordering of the same sum. Carvalho, Silva & Moreira (arXiv 2202.06121 v2, 2025) give adaptive truncation rules with error guarantees, which could replace the ad hoc mu+10 sd stopping rule for robustness. That is not a speedup.

findings.candidate: Route the fallback through EDI's own C++ NB2 MLE (fast_neg_bin_cpp, no new dependency), or through fastglm::fastglm_nb (fastglm 0.1.4, GPL (>= 2)). fastglm_nb runs the same IRLS/theta alternation in C++ with an inner Brent search for theta and a moment-based start.
findings.claimed_speedup: Source claim, not measured here. The fastglm benchmarks vignette reports median 1.62 ms (fastglm_nb) vs 7.71 ms (glm.nb) at n=1000 with an intercept plus 3 covariates (about 4.8x), and 13.2 vs 63.8 ms at n=10^4. The convergence vignette reports 200/200 vs 165/200 converged at n=200, p=9, theta=1; fits that both methods completed agree to max |Δloglik| 1.5e-6.
findings.suggested_action: Low priority: replace MASS::glm.nb in robust_negbinreg with fast_neg_bin_cpp (preferred, already in EDI), or with fastglm_nb. Then re-run the KK21 count-matching fixtures.

blossom-matching.note: Same day as previous result (2026-11-16), and no code commits since. Re-checked: Blossom VI (arXiv 2604.20351, v2 21 Jul 2026) still targets graphs of up to ~10M edges, its arXiv page links no code, and it shows no gain at EDI's n (tens to hundreds; m = n/2 pair averages for compute_halves). nbpMatching 1.5.6 (2024-09-25, GPL>=2) is unchanged on CRAN. On EDI's complete (dense) graphs, the O(n^3) Gabow/Galil-type blossom (NetworkX/van Rantwijk, rustworkx) is the right asymptotic class. Sparse-graph O(nm log n) and scaling O(m sqrt(n) log(nN)) (Duan-Pettie-Su, arXiv 1411.1919) algorithms bring no gain on dense graphs with n<=~1000. Greedy and approximate Euclidean algorithms change the pairs: an estimator/design change, not a speedup. designmatch (0.5.5, 2026-02-20) uses MIP solvers (highs), which are not faster for exact pair matching at these sizes. The p=1 sort-and-pair path is O(n log n) and optimal. compute_halves is computed once and cached, so it is not on the resampling hot path. Keep.

nonparametric-bootstrap.note: The previous conclusion stands: for the same bootstrap distribution, nothing beats i.i.d. multinomial resampling plus B refits warm-started at the full-data MLE. Balanced resampling (Davison, Hinkley & Schechtman 1986, doi 10.1093/biomet/73.3.555) is still the tracked variance reduction under audit J / TODO-4, and no newer evidence changes it. Do (1992) finds balanced more efficient in most cases, but quantile/percentile gains are modest. The KK compound kernel is O(n) per replicate in C++, and its O(B·m·n) R index build is an implementation fix (I9). The studentized loop's cost is an implementation issue (I7: serial, an R6 duplicate per replicate, no seed); fwb 1.0.0 (2026-10) shows the seed-per-draw, core-count-independent design EDI wants. New since the last run: the Studentized Cheap Bootstrap (He, Lam & Yan, arXiv 2606.25968, June 2026) gives higher-order coverage for studentized intervals from very few resamples. It strengthens the cheap-bootstrap finding and extends it to the (θ*, se*) path. Both findings (cheap bootstrap, k-step bootstrap) are estimator changes and are re-reported. Bag-of-little-bootstraps (Kleiner et al.; the cBLB kernel extension in arXiv 2603.13662, rev. 2026-11) targets data sizes far beyond EDI's and changes the estimator, so it was not adopted. Importance (tilting) resampling is already in the P3 options table.

rejection-sampling.note: Unchanged. The mean-diff rejection loop is effectively unreachable (I10). The g-comp rejection of unusable resamples is a statistical choice: any scheme that avoids it changes the bootstrap distribution. van Smeden et al. (BMC MRM 2016) and the Gelman blog note that discarding separated resamples can bias results, a robustness issue already flagged as incidental, not a speed gain. The new 2026 rerandomization rejection alternatives (Metropolis–Hastings + SIR, arXiv 2602.07613; BRAIN; FastRerandomize) address covariate-balance assignment sampling, not degenerate-bootstrap rejection, so they don't apply to these entries.

ridit-scoring.note: Unchanged. The per-replicate O(n log n) ridit rebuild has a known faster equivalent: the O(n+L) level-slot counting rebuild, already tracked as ridit_kernel_level_slots.md TODO-3. Searches (ridit bootstrap, multinomial count resampling, pim/DescTools/Ridit) found nothing faster. The Ridit CRAN package is archived (2022).

value-space-bisection-selection.note: Unchanged. X+Y selection theory (Frederickson–Johnson 1982; soft-heap selection, arXiv 1802.07041; cache-oblivious FJ, arXiv 0804.0936) and Monahan's Algorithm 616 (used by DescTools) are the catalog's known alternatives. None has practical benchmarks beating nth_element / value bisection at EDI's n, and the plain HL bootstrap kernel is dead code. The IVWC variance loops are tracked as TODO 5.

findings.candidate: Cheap bootstrap (Lam 2022): ψ̂ ± t_{B,1−α/2}·S with S² = (1/B)Σ(ψ*_b − ψ̂)². It is asymptotically valid with B as small as 1, typically B ≈ 5–10, and Lam & Liu (ICML 2023) give finite-sample coverage bounds. New since the last run: the Studentized Cheap Bootstrap (He, Lam & Yan, arXiv 2606.25968, 2026-06-24) gets higher-order coverage, as conventional studentization does, from very few Monte Carlo replications. That makes a cheap counterpart for the (θ*, se*) studentized CI path possible too. Both would be offered as new opt-in CI types for classes with expensive refits.
findings.claimed_speedup: Refits drop from ~501 to ~5–10 (~50–100x fewer), by arithmetic, not a measured benchmark. Lam's ar5iv simulation (previous run): coverage 0.92 at B = 5 and 10 against 0.69/0.80 for the percentile bootstrap at the same B. The studentized version's abstract gives no numbers ('very few Monte Carlo replications').
findings.suggested_action: Consider an opt-in cheap-bootstrap CI type (B ≈ 10) for classes with expensive refits (GLMM, survival, ordinal). Track the Studentized Cheap Bootstrap (arXiv 2606.25968) as its studentized companion. Validate coverage against the B = 501 percentile, BCa and bootstrap-t intervals in the A/B harness, then record the result in the catalog §9 / P3 options table.

findings.candidate: k-step bootstrap (Davidson & MacKinnon 1999; Andrews 2002, Econometrica 70(1):119–162): a fixed k Newton / line-search Newton steps from θ̂ per replicate. It is higher-order equivalent to the standard bootstrap for t-CIs and Wald tests under the iid and block bootstraps.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. Andrews calls it 'a very attractive alternative computationally'. With EDI's warm start, the gain is only the iterations beyond k plus convergence checks: likely ≈1–3x for Newton/IRLS families and more for L-BFGS families. This is an estimate, not measured.
findings.suggested_action: First measure how many iterations warm-started bootstrap refits actually take on representative fixtures. Only if that is well above 3 for some family, prototype an opt-in k-step mode for studentized/t-based bootstrap CIs; otherwise record 'no gain at EDI's warm-start setup' in the catalog §9 J options table.

erfc-normal-cdf.note: This updates the previous finding with new evidence, not a pure speedup. SciPy's xsf log_ndtr (stats.h) computes log Phi(x) = log(erfcx(-t)/2) - t^2 for x<-1. Stan Math PR #3406 (opened 2026-09-18, not merged) rebuilds std_normal_lcdf and its gradient on a shared erfcx kernel (Cody 1969 rationals plus a small-|z| Chebyshev polynomial). The PR reports gradient relative error at most 3.7e-15, a finite and accurate value down to z=-1.9e154, and 1.35-1.44x faster double evaluation than Stan's previous code. That speedup is against Stan's own code, not against EDI's Cephes erfc. The same erfcx value also gives the Mills ratio phi/Phi = sqrt(2/pi)/erfcx(-x/sqrt2) with no exp, which is what the probit score needs. EDI's pnorm_fast and fast_log_pnorm, including the new vectorized fast_log_pnorm_vec_cpp, are still clamped at |x|>=8. R 4.5.0 NEWS says 'pnorm(x) underflows more gracefully', so re-check v1.0.5-TODO-22's R::pnorm reference grid against current R.

rational-approximation.note:
I checked for anything new since 2026-11-16.
- R NEWS through R 4.6.2: no qnorm change for non-log p. R 4.3.0's Maechler asymptotic formulas (DPQ qnormAsymp) only affect log.p extreme tails, so AS241 seed parity with R's Inversion generator still holds.
- Cephes erfc: Boost.Math erfc has a peak error of 0.98 eps, about the same as Cephes, and its docs give no speed data. SLEEF erfc and LitMath (1e-13) are SIMD options, but neither has a benchmark at EDI's scalar per-observation call sites. VDT has no erf, erfc or quantile.
- Acklam: used only for warm starts. Wilson CI exact z is already adopted as catalog TODO 7. No new CPU benchmark of Acklam+Halley vs AS241 found.
Nothing new beats Cephes, Acklam or AS241 for these jobs.

findings.claimed_speedup: Not measured against EDI. Stan PR #3406 reports std_normal_lcdf (double) 1.35-1.44x and Phi 1.27-1.43x faster than Stan's previous implementation (A&S 7.1.26 plus Taylor pieces) on an AMD EPYC 9965. Later commits report 1.2-1.4x for z in [-30,30]. Jenkins suite-level ratios were about 1.0, and a bot review notes the benchmark source is missing from the PR. Against EDI's Cephes erfc+log, expect about equal cost: one rational evaluation, and the exp is removed from the log Phi and Mills-ratio paths.
findings.suggested_action: When implementing v1.0.5-TODO-22, prefer an erfcx kernel (port xsf faddeeva erfcx, or Stan's Cody-based one after merge) over the 4-term asymptotic series, and return log Phi and the Mills ratio from one call for the probit/dep-cens score. Gate: R::pnorm(log.p=TRUE) grid on [-40,40] at 1e-12 rel, re-checked against R >= 4.5.0 given its pnorm underflow change. Also microbenchmark against the current fast_log_pnorm on [-8,8].

finite-differences.note: Rechecked on 2026-11-16 (code_commits_since is empty; the code is unchanged). Every EDI entry takes finite differences of an ANALYTIC gradient: central differences cost 2P gradient evaluations (numerical_hessian, the GLMM engine, ordinal GLMM, ZINB, Weibull frailty) and forward differences cost P+1 (Clayton, dep-cens), at P up to about 25, mostly once per fit. Alternatives checked this run, none faster at EDI's sizes: (1) Hyper-dual or forward-mode AD (TinyAD, nabla, autodiff) needs about P(P+1)/2 hyper-dual passes of a templated VALUE function, or P forward passes over the gradient, so it is no cheaper than 2P analytic-gradient calls and needs every functor templated (catalog NEW-fd-hessian already rejected forward-over-reverse AD). (2) Complex step cannot be applied twice for a Hessian; the pracma docs and Ridout 2009 (doi:10.1198/tast.2009.0013) apply a finite difference over a complex-step gradient, which saves at most a factor of 2 versus central differences and needs complex-safe functors (already rejected in the catalog). (3) sparseHessianFD-style graph colouring (Braun 2017, JSS doi:10.18637/jss.v082.i10) cuts gradient calls only when the Hessian is sparse; EDI's observed-information Hessians (GLMM fixed effects plus sigma, ZINB, survival) are dense, and the package was archived from CRAN on 2025-12-25. (4) pnd 0.1.3 (2026-05) adds step-size search and parallel evaluation; that is an accuracy and parallelism tool, more evaluations rather than fewer, and parallelism per fit would conflict with EDI's per-replicate threading. (5) Forward instead of central differences would halve the cost of the 2P entries but makes the error O(h) instead of O(h^2), so it fails the accuracy bar. The one repeated use, the ordinal-GLMM damped-Newton polish (fast_ordinal_glmm.cpp:459, up to 50 × 2d gradient calls), fires only when L-BFGS leaves a residual score above tolerance, and the already-Adopted analytic Louis-identity Hessian (v1.0.5-TODO-2) remains the right fix there. Reusing or quasi-Newton-updating the first FD Hessian across polish iterations is an optimizer change, not a derivative method, and has no source quantifying a gain. Previous conclusions for all five labels (FD Hessian + LU inversion, central FD, central FD of gradient, central FD Hessian, forward FD Hessian) stand.

bordered-normal-equations.note: Checked again on 2026-11-16 against the problem-level literature (Freedman-Lane/permuco, PALM, residual permutation test, Zhao-Ding covariate-adjusted FRT, arXiv FWL listing, MacKinnon fast pairs cluster bootstrap). For the permutation kernel the fastest exact form is the FWL rewrite: y_res = M y hoisted, numerator = masked sum over treated, denominator = n_T - ||L^{-1} X_c^T w_b||^2, i.e. O(n_T p + p^2) per draw. That is already planned (ols_distr_kernel_fwl.md, v1.2.0-TODO-9). Batching all B draws through one GEMM/TRSM gives the same flops, and masked sums beat GEMM for binary w. PALM's no-permutation, gamma and tail methods are approximate, so they lose exactness; catalog P4 already rejected saddlepoint/moment fits. For the bootstrap kernel the rows change, so its O(np^2) per draw is inherent. Rank-one Cholesky up/downdates cost O(p^2) per changed row, and about n rows change, so they are no gain. No new source overturns catalog §7 P5.

cholesky-ldlt.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. Use in this problem (BRT kernel): X[i_b] changes every replicate, so the factorization cannot be reused across draws. Rank-1 up/downdate per changed row totals O(np^2), the same as rebuilding. MacKinnon's fast pairs bootstrap only helps when G << n. The Eigen benchmark (fetched) confirms that LLT/LDLT is already the cheapest per-replicate solver (about 5x cheaper than QR at 10000x8).

qr-decomposition.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. Use in this problem: compute_rand_bootstrap_ci_affine_coefs (R loop, one qr() per draw with a 2-column RHS). Rows differ per draw, so one factorization per draw is needed; nothing algorithmically faster keeps QR's accuracy. Switching to normal equations plus LDLT is about 5x per the Eigen benchmark but squares the condition number. Porting the loop to C++ (catalog §10 TODO-9, mirroring compute_rand_bootstrap_ols_parallel_cpp) remains the implementation-level win; no new evidence.

cholesky-ldlt.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. I re-checked the Eigen DenseDecompositionBenchmark this run: LLT/LDLT on the normal equations, with AᵀA formation counted, is 4.3–5.4x faster than (ColPiv)HouseholderQR at 10000x8 and 10000x100, so fast_ols.cpp already uses the fastest dense method. On per-replicate use in this problem: get_likelihood_test_spec/simulate_under_lik_null call fit_null(δ) on the fixed X[,-j] for every δ, an O(np²) refactor each time (one factorization plus β(δ) = A·y − δ·A·x_j would make each δ O(p)). That is subsumed by catalog §10 TODO candidate 8 (closed-form CIs, 'Adopt'), which removes these refits entirely, so it is not re-reported. No code commits since the last research.

qr-decomposition.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. A single fit is still fine: one O(np²) LINPACK/Householder QR plus the C++ HC2 post-fit, sub-millisecond at EDI sizes. What is new is how this problem repeats it. Lin's randomization null (catalog §10 row continuous_lin.R compute_fast_randomization_distr, Prototype TODO candidate 9) calls lm.fit on the n×(2p+2) interacted design for every draw, about 2n(2p+2)² = 8n(p+1)² flops. Lin's estimator equals OLS fitted separately in each arm (Ding, A First Course in Causal Inference §30.2.2). So each draw needs only the two arm Gram matrices (n(p+1)²/2 in total, or only the smaller arm if G0 = G − G1) and two (p+1)×(p+1) solves. That is roughly 16x fewer flops (theoretical), on top of removing the R overhead that candidate 9 already targets. Filed as a finding to shape that kernel; the KK stacked fits (fit_combined) have no such arm structure and are unchanged.

findings.candidate: Arm-wise (block-diagonal) solve. With covariates centered at the full-sample means (w-independent), the interacted design spans the same column space as the block-diagonal [(1−w)[1,Xc], w[1,Xc]], so τ̂_Lin = (γ̂1) − (γ̂0) from separate per-arm OLS fits (Ding §30.2.2). Per draw: precompute G = ZᵀZ and Zᵀy once (Z = [1, Xc]); form the smaller arm's Gram G_a and Z_aᵀy in O(min(n_T,n_C)(p+1)²/2) (or both arms directly, n(p+1)²/2, for accuracy); get the other arm by subtraction; then two (p+1)×(p+1) LDLT/LLT solves. If the studentized statistic or HC2 is needed, per-arm leverages h_i = z_iᵀG_arm⁻¹z_i give the HC2 sandwich of the interacted fit, since the EHW sandwich is invariant to the reparametrization. That equivalence is my algebra, not a fetched statement; verify it numerically. Build this into the C++ batch kernel that candidate 9 already plans.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. Theoretical flop ratio about 8n(p+1)² / (n(p+1)²/2) ≈ 16x per draw (≈32x with the smaller-arm subtraction), on top of the 10–100x the catalog expects from moving the loop to C++. The Eigen benchmark shows normal-equations LLT at 4.3–5x faster than HouseholderQR even before the column-count halving.
findings.suggested_action: Fold into catalog §10 TODO candidate 9 (C++ batch randomization kernel for Lin): implement the per-draw step as arm-wise Gram + two small LDLT solves rather than a QR of the interacted design. Gate it on equality with the current lm.fit path (tolerance about 1e-10) on fixtures that include within-arm-constant covariates.

brute-force-distance.note: Euclidean²/L1 (optimal_blocks_distance.cpp, pair_dist_helpers.cpp): the output is n², so the brute-force O(n²p) loop is order-optimal. KD-trees, ball trees and ANN only help for k-NN or fixed-radius queries, not for a full matrix. The GEMM/Gram form stays rejected (catalog P1/P12). scikit-learn's docs (fetched) still warn of catastrophic cancellation and asymmetry, and SimSIMD/NumKong (fetched) explicitly rejects the |a|²+|b|²−2<a,b> decomposition for distances. New this run: Chen & Güttel's SNN preprint (arXiv 2212.07679 §4) claims the inner-product form has the same relative bound γ_{d+2}‖x−y‖² as the direct form. A 1-D example contradicts this: x = 1e8+1, y = 1e8 gives 100% relative error in double, so the claim does not overturn the rejection. The column-major stride remains incidental 9. The R-callback path's earlier finding still stands and is updated: per-call evidence shows Rcpp::Function is costlier than Rf_eval, so the XPtr path plus hoisted buffers remains the option. Low priority, because the ompr MILP dominates.

gauss-jordan-elimination.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. In this problem it is inverted once per design (O(p³)), not per replicate. Its replacement by LLT is already Adopt (v1.0.5-TODO-29 / catalog §8 TODO-1) and is covered by the Mahalanobis finding below. Eigen benchmark re-fetched: at 8x8, LLT takes 0.05 ms against 0.08 ms for PartialPivLU.

mahalanobis-quadratic-forms.note: The per-pair d'S⁻¹d is O(n²p²). Cholesky whitening once, then a direct Euclidean² loop, gives O(np²+n²p). This is the existing Adopt verdict (v1.0.5-TODO-29), and searches and fetches this run (skfolio relative-ridge Cholesky, Eigen benchmark, practitioner discussions) again confirm it as standard practice. Nothing new since the earlier result today: no 2025-26 paper changes the picture. Sketch-based online Mahalanobis estimation (arXiv 2309.01030) is approximate, so it is an estimator change and is not acceptable. Re-reported as confirmation only.

findings.candidate: Also accept a compiled user distance: an RcppXPtrUtils::cppXPtr pointer routed through EDI's existing user-compiled-fn plumbing, as parallelDist does for custom distances. Keep the R-function path, but hoist the xi/xj buffers out of the loop and evaluate through a pre-built call (Rf_lang3 + Rf_eval) rather than Rcpp::Function::operator().
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for this kernel. Mailing-list measurements seen in search results (not fetched; indicative only) put Rcpp::Function at several times the cost of a direct call. The XPtr path removes R interpreter overhead per pair entirely.
findings.suggested_action: Low-priority re-look: add XPtr custom-distance support and hoist the per-pair allocations. Otherwise keep the verdict 'Keep (inherent to a black-box R fn)'.

findings.candidate: LLT of (S + relative ridge × mean diag S), whiten once (Z = X L⁻ᵀ), then a direct per-pair squared-Euclidean loop on the rows of Z, not the Gram expansion: O(np² + n²p). This is the existing Adopt verdict, confirmed again.
findings.claimed_speedup: About p× on the pair loop (the audit's theoretical estimate). The Eigen benchmark at 8x8 gives LLT 0.05 ms against PartialPivLU 0.08 ms, which affects only the O(p³) part.
findings.suggested_action: No new action: this confirms v1.0.5-TODO-29 (catalog §8 TODO-1). Implement with a relative ridge and keep the direct-difference loop on Z.

list-scheduling.note: Unchanged since the earlier 2026-11-16 result: inference_suite.R has no commits since then (last commit 168c2e92), and run_all_inference_fork_dispatch still dispatches in build order (pending = seq_len(n_total)). The best acceptable improvement is still LPT order, and the catalog already has it as Adopt (§11 TODO-5; v1.0.5 audit TODO-34, scheduled as release_v1_2_0 TODO-22), so it is not re-reported. Newer work does not change this. Della Croce and Scatamacchia's LPT refinement (arXiv 1801.05489) only tightens the 4/3 − 1/(3m) bound to 4/3 − 1/(3(m−1)) and needs exact runtimes. The 2025 work on non-clairvoyant makespan with predictions (arXiv 2504.10945) gives competitive ratios as a function of prediction error, not a practical improvement over LPT driven by estimates. Work stealing, OpenMP dynamic schedules and mirai's FIFO dispatcher do not help: dispatch here is already dynamic, one task at a time. An R-bloggers benchmark found that longest-first plus dynamic load balancing comes within 1% of the optimal makespan, versus 151% of optimal for dynamic balancing in the original order. That supports the existing LPT verdict. Implementation caveat: the existing manifest (R/package_tests/ci/test_runtimes.csv) holds runtimes per test, not per (class, method, type) task, so LPT needs per-task estimates, e.g. the fit_secs column of past results. Each estimate should be capped at max_secs_per_class, since timed-out tasks are killed at that limit.

inverse-transform-sampling.note: No code commits since the last research (2026-11-16). Cox event-time inversion: replacing the linear which(cumhaz >= tgt) scan with findInterval (O(n log K)) is already Adopt (§12 TODO-7) and still the right fix. mets::rchaz/sim_phreg (Apache-2.0) invert a piecewise-LINEAR interpolation of Breslow. That is an estimator change: it simulates continuous times, not draws from the step-function Breslow fit, so it is not a drop-in. Ordinal categorical draws: each observation has its own probability vector, so the alias method's per-draw table rebuild gives no gain. Gumbel-max needs K exponential/Gumbel draws per observation and changes RNG consumption, so it is no faster than one runif against cumulative probabilities (already incidental I16). Clayton pairs: closed-form conditional inversion uses 2 uniforms, against 3 draws plus a gamma for Marshall–Olkin. The copula qrng vignette's general preference for stochastic representations applies to higher dimensions, not to the bivariate case.

parametric-bootstrap.note: Re-checked for anything new since 2026-11-16. The arXiv title listing ('parametric bootstrap', newest first) has nothing on reducing refit cost after 2025; the newest item, 2609.10038, is an applied CI. The k-step bootstrap (Davidson & MacKinnon 1999) still stands as an opt-in estimator-change option (re-reported). Already tracked: SMC early stop (TODO-8), memoization (TODO-1) and the fixed critical value (TODO-9). Besag–Clifford, which the catalog rejected, is exactly pbkrtest::seqPBmodcomp's rule (stop after h exceedances). Stoepker & Castro (arXiv 2409.18908) give anytime-valid sequential MC p-values and belong with TODO-8, not a new finding. Kojadinovic's weighted multiplier bootstrap (arXiv 1202.5682) is a large-sample substitute for GoF tests, not for LR calibration at small n, so it is not acceptable. Gaussian/count null-simulation draws cost O(nK) and are negligible next to the refits.

random-variate-generation.note: Simulation DGP only, O(n) per dataset. Ziggurat generators (zigg, GPL>=2, claims about 7.4x faster normals; dqrng, AGPL-3) and PTRS Poisson would change the random stream, breaking parity with R's set.seed, and zigg's own page warns of lower quality and shorter periods. No gain at EDI's sizes, where the refits dominate.

findings.candidate: k-step parametric bootstrap: per replicate, take a fixed small number k of Newton steps from the original-sample estimate instead of iterating to convergence. Offered as an opt-in mode (re-reported from the previous run; still stands).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by the sources. Davidson & MacKinnon (1999) say only that very few steps are needed, fewer for LR tests and with Newton than quasi-Newton. The saving is the iterations beyond k per refit, which is modest because replicates are already warm-started.
findings.suggested_action: Record the k-step bootstrap in the catalog §9 J options table as an estimator-change option. Before prototyping, measure the iteration counts the warm-started workers actually use. If they converge in 2–3 Newton steps already, drop it.

qr-decomposition.note: Researched in dense-linear-algebra. How this problem uses it matters, because the QR is repeated per arrival in 4 subsets, so I re-checked row-append/updating QR. Re-checked: arXiv 2412.05905 (R-only QR updating) and fastQR 1.1.5 (CRAN, 2026-11-10). Neither mentions pivoting or rank-deficient updates, and neither handles the per-t re-centring/re-scaling that changes every row. No 2026 work on updating rank-revealing QR after row appends turned up. The previous conclusion stands: the practical wins are already tracked, namely dropping the redundant second QR (v1.0.5-TODO-29) and recomputing only when the varying set changes (kk14_incremental_covariance.md TODO-1/2).

streaming-moments.note: Trivial: scale_columns is a closed-form two-pass z-score, O(tp) per call. A new preprint (Reichel, arXiv 2605.00247, 2026-04) compares Gram, Welford and Chan-Golub-LeVeque streaming covariance. It finds Gram fastest but Welford uniquely robust to cancellation. That supports the Welford update already chosen in kk14_incremental_covariance.md; it is not a new speedup.

ab-timing-comparison.note: Marked trivial (developer tooling), but it is the cost driver of the tuner: repetitions per cell × fit time. The previous finding still stands and is restated with stronger sources. Interleaving is already done, but the unpaired median ± 2·IQR rule throws away the pairing. A paired analysis of per-round differences reaches a decision with fewer repetitions. Options: a paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test, or a bootstrap CI, with a noise band and adaptive stopping. Practice since the last run: perfgate-paired uses a paired t on interleaved differences and adds pairs until the CI excludes zero. Laaber et al. 2019 show that same-instance randomized interleaving detects slowdowns of 10% or less. Melis 2026 (arXiv 2606.17261) gives consistent contrast estimators for stateful benchmarking. No code commits since last_researched.

exhaustive-autotuning.note: Unchanged. Each axis has 2–3 candidates on a small family × n_grid. Bayesian optimization (Kernel Tuner BO, Willemsen et al. 2021) targets large constrained spaces, and none of the sources tested it on spaces this small. Racing (irace 4.5.1, 2026-10-29) is already catalog §12 option (m) and tracked by v1.0.5-TODO-12. The saving comes from fewer repetitions per A/B, which is covered under ab-timing-comparison.

linear-search.note: Unchanged. The n_grid has 3–5 points, so bisection saves at most 1–2 points. Probabilistic (noisy) bisection (Waeber–Frazier–Henderson) pays off only with many candidate points. Cost is dominated by repetitions per point, which the paired-difference finding addresses.

findings.candidate: Analyze the per-round paired differences a_i − b_i with a paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test, or a seeded percentile-bootstrap CI. Accept only when the CI lies entirely beyond a noise band (keep 5%). Stop adaptively: add pairs until the CI is decisive, with a minimum and a maximum number of pairs (perfgate-paired; zenbench). Randomizing the order within each round (RMIT, Laaber et al. 2019) is the established design for a noisy host. Melis 2026 gives designs whose contrast estimators stay consistent under stateful bias.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for repetition savings. Google Benchmark reports about 40% lower run-to-run variance from random interleaving, which EDI already does. Laaber et al. report detecting slowdowns of 10% or less with same-instance randomized interleaving. Adaptive stopping saves repetitions on clear wins and losses (the tools describe this qualitatively).
findings.suggested_action: No verdict change. Implement the paired-difference half of v1.0.5-TODO-12 as described (paired test or seeded bootstrap CI, 5% noise band, adaptive stopping with a minimum and maximum number of pairs), and self-check it on seeded synthetic timings.

permuted-blocks.note: Algorithmically optimal: one Fisher–Yates shuffle per block and an O(1) pop per assignment, so O(n) per draw. I found no faster algorithm in the 2025–2026 literature. Batched bounded draws (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, doi 10.1002/spe.3369) save little on blocks of a few to tens of entries and would change the stream, so I still reject them. What changed since the previous result: the random-block-size design now uses random_block_size_redraw_w_cpp. Its draw_ws_raw calls it once per replicate through replicate(r, …), and each call rebuilds a std::map<std::string,…> from the n string keys. The SPBR path (generate_permutations_spbr_internal) avoids this: it converts keys to dense integer ids once and loops over nsim inside C++. randomizr 2.0.1 made the same change (one C++ call instead of per-block R calls) and reports a 5–8× speedup. That is a constant-factor finding, not an algorithmic one. SPBR, the per-arrival assign_wt functions and the dead spbr_redraw_w_cpp are unchanged.

findings.candidate: Generalise generate_permutations_spbr_internal (generate_permutations.cpp) to accept a vector of block sizes, or add a sibling that does. Map keys to dense integer ids once, keep reusable per-stratum std::vector<int> state, loop over all r draws inside one C++ call, and write directly into an n×r integer matrix. This is the batched pattern EDI already uses for SPBR, and the one randomizr 2.0.1 adopted for block_ra.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not measured for EDI. As an analogue, randomizr 2.0.1 NEWS reports 5–8× (e.g. N=20,000 with 2,000 blocks: 8.9 ms → 1.1 ms) from replacing per-block R-level calls with a single C++ call. The EDI gain comes from removing r R→C++ round trips plus the per-replicate string conversion and map lookups.
findings.suggested_action: Prototype a batched random-block-size kernel with dense stratum ids, modelled on generate_permutations_spbr_internal. Check marginal and block-size distribution equivalence against the current function, and benchmark draw_ws_raw at typical n (100–1000) and r (1000–10000).

pocock-simon.note: No faster acceptable method found. Rechecked against the code at 8b718ae1 (no commits since the last research, code_commits_since is empty). (1) Per arrival: pocock_simon_assign_internal and the replay cores score only the subject's J levels for K=2, so each arrival costs O(J). This is the minimum, because the rule has to read every one of those levels. Possible constant-factor micro-optimization, not an algorithm change: for K=2, G0−G1 = 2·Σ w_j (c0_j − c1_j), so one weighted sum and a sign test would replace the two variance sums. It could break bit-identity of tie detection when weights are not integers (floating-point rounding near ties), so it is not filed. (2) Null draws: each Monte Carlo replicate has to replay the whole path, O(nJ) per draw, O(B·n·J) in total. Exact enumeration would mean up to 2^n paths. The real levers are already tracked: replicate-level parallelism with per-draw seeds (carat uses OpenMP per its JSS paper keywords; EDI tracks this under TODO-149, parallel RNG streams) and Besag–Clifford / adaptive repetition counts (Zhang–Zhao–Luo arXiv 2302.05977; tracked under TODO-156). Neither is new evidence against the catalog rows. (3) Updated vs previous: I withdrew the previous SIGA finding (Kojima arXiv 2608.05527, still v1 only with no code). It replaces the randomization distribution with a Gaussian approximation for power evaluation, so it is an estimator change with no exact-test analogue. EDI also runs no nested-rerandomization power evaluation, so there is nothing for it to speed up. The previous record also filed a finding while marking the method no_faster_acceptable_found, which was inconsistent. New 2026 minimization papers change the design rather than the computation: Tao and Zhang arXiv 2611.08378 (Nov 2026, improved minimization without shift), Zhang arXiv 2602.10760, and Fang and Ma arXiv 2602.22648. (4) R-side cost: draw_ws_raw still calls get_subject_levels_idx once per row (a vapply over the strata columns with a lookup in a named vector). A per-column vectorised match() would remove the per-row R overhead. That is catalog incidental #9, an implementation issue. The inventory's "rescans all t rows … O(n²k)" wording for ensure_factor_metadata is stale: since the full_scan guard, only row t is registered after the first call.

pvalue-combination-rules.note: Marked trivial: the combination rules themselves are O(1)/O(k) closed forms (Fisher chi^2_4, Stouffer, min-p, CCT) and nothing is faster. No code changed since the last run (code_commits_since empty); the CCT tail-accurate form (Adopt, v1.0.5 TODO-7) is still unimplemented, since inference_suite.R:4062-4063 still uses tan/atan directly. This run confirmed the ACAT reference code (threshold 1e-15, 1/(p*pi), pcauchy upper tail). New this run: (1) a speed point in the same inventory rows. fisher_noncentral_two_sided_pval (zhang_exact_speedups.cpp:41) recomputes 3(S+1) lgamma calls on every call, although only the x*log_or term depends on delta_0, and it is called at every step of the Zhang CI bisection. R's fisher.test caches logdc once and adds log(ncp)*support per ncp. (2) Precision: the Stouffer branch's qnorm(1-p/2) and min-p's 1-(1-p)^2 lose accuracy for tiny p (robustness, not speed). (3) The previous DPComb/Contador-Wu estimator-change finding still stands; DPComb is still 1.0.1 (2026-08-22). New comparators are TCCT (arXiv 2506.12489) and the mid-p convex-order bounds (Rubin-Delanchy et al.), both estimator changes.

findings.candidate: Compute the central log-choose terms (log C(row1,x) + log C(row2,col1-x)) once per data set, cached alongside incid_exact_zhang_stats or computed in a per-CI-search C++ helper. Each delta_0 then needs only log_w[x] = logdc[x] + x*log_or, a log-sum-exp and the two-sided sum. This is the pattern R's own fisher.test uses: logdc is computed once by do.logdc, and dnhyper adds log(ncp)*support for each ncp.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. Per evaluation it replaces about 3(S+1) lgamma calls with S+1 multiply-adds; the log-sum-exp and exp calls remain, so the expected gain is roughly 2-4x on that function. It is multiplied by the number of bisection steps in each CI search, which is the hot path for this row.
findings.suggested_action: Low-priority micro-optimisation. When touching zhang_exact_speedups.cpp, add a variant that takes precomputed central log-weights (or a vectorised p(delta_0) over the bisection), and test it for equality against the current function.

findings.candidate: Tail-accurate equivalents at the same O(1) cost: qnorm(p/2, lower.tail=FALSE), and 2*pnorm(abs(z), lower.tail=FALSE) for the combined p; -expm1(2*log1p(-p)) for min-p; and optionally the df=4 closed form p1*p2*(1 - log(p1*p2)) for Fisher. For CCT, use the ACAT form: 1/(p*pi) for p < 1e-15 and pcauchy(T, lower.tail=FALSE).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not a speedup; same cost. This is a numerical robustness finding.
findings.suggested_action: Fold into v1.0.5 TODO-7 (CCT tail numerics): apply the same lower.tail/log1p rewrites to the Stouffer and min-p branches of zhang_combine_exact_pvals, with unit tests at p = 1e-20.

findings.candidate: Re-reported from the previous run, still standing. It is the Wasserstein-adjusted discrete combination of Contador & Wu (SJS 2025, DOI 10.1111/sjos.12787; arXiv 2309.07692), extended to Stouffer and the other rules in arXiv 2508.02647 (under revision at JCGS), and implemented in DPComb 1.0.1 (CRAN, MIT), which supports binomial and noncentral-hypergeometric components. Related: mid-p combination with convex-order bounds (Rubin-Delanchy, Heard & Lawson, arXiv 1505.05068), which are conservative yet more powerful. If the exact joint convolution option in catalog §11 is chosen, it can be computed in O(d log d + S log S) rather than O(d*S): sort each component's support by its log-p, take cumulative masses, and use a two-pointer sweep over the threshold log pM + log pR <= obs.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not a speedup over the current O(1) combination; this is an estimator (test) change. The sources give no runtime numbers. The sort and two-pointer note is my own complexity remark on the catalog's O(d*S) exact option, not a sourced claim.
findings.suggested_action: Keep as a comparator for resolving the Investigate verdict in catalog §11. Use DPComb as a test oracle if a mid-p or adjusted variant is added. Use the two-pointer sweep if the exact convolution is adopted.

barrodale-roberts-simplex.note: The single-fit verdict is unchanged. quantreg 6.1 (2025-03-10) ChangeLog has no br changes, and fn/pfn/sfn/conquer stay rejected at EDI sizes. CFM 2022 single fit at n=500, k=8: simplex 0.05 s, fn 0.02 s, pqreg 0.02 s. Updated so the conclusion matches the finding: the exact preprocessing bootstrap (CFM 2022 Alg. 4) is benchmarked against a simplex bootstrap (Stata bsqreg). It applies to EDI's br replicate fits (bootstrap and randomization loops) as much as to the fn path. Low confidence at EDI's small p. New since the last run: Naik–Kundu coordinate-descent LAD (arXiv 2603.19336, 2026) has no timings and no exactness guarantee for the LP vertex, and Shetiya et al. strongly polynomial QR is O(n^{d-1} log² n), impractical for d>2. The Adopt item (rq.fit on the matrix instead of formula rq) still stands.

induced-smoothing.note: Code changed since the audit: aftsrr_for_matched_pairs/_reservoir now pass se='ISMB', B=100 when a variance is needed, and se='NULL', B=0 for estimate-only. F22 (B=0 gives an NA SE) is therefore fixed, inside a digest-seeded RNG wrapper. With B=100, the aftgee source runs viEmp's for(i in 1:B) loop: 100 extra O(n²p) smoothed-Gehan estimating-function evaluations per variance fit. ISCF (Johnson–Strawderman closed-form V, viClo) needs one O(n²) pass, gives the same β̂, needs no RNG and supports cluster ids. That is the finding. The point solve itself has no faster equivalent: aftgee 1.2.1 is still current, and nothing new gives O(n log n) for the smoothed Gehan equation, whose pairwise r_ij scale prevents a sort-sweep. fastAFT (Huang 2013, 2–3 orders of magnitude faster) is a different estimator (asymptotics-guided Newton on weighted log-rank), so using it would be an estimator change.

interior-point-lp.note: The previous run filed the preprocessing-bootstrap finding but marked this method no_faster. Corrected here: the finding is re-reported with sources re-fetched this run (ar5iv 1909.05782 tables; DOI 10.1007/s00181-020-01898-0). At EDI's n a single fn fit is no faster than br (n=500, k=8: fn 0.02 s, pfn 0.04 s). The fn point fit vs br BB-replicate inconsistency in inference_proportion_quantile_regr.R is a correctness issue and remains the existing Prototype (v1.0.6-TODO-6 per the row). The HiGHS (MIT) and scikit-learn highs solvers are generic LP codes with no published win over quantreg at small dense n.

sandwich-estimator.note: Hendricks–Koenker nid (quantreg): no change since 5.74 and nothing faster that is the same estimator ('ker' and bootstrap are different; the extra τ±h fits are inherent). Updated because the rank-AFT SE in this problem is also a sandwich (Johnson–Strawderman A⁻¹VA⁻ᵀ). Its V is currently the empirical multiplier version (ISMB, B=100). The closed-form V (ISCF) removes the B-loop; see the finding. That changes the SE estimator, not β̂.

findings.candidate: aftsrr(se='ISCF', B=1): the Johnson–Strawderman sandwich with closed-form V (viClo: one getSi pass building N² pairwise differences, aggregated by cluster through rowsum(id)). Same smoothed Gehan β̂ and same induced-smoothing slope A. B is unused by viClo, but aftsrr only runs the variance branch when B>0, so B must be ≥1. Optionally keep ISMB as a fallback when ISCF returns a non-finite value.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. From the aftgee source fetched this run, the variance step drops from B=100 O(n²p) estimating-function evaluations to one O(n²) closed-form pass, so variance-path fits should drop roughly by the share that the 100 resamples take of the total (the point solve is ~10–50 evaluations under BBsolve). The win grows with n because every evaluation is quadratic.
findings.suggested_action: Investigate: on EDI fixtures (matched and reservoir, n 50–1000), compare ISCF vs ISMB(B=100) SE values and timings. If they agree within the A/B tolerance for coverage, switch to se='ISCF', B=1 and drop the RNG wrapper from the SE path. Catalog this as an option on the NEW-rank-AFT row.

findings.candidate: Preprocessing bootstrap (Chernozhukov, Fernández-Val & Melly 2022, Algorithm 4, extending Portnoy–Koenker 1997). Predict residual signs in each replicate from the full-sample β̂(τ), solve the reduced LP on the M ≈ m·(kn)^{1/2} uncertain observations plus two glob observations, then verify the signs and repair any that are wrong. The paper reports numerically identical estimates to the standard solver.
findings.claimed_speedup: CFM 2022 (ar5iv 1909.05782), bootstrap panel for median regression with k=20 and 50 replications: Stata bsqreg simplex 2.63 s vs preprocessing 0.42 s at n=500 (~6×), 3.14 vs 0.63 s at n=1,000 (~5×), 8.19 vs 1.89 s at n=5,000 (~4×). For a single fit at n=500, k=8, preprocessing gives no gain (fn 0.02 s vs pfn 0.04 s).
findings.suggested_action: Do not implement now. Record it in the catalog options tables (NEW-quantile-LP / NEW-quantreg) as considered: exact, cited DOI 10.1007/s00181-020-01898-0, gain unproven at EDI's small p. Re-look only if profiling after the rq.fit Adopt shows replicate QR fits dominate at n ≳ 1,000.
