inverse-transform-sampling.note: norm_rand (AS 241 inversion) must reproduce R's 'Inversion' N(0,1) stream bit for bit. A ziggurat is at most marginally faster: an informal MT benchmark in the chasethedevil blog gave AS241 0.49 s vs ZIGNOR 0.44 s. Box-Muller and the ziggurat both change the stream, and no hot loop calls norm_rand. Checked what is new since 2026-11-16: nothing overturns the catalog P1 row. The alias method and binary-search inversion do not apply, because EDI does no weighted categorical sampling (catalog P2, N/A). Keep.

lemire-bounded-integer.note: Single draws are already optimal. Lemire's method is also what numpy Generator.integers cites, and what Randompack (arXiv 2605.05099, May 2026) uses. Bitmask rejection, R's R_unif_index, uses more bits on average. The previous finding still stands: batched ranged generation (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, doi 10.1002/spe.3369) can cut generator words per fisher_yates_shuffle. It changes the stream and is not measured with MT19937. Updated this run: the DOI is confirmed via Crossref, and Apache Commons RNG opened RNG-187 to adopt it, estimating 'up to 2-fold for smaller arrays' (an estimate, not a measurement).

mersenne-twister.note: mt_genrand, unif_rand (R fixup) and the RRng(uint32) LCG-scramble seeding all exist to reproduce R's MT stream bit for bit. SFMT, xoshiro, PCG and Philox are faster (Randompack Table 7: xoshiro256++ 0.3-1.07 ns per 64 bits), but each was already rejected in catalog P1 for parity and is tracked as performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md TODO-149(c). Nothing dated after 2026-11-16 overturns that. The 2026 arXiv entries (2605.05099, 2605.18227) do not benchmark R's MT. The seeding cost matters only where a fresh RRng is built per draw index; that is covered under seed-derivation.

seed-derivation.note: The SplitMix64 mix is O(1) and fine. The cost lies downstream, and I re-checked the code: rerandomization_helpers.cpp:230, design_fixed_greedy.cpp:97/147, optimal_design_search.cpp:167/214 and binary_match_search.cpp:39 each build a fresh 2.5 KB MT RRng per draw index. That is 675 LCG steps plus a 624-word twist, before about n bounded draws and an n×p mat-vec. New evidence: one benchmark finds mt19937 seeding several hundred times slower than xoshiro256ss (quuxplusone); Random123 keyed generators have 'little or no overhead' per instance; and arXiv 2603.11084 (Mar 2026) argues for counter-based RNGs keyed by event id, which matches EDI's index-keyed design. Robustness note: seed_for_index truncates to 32 bits, so with D draws P(duplicate stream) ≈ 1−exp(−D²/2^33), about 0.69 at D=10^5. seed_from_unif01 and draw_seed_from_r cost O(1), one R uniform each; nothing faster is needed.

findings.candidate: Key a small-state or counter-based generator directly by (master_seed, draw index), with the within-draw position as the counter. Options are Philox4x32-10 or Threefry from Random123 (header-only, BSD-3-Clause), or xoshiro/PCG seeded through SplitMix64. Child streams need no R parity, because R never produces them. Index-keyed determinism, and therefore thread-count invariance, is kept. Widening the key to 64 bits or more also removes the 32-bit birthday-collision risk.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for this workload. Random123 docs (fetched) say 'little or no overhead to creating billions of unique' generators and 'a few cycles per byte'. The quuxplusone benchmark (QuickBench) says mt19937 is about '500 times slower to seed' than xoshiro256ss and about half its output speed. Randompack (arXiv 2605.05099) Table 7 gives Philox-4x64 at 1.07-2.75 ns and xoshiro256++ at 0.73-1.07 ns per 64 bits on non-Windows platforms. My own reading of the code, not a measurement: at n=100, p=5 the setup is about 1,300 word operations, against about 100 draws plus 500 FMAs of real work per candidate.
findings.suggested_action: Micro-benchmark RRng(seed_for_index(...)) construction plus the first draw against the per-candidate work in rerandomization_helpers.cpp at n in {50, 200, 500} and p in {2, 10}. If setup is more than about 30% of a candidate, prototype a Philox-keyed (master, index) child stream behind the seed_for_index call sites, with a key of 64 bits or more. Fix the 32-bit seed truncation in any case. Salmon et al. 2011 is doi 10.1145/2063384.2063405.

findings.candidate: Batched ranged random integer generation (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, Software: Practice and Experience 55(1), doi 10.1002/spe.3369; arXiv 2408.06213). It draws k unbiased bounded integers from one word when the product of the ranges is at most 2^L. With L=32, two draws fit per word whenever the remaining length is at most 2^16, which always holds at EDI's n.
findings.claimed_speedup: The arXiv abstract says it can 'more than double the speed of unbiased random shuffling' for small to moderate arrays. Apache Commons RNG-187 estimates 'up to 2-fold for smaller arrays', and adds that slower generators gain more. Neither benchmarks MT19937 with 32-bit words, so the gain for EDI is not quantified.
findings.suggested_action: Add as an option row under catalog P2 and bundle it with the stream-changing RNG work under TODO-149(c). The MIT-licensed batched_random repository is a reference implementation to port and test against.

monte-carlo-randomization.note: The previous result was dated 2026-11-16, and no code commits have touched these files since. This run checked work dated after that result and looked again across the whole problem. (1) The previous finding still stands: Fischer & Ramdas, sequential Monte Carlo testing by betting (JRSS-B 2025, doi:10.1093/jrsssb/qkaf014; arXiv v5 is still the latest, re-fetched). It is anytime-valid and can stop early under both the null and the alternative, whereas Besag–Clifford (v1.0.6 TODO-156) stops early only for futility. No R or C++ implementation was found. The rule is closed form and changes the reported p-value, so it would be opt-in. (2) New candidates checked and rejected: (a) Cheap Permutation Testing (Domingo-Enrich, Dwivedi & Mackey, arXiv 2502.07672 v3, Jul 2026) permutes bins of units instead of units. That is a different reference distribution, not the design's assignment distribution, so it is an estimator change and breaks design-based randomization inference for Efron, KK and other restricted designs. (b) Koning, 'More Power by using Fewer Permutations' (arXiv 2307.12832) uses a small algebraic subgroup of permutations. That is likewise a different test and needs group structure that sequential designs lack. (c) Hash-augmented adaptive multilevel splitting (Golikov et al., arXiv 2607.12853, hamstest, MIT) gives accurate *small* p-values. A 501-draw test never resolves p ≈ 1e-6, so this does not speed up EDI's regime. (d) Barber & Ramdas, arXiv 2607.23010, is validity theory without joint exchangeability (P ≤ 2α), not a speedup. (e) Saddlepoint and exact DP/FFT approaches are already in catalog P4, and nothing newer was found. (3) Per-replicate kernels: the masked-sum mean difference (O(n), memory-bound; bit-packed popcount only yields n_T), the rank kernels (hoisting already tracked) and per-replicate rematching (the sort is required) have nothing faster. The O(r) two-sided tail count is already the floor. The user-statistic path needs r × cost(stat). (4) Robustness side note, filed as a separate finding: EDI reports b/r with a 1/r or 2/r floor, not (b+1)/(r+1). Phipson & Smyth show b/r understates the p-value by about 1/r, so the test is slightly anti-conservative. Catalog P4 wrongly says the current rule is (b+1)/(r+1); the inventory row says 'Not (b+1)/(r+1)'.

findings.candidate: Anytime-valid sequential Monte Carlo testing by betting (Fischer & Ramdas, JRSS-B 2025). Test martingales bet on whether each redrawn statistic is ≥ or ≤ the observed one. The p-process 1/sup W_t is valid at any stopping time, including a budget cap at r. The binomial and binomial-mixture strategies, and the anytime-valid Besag–Clifford variant, are closed form and O(1) per draw. Draws can be generated in batches from the design, so the kernels stay unchanged.
findings.claimed_speedup: From the paper, not measured in EDI. In the previous run's reading of arXiv 2401.07365v5 §7.4 (Fisher sharp-null example, 53 units, p = 0.026, α = 0.05), the binomial strategy needed a mean of 85 permutations, the binomial mixture 147 and Besag–Clifford (h = 10) 200, against EDI's fixed 501, so roughly 3–6× fewer draws. Gains are smaller at α = 0.01, with some power loss. This run re-checked that the paper is unchanged at v5 and published as JRSS-B qkaf014.
findings.suggested_action: When v1.0.6 TODO-156 (Besag–Clifford) is designed, include the Fischer–Ramdas binomial-mixture / anytime-valid BC rule as a compared option for the standalone p-value. Add it to catalog P4, and correct P4's claim that Besag–Clifford saves draws when the result is clearly significant. Keep fixed r as the default.

findings.candidate: Use the Phipson–Smyth exact Monte Carlo p-value (b+1)/(r+1) per tail, two-sided 2·min(b_ge+1, b_le+1)/(r+1) capped at 1, as SciPy permutation_test and perm do. This is a robustness and validity fix, not a speedup.
findings.claimed_speedup: None (cost unchanged, O(r)). Phipson & Smyth say b/r understates the p-value by about 1/r; at r = 501 that is about 0.002, which makes the test slightly anti-conservative near α.
findings.suggested_action: Fix the catalog P4 description of the current rule. Decide, as a policy question, whether to switch to (b+1)/(r+1), or document why b/r with a floor is retained. Bundle the decision with the v1.0.6 TODO-156 stopping-rule work, since both change the reported p-value.

mahalanobis-quadratic-forms.note: Rechecked on 2026-11-16 with no code commits since then. rerandomization_search_cpp already whitens once (LLT, M = L^-1 X'/n) and computes squaredNorm of M(2w-1), which is the best form. The one GEMM-based upgrade for compute_objective_vals_cpp is already tracked in rerandomization_objective_vals_gemm.md. New searches on batched Mahalanobis via GEMM/whitening and on rank-one/rank-two T^2 updates turned up only generic guidance (whiten, then take Euclidean norms) and no new benchmark. fastrerandomize's October-2026 dev notes report GPU balance-GEMM throughput, but that is accelerator hardware, not an algorithm EDI can use.

rejection-sampling.note: The earlier findings still stand: early abandoning of the O(np) check (exact, unquantified) and PSRSRR (arXiv 2602.07613, still only v1; a design-law change). New since then: Langevin-Gradient Rerandomization (arXiv 2604.07524, Apr 2026). It is explicitly non-uniform over the acceptable set and valid only with FRTs conditional on the LGR mechanism, so it is a design-law change, not a speedup. The 2025 review arXiv 2512.05290 says neither PSRR nor BRAIN samples uniformly, which confirms the catalog's MCMC rejection. The review also cites 'mirror allocations' (Johansson & Schultzberg 2020, doi 10.1080/10618600.2020.1753531): for symmetric criteria with n_T = n/2, f(1-w) = f(w), and this is exact for EDI's d = M(2w-1) because d flips sign. That halves the candidates generated, but the r draws come in complement pairs and are not i.i.d. For a difference-in-means FRT under the sharp null, T(1-w) = -T(w), so a mirror adds no information to a two-sided test. It is not an acceptable speedup and is noted for the catalog only. i.i.d. Fisher-Yates rejection remains the exact sampler.

selection-algorithm.note: A full order() on N scores, O(N log N), is dominated by the O(N·np) scoring. New check: R's sort(partial=) falls back to a full sort when more than 10 positions are given, and order() has no partial mode. Getting a gain would therefore need C++ nth_element (or Floyd-Rivest, e.g. miniselect, BSL-1.0) on indices, with a tie-handling rule. That is still a trivial gain; nothing new overturns the catalog's verdict.

findings.candidate: Early abandoning (re-reported from 2026-11-16). Accumulate the per-component terms of f (d_j^2 or |d_j|) one row of M at a time and reject once the running sum exceeds the cutoff. The terms are nonnegative, so the decision is unchanged except for floating-point rounding exactly at the cutoff.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for this problem. arXiv 2102.05221 reports a 'substantial speedup' from early abandoning in threshold search, but for elastic distances. The gain is bounded by the O(np) share of each draw, since Fisher-Yates O(n) remains.
findings.suggested_action: Add a catalog §P6 row. If it is prototyped, benchmark at n = 100-1000, p = 5-20, p_acc = 1e-2 to 1e-4.

findings.candidate: MCMC and gradient samplers: PSRSRR (arXiv 2602.07613, pair-switching MH plus an asymptotic uniformity correction) and, new this run, Langevin-Gradient Rerandomization (arXiv 2604.07524, SGLD on a continuous relaxation, explicitly non-uniform on the balanced set).
findings.claimed_speedup: PSRSRR: 10-10,000x, about 66x on STAR with n ~ 974 (arXiv 2602.07613). LGR: 'orders of magnitude' in high d, unquantified in the text (n = 500, p_a = 0.01; Figures 1-2 of arXiv 2604.07524).
findings.suggested_action: Keep the default sampler. Add arXiv 2604.07524 (doi 10.48550/arXiv.2604.07524) next to PSRSRR in catalog P6's MCMC row as 'invalid for the uniform design law'. If an alternative design is ever offered, it should be a separate, opt-in design.

barrodale-roberts-simplex.note: The previous finding stands: the intercept-only sign-flip refit is a closed-form τ-quantile (nth_element), folded into the existing Adopt. Checked this run: there are no code commits since the last run. quantreg is still 6.1 (2025-03-10) on CRAN. Chernozhukov–Fernández-Val–Melly preprocessing (arXiv 1909.05782) has headline gains only at n=50,000, p=20. New since the last run: PALB (arXiv 2512.20682, Dec 2025), an exact LAD *line* fit reported faster than BR/LP. It covers only τ=0.5 and a single line, so it does not apply to EDI's general-τ, multi-covariate refits. The p=0 case is already better served by the closed form. HiGHS (sklearn) has no small-n benchmark against br.

bayesian-bootstrap.note: BB and PB refits are already warm-started at the full-data MLE. New this run: fwb 1.0.0 (CRAN 2026-10-14) refits through glm.fit with the original coefficients as the start, which is the same strategy EDI uses. WBB / constrained WBB (arXiv 2606.04237) and BLB change the estimator or the target. No exact-refit speedup found.

lbfgs.note: Code unchanged: params0.setZero() and 'lbfgs' at fast_weibull_regression.cpp:706-713. LBFGSpp is still v0.4.0, with no performance changes; v0.4.0 adds final_approx_inverse_hessian(), which could seed warm starts. New supporting evidence for the already-Prototype warm start (catalog §5 TODO-3): IceCube arXiv 2609.12941 reports a median 3.6× reduction in likelihood evaluations from warm-started L-BFGS-B, though on a different problem. The k-step bootstrap remains an estimator change.

newton-raphson.note: The previous O(K) aggregated-Newton finding for p=1 compute_coxph_rand_bootstrap_cpp stands; that function still has no caller. Update: FastSurvival 2.0.0 (CRAN 2026-11-16) switched coxph_fast from the closed-form Pike–Halley approximation to Newton-Raphson, with coxph's start, convergence criterion and 20-iteration cap, plus Efron/Breslow ties. The reference implementation now matches the coxph estimator exactly. It makes no new speed claims. Trust-region Newton (Lin et al.) targets large sparse problems, so it gives no gain at EDI's small p.

parallel-refit-loop.note: The previous FRB finding (an estimator change, opt-in only) stands; FRB 2.0-1 (2024-10-07, GPL ≥ 3) is unchanged. New: ROBU (Christidis & Salibián-Barrera, arXiv 2606.26611, Jun 2026) speeds up MM initialisation, which is relevant only if a true MM is adopted. The HPC task view (2026-10-28) and the mirai/future vignettes offer R-level parallelism, which is no faster than EDI's in-C++ OpenMP. The stereotype parallel L-BFGS loop is still dead code.

warm-start-continuation.note: Sequential null anchoring is the standard continuation answer. Searches turned up only general warm-start evidence (arXiv 1803.08021, which reuses the original solution as the start, and arXiv 2609.12941). The k-step and one-step bootstraps (Davidson–MacKinnon; Andrews 2002) change the statistic. Nothing new found.

worker-reuse.note: Permuting w changes the interaction columns, so QR reuse and the wild-bootstrap precompute tricks (fwildclusterboot, now archived on CRAN) do not apply. No exact permutation shortcut exists for interaction models (lmPerm docs, permuco JSS). The recorded C++ batch-kernel Prototypes stand. quantreg has no new release.

findings.candidate: (Re-reported, still stands.) The intercept-only refit is the sample τ-quantile, computable with one std::nth_element (O(m)), with all draws batched in C++ using per-draw-index seeds. For p>0 refits, Portnoy–Koenker preprocessing seeded by the observed fit (Chernozhukov, Fernández-Val & Melly) is exact, but its gains appear only at large n.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for the closed form. It removes the model.frame and simplex overhead; the catalog's own estimate for the formula overhead alone is 3–10×. The preprocessing headline (÷100) is at n=50,000, p=20, not at EDI's sizes.
findings.suggested_action: Fold into the existing Adopt (v1.0.5-TODO-19 / catalog TODO-6b). Special-case p==0 to nth_element after a tie-rule identity test, and otherwise keep rq.fit.

findings.candidate: (Re-reported, updated.) Collapse each draw to per-distinct-event-time arm counts and run Newton at O(K) per iteration. FastSurvival 2.0.0's coxph_fast now does exact Newton-Raphson with coxph's start, convergence rule and Efron/Breslow ties, so it can serve as a reference implementation.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for this kernel. FastSurvival 2.0.0 NEWS makes no speed claim for the Newton version. The gain is O(n) to O(K) per iteration, which is small unless ties are heavy.
findings.suggested_action: Note this in small_kernel_hoists_batch.md Item C, and act only if compute_coxph_rand_bootstrap_cpp gains a caller. Use FastSurvival (MIT) as a test oracle.

findings.candidate: (Re-reported, still stands.) Fast robust bootstrap (Salibián-Barrera & Zamar 2002; CRAN FRB): one weighted LS solve per replicate using the full-sample robustness weights, plus a linear correction.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified; roughly K× fewer weighted solves than K-iteration IRLS, in theory.
findings.suggested_action: Record FRB in the catalog options table as an estimator-change option. Revisit only if a true MM estimator is adopted; ROBU (arXiv 2606.26611) would then also be relevant for its initialisation.

The searches for weighted / Bayesian-bootstrap U-statistics, Fenwick and sort-based two-sample U computation, and AUGUST / Even-Zohar O(n log n) found nothing that beats O(n+K) for ordinal data with K levels. Nothing new to report; the existing Adopt item is still open.

closed-form.note: Trivial: compute_jt_statistic2_from_counts is O(K) and the fast_ridit_analysis_result contrast is O(n). Both are at the cost of reading the input, so nothing is faster.

delong-structural-components.note: On speed nothing changed: EDI gets V10/V01 as cross-arm midrank CDFs in O(n log K) plus O(n), at or below pROC's Sun-Xu delongPlacementsCpp, which costs O(N log N) for its sort. The finding filed here is about robustness and accuracy, not speed. Brunner & Konietschke (Statistical Papers 66(1), 2025) give an unbiased, non-negative, tie-valid estimator of the Mann-Whitney variance. It uses the same placements, so its cost is the same O(n), and they show the DeLong estimator is biased at small n in a way that depends on the distributions. Adopting it changes the SE estimator (not the point estimate). Oku (arXiv 2609.19986, Sept 2026) only reinterprets the Brunner-Munzel variance and brings no computational gain.

ridit-scoring.note: Scoring is O(n log K) by binary search over K levels, and the per-replicate rebuild is O(n log n). The O(n+K) level-slot counting version is already tracked (ridit_kernel_level_slots.md TODO-1..3), as is hoisting the per-element reference string compares; ridit_distr_parallel.cpp:85 now caches treatment_reference as a bool, but :91/:93 still compare strings. The new searches (ridit variance, mid-rank / pseudo-rank scoring, the pim, DescTools, Ridit and ridittools packages, arXiv 2025-2026) found no faster scoring algorithm. Ridit and ridittools are both archived on CRAN.

findings.candidate: The Brunner & Konietschke (2025) unbiased rank-based estimator of the Mann-Whitney variance. It is built from the same placements, is valid with ties, is non-negative for n_i >= 2, and is L2-consistent.
findings.claimed_speedup: None. It costs the same O(n) after the placements EDI already computes. The gain is accuracy: the authors show that existing estimators, including DeLong's, are biased at small samples (not quantified here).
findings.suggested_action: Investigate: add the unbiased Brunner-Konietschke variance as an option (or as the small-n default) beside the DeLong SE. Compare the type-I error and CI coverage of both at small n_T/n_C with heavy ties, in the TODO-106 simulation.

bisection.note: No code commits since 2026-11-16, and the code is unchanged: mn_constrained_mle_pc_cpp still runs a 60-step bisection on the score, and mn_ci_internal still runs a ≤50-step bisection on δ in which each step calls the inner bisection. The new evidence is CRAN lrstat 0.3.4 (2026-09-15, GPL >= 2). Its C++ remlRiskDiff solves the constrained MLE with the closed-form trigonometric cubic (acos argument clamped, repeated-root branch, pooled estimate when |δ|<1e-8). Its mnRiskDiffCIcpp finds each CI bound with Brent on z(δ) ∓ z_{1-α/2}. Together these are exactly the v1.0.5 audit TODO-3 plus the brent_ci_inversion.md scope extension, and they give a C++ reference to port and test against. cicalc 0.2.2 (Apache-2.0) does the same in R (acos cubic + uniroot). ITP (Oliveira & Takahashi 2021, CRAN itp) keeps bisection's worst case with superlinear speed, but Brent is enough here because z(δ) is smooth and monotone.

closed-form.note: Trivial. The unpooled Wald SE for RD and the RD point estimate with the MN N/(N−1) variance factor are O(n) single-pass formulas, bounded below by reading the counts. Nothing faster.

miettinen-nurminen-score.note: The previous finding stands, with a stronger reference. The z statistic costs O(60) only because of the inner bisection. lrstat 0.3.4 (C++, GPL >= 2) has a closed-form cubic constrained MLE with a Brent outer CI root and supports stratified MN with MH weights. cicalc 0.2.2 (Apache-2.0) and ratesci 1.1.1 (GPL >= 3) use the same closed-form cubic. ratesci 1.1.1 NEWS adds no change to RD root finding. Its new Brown-Li Jeffreys method for RD is a different estimator, not a speedup. The arXiv 2609.10865 'Elliptically Optimal' closed-form interval is also an estimator change and is not adopted. Absolute cost is microseconds, so priority stays low. The p floor at |z|>8 is v1.0.5 audit TODO-22 (pnorm_fast).

newcombe-hybrid-score.note: No speedup exists: the independent CI is a closed form from two Wilson limits, O(1), and the p-value inverts that CI over α with Brent (uniroot) in about 10–15 evaluations. Searches found no closed-form inverse and no package that gives a Newcombe p-value; ratesci says MOVER has no corresponding test. This method is marked faster_option_found only because the accuracy finding below applies to it. That finding is re-reported unchanged: newcombe_speedups.cpp:128-129 still uses the uncorrected Pearson φ, whereas Newcombe method 10 (ratesci MOVER-NW / 'MOVER_newc') applies Newcombe's correction to the correlation. F9 (p = 1 when there is no sign change) and uniroot's default tol are already-logged accuracy bugs.

wilson-score-interval.note: Trivial closed form, O(1); nothing faster. The open item is accuracy: newcombe_speedups.cpp:23 still calls fast_qnorm (Acklam), so v1.0.5 audit TODO-7 is still open.

findings.candidate: Closed-form Farrington–Manning/MN cubic for p̃_C in trigonometric form, plus Brent on z(δ) ∓ z_{1−α/2} for each bound. Both are already implemented in C++ in CRAN lrstat 0.3.4: remlRiskDiff clamps the acos argument, handles the repeated root, and uses the pooled estimate at δ≈0; mnRiskDiffCIcpp calls brent(f, -1, est, 1e-6). cicalc 0.2.2 (R) and ratesci 1.1.1 (R) use the same cubic.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. The catalog's theoretical estimate is ~30–60× fewer flops for the inner solve, and Brent cuts the outer loop from ~50 to roughly 8–15 evaluations. Absolute cost is already microseconds.
findings.suggested_action: When implementing v1.0.5 audit TODO-3 and the brent_ci_inversion.md scope extension to mn_ci_internal, port lrstat's remlRiskDiff (src/miettinen_nurminen.cpp) and its Brent outer root. Test against lrstat::mnRiskDiffCI and remlRiskDiff over an (x_t, n_t, x_c, n_c, δ) grid that includes the boundary cases. Low priority.

findings.candidate: Newcombe (1998b) method 10 with the corrected φ. When AD−BC > 0, the numerator becomes max(AD−BC−N/2, 0). This is ratesci's MOVER-NW ('MOVER_newc') and statsmodels' 'newcombe'.
findings.claimed_speedup: none: this is an estimator/accuracy correction, not a speedup (O(1) either way)
findings.suggested_action: Resolve the Investigate verdict: apply the N/2 correction to the positive φ numerator, and add a test against ratesci::moverpairci (Wilson base, Newcombe correction) or statsmodels confint_proportions_paired(method='newcombe').

irls.note: The previous result (2026-11-16, same day) still stands, and no code commits touched these files since. Two leads are re-reported. (1) For the Huber 'M' path, finite-termination Newton (Madsen & Nielsen 1990, BIT, doi 10.1007/BF01933216; Chen & Pınar 1998, BIT, doi 10.1007/BF02510408). It gives the same estimator at the same per-iteration O(np²), and its convergence is exact rather than tolerance-based, which helps the KK classes that cap maxit at 10–25 with acc 1e-3. (2) For the planned true-MM prototype (catalog §1 TODO-4), a deterministic start: Peña–Yohai via RobStatTM/pyinit, plus a new reference implementation found this run, statsmodels RLMDetS/RLMDetSMM (BSD-3; DetS-style starts from robust Mahalanobis subsets, as in Hubert et al. 2012). This fills the '[cite needed]' in catalog O8's DetS row. Checked for news: robustbase NEWS 0.99-5…0.99-7 (2024-11 to 2026-02) has no algorithmic change to lmrob/FAST-S. ROBU (arXiv 2606.26611) targets large p and is still subsampling-based, so it does not help at p≲10. A web search found no IRLS-vs-Newton benchmark for Huber or Anderson-accelerated IRLS for Huber; one source reports Huber IRLS typically converging in 4–5 iterations, which caps the possible win. Per-replicate warm starts are already implemented (warm_start_beta / weights / fisher_info in fast_robust_regression_internal), so catalog §1 New TODO 8 is a matter of wiring, not a new algorithm.

sandwich-estimator.note: Closed form, O(n + p³), reusing the cached OLS R factor, so nothing can be faster. This run found no new small-sample correction specific to M-estimators. The issues already recorded (no guard for mean ψ′→0, Incidental 10; Koller–Stahel anti-conservatism, catalog O8) concern accuracy, not speed.

selection-algorithm.note: One median per fit: std::sort below n=512, nth_element above. That is O(n), negligible next to the O(K n p²) IRLS. The only newer selection work found (a fixed-pivot select, QuickselectAdaptive) gives constant-factor gains, which catalog O9 already judged not worth the code at n≤10⁴.

findings.candidate: Finite-termination Newton for the Huber M-estimator (Madsen & Nielsen 1990; Chen & Pınar 1998). It is an active-set Newton on the piecewise-quadratic Huber objective: once the inlier set is correct, one step lands exactly on the minimizer. Each step costs O(np²), the same as IRLS.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. Chen & Pınar's abstract claims only 'improving the efficiency' and proves finite termination with no assumptions on the problem. A separate source reports Huber IRLS converging in 4–5 iterations, so the iteration saving at EDI's sizes may be small. The main gain is exact convergence under capped maxit.
findings.suggested_action: Revisit catalog O8's 'Newton instead of IRLS' row for the Huber path only. Prototype Madsen–Nielsen/Chen–Pınar Newton and A/B its iteration counts and estimate differences against IRLS at n≈50–1000, p≲10, especially in KK randomization draws where maxit is capped.

findings.candidate: A deterministic S-step start for the true-MM prototype: Peña–Yohai candidates (RobStatTM::lmrobdetMM, pyinit) or DetS-style robust-Mahalanobis subsets (statsmodels RLMDetS/RLMDetSMM), then a bisquare M-step at the S-scale. Both remove the need for an RNG-seed contract.

sandwich-estimator.note: No code commits since last_researched (2026-11-16). Per entry: [HC0, R helpers + OLS LPM] closed form, O(np²+p³); nothing faster, unchanged. [HC2 C++] exact leverages in O(np²) are the minimum; unchanged. [cluster-robust GLM / gcomp cluster + delta] one score-sum pass plus G rank-1 updates; unchanged. [CR2 + Satterthwaite df, cluster_robust_cr2_variance] UPDATED: new evidence strengthens the previous finding. estimatr 2.0.0 (CRAN, 2.0.1 published 2026-10-10, MIT) replaced its O(J²) cluster-level df matrix with r×r Gram products (trace(P)²/‖P‖²_F without forming P). Its NEWS reports about 2× end-to-end at n=1000, G=100, which is EDI's size range. Its C++ also reduces large clusters to a k×k eigenproblem through a thin QR of [U_c, X_c]. EDI still forms the dense n×G Umat (O(nGp) build, O(nG²) crossprod) and runs a per-cluster n_g×n_g eigen(). The function runs in shared() whenever the SE is requested (estimate_only = FALSE), so in any studentized resample. [Lin–Wei prefix sums] previous optional finding stands (monotone pointer, from survival coxscore2.c). The survival 3.8 NEWS has nothing new on speed; coxdev 0.4.0 (2026-11-07, GPL≥3) offers O(n)-per-column score residuals, the same order as EDI's.

findings.candidate: The p×p (r×r) formulation, as now shipped in estimatr ≥2.0.0 C++ (lm_robust_helper.cpp). Bell–McCaffrey df: trace(P) and ‖P‖²_F come from a few p×p Gram products of per-cluster p-vectors, P = S − U − Uᵀ + D, without forming the G×G or n×G objects. Meat: clusters with n_g > k are reduced to a k×k eigenproblem via a thin QR of [U_c, X_c], giving A^{-1/2}X = X + Q(B^{-1/2} − I)QᵀX. Equivalently, use dfadjust vignette Lemma 2 (generalized inverse), which handles singular I−H_gg. Same CR2 estimator and the same df.
findings.claimed_speedup: estimatr 2.0.0 NEWS: about 2× end-to-end on a 1,000-observation, 100-cluster model from the df change alone (a 500×500 cluster matrix replaced by five 3×3 matrices). MacKinnon–Nielsen–Webb (arXiv 2301.04527): the n_g×n_g route is fastest only for cluster size ≤4. Neither number was measured in EDI.
findings.suggested_action: Prototype. Port the estimatr r×r Satterthwaite df (MIT, attribute) and the large-cluster k×k reduction into C++ (or vectorised R). Drop Umat. A/B test against the current function and clubSandwich::coef_test(vcov='CR2', test='Satterthwaite'), including a singular I−H_gg case. Priority rises if the CR2 SE is used inside studentized bootstrap / randomization loops.

findings.candidate: Monotone pointer over the sorted event times, or survival's single backward pass (coxscore2.c), O(n+K) with identical results.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. It removes a log K factor from a non-dominant term.
findings.suggested_action: Optional: do it together with the I-6 fix in compute_robust_vcov; no standalone change.

bernoulli-coin-flips.note: Trivial, as the taxonomy says: one draw per subject, O(n) per null draw, already in C++. The per-arrival O(t) recount in R runs once per real arrival and is not hot. dqrng (AGPL-3, so only conditionally usable) offers fast sampling but no Bernoulli advantage over EDI's own edi_rng. Nothing new since 2026-11-16.

efron-biased-coin.note: The C++ kernel (generate_permutations_efron_cpp, running counts) is O(n) per draw, which is the floor for writing an n-vector. I re-checked the exact-distribution route: the Hollander & Peña (1986) recursion and the Markaryan & Rosenberger (2010) closed forms. The recursion works over states (t, imbalance, partial statistic), so it applies only to linear (rank) statistics on a lattice. At n=100 that is about n^4 = 1e8 operations, compared with about 5e4 for r=501 Monte Carlo draws. It buys exactness, not speed, and is already tracked under catalog §7 TODO-6. Kojima's arXiv 2608.05527 (Aug 2026, SIGA) is a Gaussian approximation for design-stage power under minimization: an estimator change, and outside EDI's inference use. carat 2.3.0 (2026-09-08) is a C++ rival but implements covariate-adaptive procedures. No code changes since the last review.

sequential-replay.note: The generic R double loop (design_seq_one_by_one_abstract.R:247) is now used only by the urn design (RandomBlockSize has gained its own draw_ws_raw). Because the urn's assign_wt recounts sum(private$w==1) over the whole w vector, the loop costs O(r n^2) R operations. A C++ urn kernel with running counts (O(rn), same distribution, different RNG stream) is still the fastest acceptable option. It is already scheduled (v1.0.5 TODO-10 / release_v1_2_0 TODO-22) and is re-reported here only because a new correctness observation comes with it: the generic loop overwrites private$w on the object it is called on and never restores it. The main randomization path calls it on des_obj$duplicate(), which is safe. But inference_incidence_cmh.R:196 calls private$des_obj$draw_ws_according_to_design() directly, which would replace the observed urn assignment with the last null draw. I have not verified this by running it.

urn-design.note: The urn rule itself is a Markov chain in (nT, nC) with O(1) work per arrival. Wei's UD is a Friedman-type urn, not a Pólya urn, so it is not exchangeable and there is no beta-binomial-style shortcut that would skip the sequential simulation. The O(t) recount in assign_wt runs once per real arrival. The speed gap is in the replay, recorded under sequential-replay. Rivals: randomizeR 3.0.2 (2023-09-18, pure R, genSeq is Monte Carlo and getAllSeq enumerates all sequences) and RARfreq 0.1.5 (pure R, DBCD/SEU only). Neither is faster. Oden & McIntosh (2006) give exact moments, not a faster sampler.

findings.candidate: A dedicated C++ urn draw kernel with running counts (nT, nC), per-draw seeding like generate_permutations_efron_cpp: O(rn). It never touches private$w, which also removes the side effect.
findings.claimed_speedup: O(r n^2) R-level ops to O(r n) compiled; from the complexity analysis in catalog §12 options table (k)/(l), not measured
findings.suggested_action: Keep TODO-22 (C++ urn kernel). Separately, check whether inference_incidence_cmh.R:196 and the bootstrap draw sites in inference_all_abstract_rand_bootstrap.R are reached with a live urn design, and either call them on a duplicate or have the generic draw_ws_raw restore private$w.

sequential-monte-carlo-stopping.note: The earlier finding (Fischer & Ramdas betting tests) still stands. Its sources are now confirmed as published: JRSS-B 87(4):1200, 2025, doi:10.1093/jrsssb/qkaf014. The multiple-testing follow-up is in EJS 20(1), 2026, doi:10.1214/26-EJS2514. There were no code commits since the last run. New this run: I read the code. The rule is enabled only inside CI searches, with mc_stop_threshold = α, so EDI needs a decision on p(δ) vs α; the catalog's objection that 'Gandy is decision-only' does not apply. I also derived the stopping points from the closed forms. With the defaults (99% Clopper–Pearson, batch 45 at r=501, mc_min_draws=100), the current band cannot stop to reject until n ≥ 210 draws, even with 0 exceedances, so 225 draws after batching. The binomial betting strategy (p=1/55) reaches wealth 1/α=20 after 44 draws with 0 losses, 53 with 1 and 80 with 2. The binomial mixture with c=0.04 needs 39 draws with 0 losses and 73 with 1. That is about 3–5x fewer refits for clearly significant δ during CI bracketing, and the betting rule also controls error across repeated looks. Stoepker & Castro (arXiv 2409.18908) is another anytime-valid option, but it is not quantified. MChtest (truncated SPRT) and rfvimptest (SPRT/SAPT) are older rivals with no evidence of beating betting.

findings.candidate: Anytime-valid sequential Monte Carlo test by betting (Fischer & Ramdas, JRSS-B 2025). Use the binomial strategy with p=1/⌈√(2πe^{1/6})/α⌉, where wealth = (T+1)·p^ℓ(1−p)^{T−ℓ}·C(T,ℓ), or the binomial mixture with c<α, where wealth = (1−Bin(ℓ;T+1,c))/c. Stop to reject when wealth ≥ 1/α and for futility when wealth < α. Keep EDI's batching (validity holds at any stopping time) and fall back to the fixed-r p-value if there is no decision by r. The rule is a deterministic function of the draws, so it keeps thread- and seed-determinism. The paper proves zero resampling risk for limiting p-values below p (binomial) or below c (mixture), which addresses the multiplicity gap the catalog records for the current band.
findings.claimed_speedup: Minimum draws to reject at α=0.05, from the paper's closed-form wealth (my arithmetic, not a benchmark): binomial strategy 44 / 53 / 80 draws with 0 / 1 / 2 losses; mixture with c=0.04 needs 39 / 73 / 105 (the paper itself states 39). The current band needs ≥ 210, i.e. 225 after batching. That is about 3–5x fewer refits for clearly significant δ in the CI bracketing phase. Futility stops can also come before the current 100-draw floor. Near the CI boundary (p≈α) neither rule stops early, so the end-to-end saving per CI search is not quantified. Paper Section 7.4 (Fisher sharp null, α=0.05): binomial mean 85 / median 53 permutations vs 200 for Besag–Clifford (h=10).
findings.suggested_action: Under performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md TODO-156, add Fischer & Ramdas 2025 (and Gandy–Hahn–Ding 2020 buckets) to the NEW-seq-mc-stopping options table. Correct the table's objection to decision-only rules: the SMC path only decides p(δ) vs α inside CI searches. Prototype the binomial or binomial-mixture stop in sequential_mc_band_excludes_threshold. Measure draws per CI search and endpoint agreement against fixed r=501 on the GEE and other refit-per-draw classes.

clopper-pearson-interval.note: `summarize` calls stats::binom.test once per summary cell for coverage_pval and size_pval. The p-value sums dbinom over the support, O(Nrep), and the interval is two qbeta calls. That is negligible next to Nrep×fits. Checked binom 1.1-2 (2026-07-07), PropCIs and the 2025 fast admissible-interval work (Wang et al.): nothing beats a closed form here. Blaker or Wilson would be estimator changes and are not about speed.

closed-form.note: Trivial. Quantile cut, normal cell probabilities in O(nK) and Weibull means via gamma() are each at the input-reading lower bound. The survival-factor check (incidental #11) is about correctness, not speed. No commits since the last run.

crude-monte-carlo.note: The FNV-1a uint64 unordered_set dedupe is still O(1) per key and negligible. The precision-targeted Nrep and sequential stopping rules are already option (n) in catalog §12, and the 2025/2026 review (Wu & Kawai, arXiv 2510.22688 v3, Jun 2026) gives no evidence that overturns it. Besag–Clifford and Gandy per-replicate stopping are tracked under TODO-156. New this run: simhelpers 0.3.0–0.3.2 (0.3.2 on 2026-11-12) ships Boos–Zhang (2000) extrapolate_coverage()/extrapolate_rejection(). These estimate B=∞ coverage and power from bootstrap subsamples, which bears directly on EDI's per-replicate B_boot=201 / r_rand=201 cost. See the finding.

findings.candidate: Boos & Zhang (2000) linear extrapolation in 1/B. Inside each replicate, compute the CI and p-value on several subsamples of the B resample statistics already drawn (e.g. b = 39…B). Then regress the coverage or rejection indicator on 1/b across replicates and report the intercept as the B=∞ coverage or power, with a cluster-robust MCSE. Implemented in simhelpers::extrapolate_coverage / extrapolate_rejection (0.3.0+, exclude_above added in 0.3.2, 2026-11-12).
findings.claimed_speedup: Boos & Zhang's abstract says linear extrapolation corrects the finite-B bias and so reduces computation time in Monte Carlo power studies. In Pustejovsky's worked example (R=2500), 399 bootstrap draws per replicate plus extrapolation gave coverage 0.946 (MCSE 0.004), against 0.9516 from brute force with B=2399: about 6× fewer resamples. CI computations rose about 8×, so it only pays when draws, which in EDI are refits, cost far more than computing a CI. Not quantified for EDI.
findings.suggested_action: Investigate: add an opt-in 'extrapolated' summary for bootstrap and randomization cells. Record the p-values and CIs at nested sub-B values inside each replicate, and validate against a brute-force large-B run on a few cells. Use simhelpers::extrapolate_* (GPL-3) as the reference implementation.

linear-scan.note: Trivial: build_matching_combined_{clogit,ols}_design_cpp write each output element once, O((n_d+n_R)·p), which is the output-size lower bound. No code commits since 2026-11-16. A problem-level search on stacked pair-difference plus reservoir design turned up only the source design paper (Kapelner & Krieger arXiv 1305.4981) and unrelated ensemble 'stacked regressions' work. No faster method exists.

ordinal-binary-expansion.note: Re-checked since 2026-11-16 (no code commits). The expansions emit at most 2 rows per subject (adjacent-category) or min(y+1,K-1) rows per subject (continuation ratio), so their O(nK) cost is the size of the output. Rival software checked: VGAM 1.1-14 (vglm Fisher scoring), ordinalNet 2.14 (2026-02, coordinate descent), GLMcat 1.0.0 (JSS 2025, Fisher scoring over a per-observation design Z; no benchmark found), rms 8.2-1 (cr.setup, the same row-replication reduction EDI uses, clustered on subs), glmpathcr, brms cratio, Stata crreg (direct ML). None offers a different algorithm or a benchmark at EDI sizes. Fitting without expansion (structured Hessian) is already recorded as catalog §2 TODO-3 and is not re-reported. For the adjacent-category stacked composite likelihood, the open issue is still SE validity (Mukherjee et al.: amalgamated conditional logistic regression with a robust sandwich variance), not speed.

analytic-derivatives.note: Closed-form score, observed Hessian and expected_hessian, O(n K d^2). AD (TMB, Stan, CppAD) is reported as slower than hand-coded derivatives (TMB paper, arXiv 1509.00660). mnlogit-style exploitation of Hessian structure (JSS v75 i03, 10-50x versus generic multinomial software) applies in principle to the sparse B_j blocks, but the catalog already notes 'sparsity = incidental' and Keep. At d = 2K-3+p of about 10 the gain is a constant factor on a step that L-BFGS mostly bypasses at the cold start. Not an algorithmic improvement.

log-sum-exp.note: Trivial: max-shifted log-sum-exp, O(K) per observation, at the lower bound; nothing faster that is as accurate.

multistart.note: Stereotype multistart (.stereotype_full_data_multistart, _multistart_candidates, _null_refit_multistart). The likelihood is genuinely nonconcave: the bilinear form, plus EDI's monotone phi constraint, is not covered by the benign-landscape results for low-rank factorisation. The general multistart refinements found (MLSL clustering, METOD early termination, J Glob Optim 2021; KNITRO rule-based termination) are heuristic. They would change which optimum is reported on hard cases and need random sampling, which conflicts with EDI's RNG-free deterministic starts. Rival software (gnm, clustord nstarts, Latent GOLD) uses random multistart, which is no faster. Change from the previous result: its finding (cloglog multistart gated on a convergence certificate) concerns .cloglog_full_data_multistart, which is not an entry of this problem. It belongs to the cumulative-link problem, so it is not re-reported here and this problem's multistart is marked no faster option.

newton-raphson.note: Newton then L-BFGS fallback (fast_stereotype_logit_internal / _full_internal / _cpp / _with_var_cpp). Rival fitters checked this run: VGAM rrvglm (IRLS, alternating RR-VGLM; 1.1-14 NEWS has only a 'bhhh' option and no rrvglm solver speedup), gnm (Poisson-expanded IRLS/Gauss-Newton with random starts, and its vignette reports 73 of 100 random-start calls abandoned on a nonlinear example), clustord::osm (optim on a cumulative expit/exp phi parameterisation, numerical Hessian), Stata slogit, the elastic-net Adam fits and the de Rooij MM algorithm (arXiv 2402.07634 v3, still dated 2025-01-22, linear rate). None is faster than an analytic-Hessian C++ Newton/L-BFGS at EDI's sizes (n in the hundreds, K at most about 10). LM/trust-region and expected-information Fisher scoring are already in catalog §5 and tracked as v1.0.5 catalog TODO-6 (Prototype). The Gauss-Newton vs ALS literature (arXiv 1910.12331) supports keeping a joint Newton-type method rather than alternating. No new evidence overturns any catalog row.

profile-likelihood.note: Variance fallback only: 3 warm-started damped-Newton profile refits plus a second finite difference. The profile-CI algorithms found (Fischer & Lewis trust-region, arXiv 2004.00231; profileCI 2025, convex likelihoods only; CICO) target whole CI curves, not a single curvature. The warm-started Newton already matches their efficient regime. Not a hot path.

reparameterization.note: Cumulative-softmax ordered phi, O(K^2) per evaluation, dominated by the O(nK) likelihood. Alternatives found (clustord's cumulative expit/exp increments, Stan's log-gap ordered transform, softplus increments) are equivalent in cost. None is shown to condition better; Stan's log-gap form degrades at ties. No change warranted.

crude-monte-carlo.note: Non-blocking branch of inference_incidence_cmh.R get_standard_error: K=5000 design draws, O(nK), computed once per inference object and cached; it is not inside a resampling loop (checked compute_brt_null_statistics_with_se callers). The faster option is the O(n) deterministic closed form Var(y'w) from the design's E[ww'] for CR/BCRD/Bernoulli/blocked designs. The catalog options table already records it, and the row is already Prototype (v1.0.5 TODO-3), so it is not re-reported. Antithetic draws were already rejected because they give no gain for squared balanced statistics. The Higgins-Sävje-Sekhon block variances support the closed form but are not new. QMC and control-variate searches found nothing that applies to discrete assignment vectors from sequential designs. Those designs still need MC.

robins-breslow-greenland-variance.note: Trivial closed form over blocks, O(n), cached. Taxonomy note: the code does not use RBG 1986, which is a variance for the MH log odds ratio. It uses the extended Robins (1988) risk-difference variance from Azriel-Krieger-Kapelner (arXiv 2607.05768), averaged per block. New since the last research: Qiu et al. (arXiv 2408.12541 v2, May 2025) propose a unified robust variance for the MH risk difference, consistent under both large-stratum and sparse-stratum asymptotics; RobinCar 1.2.0 (2026-04) implements GR, mGR and Sato. That is an estimator change aimed at robustness, not a speedup, and EDI's design (equal blocks, even allocation, Robins-type estimand) differs from it. arXiv 2610.01362 (CMH vs AIPW variances, 2026-10) also has no computational content.

m-out-of-n-subsampling.note: Re-reviewed today's earlier result (no code commits since). EDI's cost is B·fit(m) or B·fit(b). Nothing found computes the same √m-scaled or FPC-scaled subsampling distribution with fewer refits. The new 2025–2026 work changes the estimator: adaptive BLB (arXiv 2608.16892), amortized neural inference (arXiv 2607.16666, all rights reserved), Politis's scalable subsampling with non-random subsamples (arXiv 2112.06434, aimed at massive n), and optimal subsampling bootstrap under a compute budget (arXiv 2302.07533, massive n). The previous finding still stands: Lam's cheap bootstrap is an estimator change. Partial Fisher–Yates for the draw primitive is already catalogued (catalog TODO-2), and the dqrng vignette confirms that design (bitset rejection or partial Fisher–Yates by selection rate). Draws are not the bottleneck next to refits.

minimum-volatility.note: EDI evaluates a 9-point grid at B=251, about 2.3k refits of size m<n. Each grid point re-calls set.seed(private$seed), so the grid already uses common random numbers when a seed is set. The alternatives are no cheaper: Bickel–Sakov is similar or higher cost (BLB paper: 'significantly greater computation'); the Jach–McElroy–Politis KS criterion uses the same grid of distributions, with only a different statistic; moonboot's Sherman double bootstrap is costlier. Adaptive BLB's AMSE-plus-stability exponent selection (2608.16892) is tied to BLB. Nothing new since today's previous result changes this.

analytic-derivatives.note: Clayton and dep-cens likelihoods are closed form and O(np) per evaluation. I checked again for new work: CopulaCenR rc_par_copula uses pracma numerical grad/hessian with BFGS, which is slower than EDI's analytic gradient. Petti et al. 2022 give analytic score/Hessian for copula additive models (GJRM), the same cost class. The 2026 dep-cens GMM preprint (arXiv 2604.04032) is an estimator change. No faster way to compute the same likelihood. The FD Hessian runs once per fit (catalog NEW-fd-hessian).

gauss-hermite-quadrature.note: The previous AGQ finding (Stringer arXiv 2310.01589 exact AQ gradient) still stands. The change is a problem-specific route found this run for the Weibull normal-frailty kernel. A Weibull AFT with a N(0,σu²) intercept on log time is exactly a PH shared frailty with a normal random intercept b=-u/σε. Charvat (Am. Stat. 2023, doi 10.1080/00031305.2022.2110939) gives the cluster modes in closed form with Lambert W0 (LAGHQ), so there is no nested mode solve and the gradient and Hessian are closed form. Charvat's own GPL(>=2) package mexhaz imports lamW. Separately, the conditional integrand depends on each cluster only through D_g=Σδ_i and H_g=Σexp(base_wi). The fixed-node kernel can therefore be collapsed to O(n p + G K) with the same estimator. This is stronger than the catalog's TODO-4 (O(nK+np)). Two findings below.

lbfgs.note: LBFGSpp: no new release with a performance claim found (latest notes are v0.3.0: More-Thuente, Nocedal-Wright default). marqLevAlg (R Journal 2021, doi 10.32614/RJ-2021-089), used by frailtypack, claims robustness and parallel speed-up, not fewer evaluations than quasi-Newton at small p. Frailty and copula packages (MultiFrailty: maxLik NR/BFGS; extrafrail: EM; CopulaCenR: BFGS with numeric derivatives) are not faster than C++ L-BFGS with an analytic gradient. For the frailty kernel, LAGHQ's closed-form Hessian would make Newton possible; that is covered by the GHQ finding.

multistart.note: The previous result's only finding (cloglog multistart concavity) applies to the ordinal cloglog entries, not to this problem's entries, so it is not re-reported here. For Clayton and dep-cens, the likelihood is truly nonconcave in the dependence parameter. Searches found MLSL/clustering multistart (arXiv 2108.13504) and multi-restart practice in copula papers, but no source showing fewer local solves at 3 starts and small p. The 1-D profile and L-BFGS-B options are already rejected in catalog NEW-nonconcave-dependence-mle. Keep.

findings.candidate: Cluster-total (sufficient-statistic) collapse. log T = Xβ + u + σε·ε with extreme-value ε is a PH model with frailty exp(-u/σε), so for cluster g at node k the conditional log-lik is const_g + Σ_i δ_i base_wi + D_g δ_k − H_g e^{δ_k}, with D_g=Σδ_i and H_g=Σ_i exp(base_wi), both computed once per evaluation in O(n). Each (g,k) term is then O(1). The gradient needs only per-cluster posterior moments E_g[e^δ], E_g[δ e^δ] and E_g[δ], giving per-observation scalars s_i = (exp(base_wi)·E_g[e^δ] − δ_i)/σε and one Xᵀs GEMV. Total O(np + GK), and the n×K r/w matrices disappear. This is the reduction Charvat (2023) uses to write the cluster integrand for a normal-intercept shared frailty. It is an algebraic identity, so the estimator is unchanged.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. My operation count: node work drops from O(nK) to O(GK), about 2× at EDI's pairs, and the gradient drops from O(nKp) to O(np), about K=20× on that term. This subsumes catalog §5 TODO-4 (O(nK+np)). Theoretical, not measured.
findings.suggested_action: Widen catalog §5 TODO-4 to the full cluster-total collapse (O(np+GK)), not just the GEMV hoist. Benchmark it against the current kernel at n=50–500 pairs, p=2–10, and check that log-lik and gradient agree to 1e-10 relative.

findings.candidate: Lambert-based adaptive GH (LAGHQ, Charvat, The American Statistician 77(1):41–50, 2023). For a shared frailty model with a normal random intercept, the cluster mode is closed form: b̂_g = D_gτ² − W0(H_gτ² e^{D_gτ²}), using the collapsed statistics above. The curvature is H_g e^{b̂}+1/τ², and the paper gives closed-form gradient and Hessian of the approximate likelihood. This removes both objections the catalog recorded against AGQ for this kernel (no nested optimization, and an exact gradient without implicit differentiation). Fewer nodes (e.g. 5–9) then suffice. Charvat's GPL(>=2) package mexhaz imports lamW and is the likely reference implementation. Boost.Math lambert_w0 (BH, BSL-1.0) supplies W0 in C++.
findings.claimed_speedup: The source gives no timings; it claims maximisation is 'convenient and efficient'. Theoretical: one W0 per cluster instead of 3–5 Newton steps, and K≈5–9 instead of 20 nodes, so roughly 2–4× per evaluation on top of the collapse. Not measured.
findings.suggested_action: Add Charvat 2023 LAGHQ to v1.0.5 TODO-153 (performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md) as the AGQ route for fast_weibull_frailty.cpp, and name the file in its scope. Prototype it after the collapse finding, check mexhaz for the formulas, then A/B against K=50 non-adaptive GH for σu up to e^1.5.

analytic-derivatives.note: WeibullAFTLikelihood / WeibullAFTLikelihoodGeneral: closed-form O(np) NLL/gradient and O(np^2) Hessian as a weighted crossprod. That is the floor per evaluation. AD (TMB/RTMB, Stan math) automates the same derivatives and cannot beat hand-coded closed forms; this run's search found no Weibull-specific AD benchmark (TMB paper arXiv 1509.00660 compares only against numerical derivatives). No code commits since 2026-11-16.

lbfgs.note: L-BFGS default in fast_weibull_regression_internal / left_interval variant (and the R wrapper). Making Newton the default, with the analytic Hessian (newton_then_lbfgs), is already Prototype v1.0.5 TODO-3 (catalog §5 'Weibull AFT optimizer choice'), so it is not re-reported. This run checked LBFGSpp (MIT; no new release info) and survival NEWS up to 3.8-12 (no survreg changes). The general Newton vs quasi-Newton sources found give no new evidence beyond what TODO-3 already assumes.

multistart.note: Re-checked the code at commit 8b718ae1. robust_survreg_with_surv_object still sets init = rep(0, p+1) (helper_robust_regression.R ~line 153) and jitters with unscaled rnorm. This overrides survreg's own default start: the survival manual (fetched this run) says init=NULL is the default and each survreg.distributions entry has an init(x, weights) function that gives the mean/variance start 'used for initial values in the iteration'. The previous finding stands; no new multistart literature specific to AFT changes it.

newton-raphson.note: The Newton–Raphson algorithm is the right one for p ≤ ~10, and survreg's Newton is unchanged through survival 3.8-12 (NEWS). The previous survreg.fit interim fast-path finding for weighted_weibull_bootstrap_surrogate_fit still stands, with one new caveat: the survival manual lists survreg.fit only under 'Internal survival functions', and its arguments 'are not guaranteed to stay the same from release to release'. That needs a version guard and the formula fallback. Trust-region Newton and Burridge reparametrization give robustness, not speed, and Burridge is already in the catalog.

sandwich-estimator.note: Pair-cluster meat via rowsum of per-observation scores plus crossprod, O(np^2), is minimal. CR2 / bias-corrected variants (clubSandwich, arXiv 2203.02560 for marginal Cox) would be estimator changes, not speedups. No new evidence.

findings.candidate: Make the first attempt with init omitted (NULL) so survreg uses the distribution's documented init(x, weights) mean/variance start. Before any jitter, add scale-aware deterministic starts: intercept = mean log-time and log-scale from the residual SD (the weibull_smart_cold_start pattern applied to lognormal/loglogistic). Keep the seeded jitter only as a last resort, scaled by SE or |start|. Re-reported from 2026-11-16; the code is unchanged.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. The expected gain is fewer failed survreg calls per fit: a zero intercept is far from log(time) at typical time scales.
findings.suggested_action: Fold into multistart_nonconcave_likelihoods.md as the concrete 'deterministic data-driven starts' prototype: init=NULL first, then a moment start, then scaled jitter. A/B the failure rate and the attempts per fit.

findings.candidate: For the unclustered case, call survival::survreg.fit(x = cbind(1, X), y = Surv(...), weights, offset = 0, init = warm, controlvals = survreg.control(), dist = survreg.distributions$weibull, ...) on the prebuilt matrix, falling back to the formula path on error. This is the same Newton–Raphson, likelihood and start, and mirrors the existing coxph.fit interim path. The end state remains the native weighted C++ kernel (bayesian_bootstrap_performance.md item 2).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified; no source benchmarks survreg.fit against survreg. The gain is removing the per-draw formula and model-frame overhead, multiplied by B.
findings.suggested_action: Add as an interim sub-item beside the coxph.fit interim in bayesian_bootstrap_performance.md item 2, guarded by a fallback. Benchmark per-draw time first; prefer going straight to the native C++ weighted kernel if that is near.

analytic-derivatives.note: Closed-form NLL, gradient and observed information at O(n·k) and O(n·k²) already use distinct-y lgamma/digamma tables and do the minimum work for an exact Hessian. Checked since the previous result: an AD-vs-hand-coded search found no evidence that TMB, CppAD or Stan AD beats hand-coded gradients on small models; Stan Math (arXiv 1509.07164) reports gradient cost of about 20× a plain evaluation. The expected_hessian functions (ZAP, ZOIB) are dead code. Nothing new.

closed-form.note: Trivial: closed-form ZIP θ→∞ limit (softplus/log-add-exp), O(n k), one pass; nothing faster.

finite-differences.note: The ZipLimitLikelihood FD Hessian is fallback-only. It costs 2k analytic-gradient evaluations, O(nk²), the same order as an analytic Hessian. The FD-vs-analytic search found only general accuracy notes (4–5 digits) and nothing ZIP-specific or faster. An analytic ZIP Hessian would improve accuracy, not speed.

laplace-approximation-tmb.note: Re-checked in the code at commit 8b718ae: both weighted glmmTMB replicate calls (inference_count_hurdle.R:436-443, inference_count_zero_augmented_poisson_abstract.R:1097-1104) still pass no se argument, so sdreport runs on estimate-only replicates. The earlier finding stands. glmmTMB on CRAN is still 1.1.15.2 (2026-09-29). TMB-users threads say DATA_UPDATE has been replaced by RTMB::DataEval, which is not thread-safe and is not reachable through glmmTMB. New: fastglm 0.1.4's fastglm_hurdle (NB with Brent θ) and fastglm_zi accept prior weights and fit in milliseconds (CRAN benchmarks vignette). They are a ready GPL-compatible reference and stopgap for the weighted C++ kernels in catalog §10 TODO-3. In the R Journal glmmTMB paper's own NB benchmark, the IRLS-class fitters (mgcv 0.03×, gamlss 0.24× of glmmTMB time) were far faster than TMB.

lbfgs.note: Updated with numbers. The previous low-confidence finding (fastglm_zi SQUAREM-EM as a possibly faster method) is now quantified by the fastglm CRAN benchmarks vignette. SQUAREM-EM is only 3.7–4.6× faster than pscl::zeroinfl for ZIP (n=1e3–1e5, p=2) and about 2× for ZINB (n=1e4). pscl is R-level optim BFGS. EDI already runs C++ L-BFGS with analytic gradients, so EM shows no speed advantage. It also only agrees with pscl to about 1e-5. Keep it as an A/B comparator for em_algorithm_zero_inflated_mixtures.md TODO-5, but it is not a speedup finding. The hurdle-Poisson block-separate Newton/IRLS (catalog §3 TODO-3) and the conditional-likelihood start and α-parametrization (TODO 1/4) are already recorded. LBFGSpp shows no new release (0.4.0).

likelihood-factorization.note: The hurdle factorization (logistic plus truncated NB) is the standard method. It is confirmed again by the Stata Journal notes, statsmodels HurdleCountModel (separate fits only) and fastglm_hurdle (independent parts). Nothing faster exists for a separable likelihood.

newton-raphson.note: Block-separable hurdle-NB Newton with count-only null refits. The comparators checked are slower or equivalent: countreg zerotrunc (BFGS), fastglm alternating IRLS plus Brent θ (its vignette shows alternation can stall when θ drifts to a boundary), and pscl optim. No newer method was found.

truncated-series-summation.note: Still dead code (no caller). The earlier finding stands. New supporting source: the trigamma-free approach of Yu, Dousti Mousavi & Yang (arXiv 2306.04798, Statistical Papers 2024) computes the trigamma expectations in NB/ZINB Fisher information efficiently, with error bounds. It is an alternative to the per-y Hessian series.

findings.candidate: Pass se = !estimate_only, and optionally glmmTMBControl(conv_check='skip', eigval_check=FALSE), on estimate-only replicates. Keep parallel=1 inside an already-parallel replicate loop.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. The glmmTMB manual documents se as 'whether to return standard errors' with no timing.
findings.suggested_action: Re-reported from 2026-11-16, still unfixed at 8b718ae. Add se = !estimate_only at both weighted glmmTMB call sites and time one B=200 run before and after.

findings.candidate: Weighted direct C++ fits (catalog §10 TODO-3). fastglm 0.1.4 already ships weighted C++ fitters: fastglm_hurdle (logistic plus truncated Poisson/NB, IRLS with Brent θ) and fastglm_zi (SQUAREM-EM, IRLS M-steps). Use them as a reference and test oracle for adding weights to EDI's own fast_hurdle_negbin / fast_zinb / fast_zero_augmented_poisson kernels, or as an interim back-end.
findings.claimed_speedup: From the fastglm CRAN benchmarks vignette (package author's machine), at p=2: ZIP n=1000 median 2.47 ms, ZINB n=1e4 78.6 ms, hurdle-NB n=1e4 32.1 ms. There is no direct comparison with glmmTMB. In the R Journal glmmTMB paper (NB GLMM), mgcv took 0.03× and gamlss 0.24× of glmmTMB's time. The speedup over glmmTMB at EDI sizes is therefore not quantified.
findings.suggested_action: In catalog §10 TODO-3, record fastglm_hurdle/fastglm_zi (weights=) as the reference for weighted kernels. Prototype weights in EDI's C++ kernels and benchmark against glmmTMB per replicate at n=50–2000.

findings.candidate: A scalar tail-probability series with an adaptive cutoff and a rank-1 update per observation, or a trigamma-free evaluation of the trigamma expectations (Yu, Dousti Mousavi & Yang).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. The arXiv abstract says 'highly efficient and much more accurate than previous methods'. Analytically, each term drops from O(p²) plus allocations to O(1).
findings.suggested_action: Delete the dead expected_hessian, or rewrite it with a tail-series or trigamma-free method if it is ever needed.
